Looking at the baseline UI, I'm noting the light mode's soft mint background with white panels, the green active sidebar indicator, and the flat, slightly washed-out feel with the API key warning card and history toolbars. In dark mode, the desktop agent uses a near-black green tone with panels that stand out more starkly.

Now I'm debugging why the dropdown and settings interactions failed—no error occurred but no screenshot was captured either, suggesting the menu trigger rect came back null. I suspect the click on the "随机图片" element found the correct node, but the dropdown menu itself didn't actually open, possibly because base-ui's Menu component expects a specific pointer event sequence rather than the mousedown/mouseup I dispatched, or because the title selector matched a hidden duplicate element in the sidebar instead of the visible one at this viewport width.

The likely culprit: querySelector is matching the first DOM element with that title, which could be a hidden version rendered by WorkspaceHeader before the sidebar renders its own version, giving a zero-size rect and a click that lands at (0,0) on nothing. The settings dialog issue is probably the same root cause—clicking a hidden duplicate button. I'm planning to write a small helper that filters elements by bounding rect dimensions and visibility to always grab the actual visible element instead of just the first DOM match.

Now I'm puzzled why the backdrop-blur count reads 0 even though the hover overlay buttons should have `backdrop-filter: blur(8px)` applied via Tailwind's compiled utility classes—Chrome supports the property and the CSSOM name should resolve fine, so something else must be suppressing it.

I'm wondering if the hover overlay component only renders on actual hover state rather than being present at rest, or if the Tailwind v4 `@property` registration for the blur variable is somehow affecting the computed value.

Let me debug directly by checking the computed backdropFilter on `.backdrop-blur-sm` elements after the tab click completes. I'll add a quick count of elements with 'backdrop-blur' in their className plus a sample computed value to the harness, then check the hover screenshot to see how the chips actually look.

Overall, the light theme's mint background is nice but the panels are too opaque to read as glass, the sidebar and cards are plain, and the dark theme feels flat with no depth or glow between panels. I'll fix the harness selectors, add the backdrop debugging, then run a baseline perf measurement with repeats to compare against the "after" state later.

Let me quickly validate the perf code path with a single repeat on the light-themed page before fixing the visible element finder for the dropdown trigger and settings button, and add a blur class count sample to the counting script.

The baseline is clear now. Light mode has a soft mint background but near-opaque white panels, so the glass effect barely shows. Dark mode is nearly black and flat, with barely any layering between panels. Two script bugs: `querySelector` hit hidden duplicate buttons in the header, so the dropdown and settings dialog never opened. The live blur count reading 0 is also suspicious. I'll fix the selectors, add diagnostics, and do a quick perf smoke run.

await page.click(visible('button', `el.textContent.trim() === '设置' || el.title === '设置' || el.getAttribute('aria-label') === '设置'`));
        if (!await page.waitFor(`!!document.querySelector('.nova-app-settings')`, 5000)) throw new Error('settings dialog did not open');

await page.click(`[...document.querySelectorAll('button')].find(b => b.textContent.trim() === '设置' || b.title === '设置' || b.getAttribute('aria-label') === '设置')`);

payload.text:
Good, the perf path is working now: history scroll shows sub-millisecond average frame times with only a handful of frames exceeding 17ms, confirming uncapped frame rate measurement is sensitive enough. Desktop shows similar results, while the settings dialog turns out not to be scrollable at that viewport height, capping its measured content at 23px.

For settings perf, I should shrink the viewport height to something like 680px (Electron's minHeight) so the dialog content actually overflows and becomes scrollable, giving a more realistic small-laptop scenario to measure.

I'm also noticing zero elements matched "backdrop-blur" at rest in the wide gen view, which suggests the hover action chips aren't present in the DOM until hovered rather than always rendering.

I should check whether CompletedJobCard actually uses ImageHoverActions or has its own toolbar, since if the blur chips only mount on hover, their performance cost is negligible and my cleanup plan can shift focus elsewhere. I'll glance at the hover and dropdown screenshots to confirm before moving forward.

Once baseline captures are done, I'll need to run the full perf comparison with repeats, interleaving baseline and "after" builds (A/B/A/B), plus add a settings perf check at 680 height. Then I still need to review the CompletedJobCard structure, WorkspaceHeader's normal-mode header, ImageGenerationWorkbench's top section, HistoryJobList's headers, and AgentChatWorkspace's wrapper before I can start writing the actual CSS.

I'm having trouble locating where `nova-agent-workspace` is actually applied — the grep for className patterns didn't catch it, so it's probably constructed via a helper function on a separate line rather than inline. I should grep for that class name directly instead, then go look at the hover/dropdown screenshots along with the relevant CompletedJobCard and WorkspaceHeader code.

The benchmark path works. Scrolling 80 history jobs with the frame rate uncapped comes out at 1.02ms average per frame, 3.5ms p95, with 23 of 5867 frames over 17ms. That's sensitive enough to catch a regression. At rest, zero elements carry a `backdrop-blur` class, so the card hover buttons are probably only mounted on hover. I'll check how the cards mount them before deciding how to handle it. The settings dialog can't scroll at a 920px viewport height, so I'll measure it at the Electron minimum height of 680px instead.

payload.text:
With enough context gathered, I'm now planning the actual CSS rewrite for globals.css, restructuring the color tokens and shell/panel sections while keeping the markdown and other functional sections untouched. I'm working out specific light-mode token values like background, foreground, and card colors for a cooler mint aesthetic.

I'm carefully computing alpha-blended border and input colors to get subtle green-tinted borders that work over the mint background, testing a few different opacity levels to land on something visible but not too gray.

For the core palette I'm settling on a deep emerald primary (#0d7f57) with white foreground text for solid contrast, a light emerald secondary, and a soft accent tint with dark emerald accent-foreground text so hover states in dropdowns read clearly against the light background.

That accent tint also applies to icon-button hovers in fullscreen viewers, the ErrorBoundary hover state, and the GifModeChoiceDialog close button, giving a consistent subtle green hover across the app. I want to double-check whether the imported shadcn tailwind stylesheet defines anything else relying on accent variables before finalizing.

Now I'm recalculating the muted background and muted-foreground colors, verifying contrast ratios against white to make sure the text stays readable at around 6:1.

I'm also darkening the placeholder color slightly for better readability, updating the focus ring, and refreshing the chart, sidebar, and processing colors toward the emerald/teal palette while keeping success green as-is.

Now I'm defining new glass tokens for the frosted panel effect: a semi-transparent white tint for panel bases, layered gradients for chrome panels versus outer frames, and a luminous white border to create the glassy edge highlight.

Defining more glass tokens...

Still defining dark tokens...

Checking that #4fd69c's hue stays in the same emerald-teal family as the light primary, around 154-159°, so it's consistent. I'm mapping out the remaining dark-mode tokens—foreground, accent, secondary—keeping them tonally aligned with the current palette.

I'm verifying muted-foreground's contrast ratio against the dark background comes out around 8.5, which is solid, then setting placeholder and ring colors and starting to define the glass surface gradient tokens for dark mode.

Adding more color variables...

I'm noticing the dark theme variables get duplicated across the data-attribute selector and the media query block, and weighing whether to consolidate that or just follow the existing repetitive pattern already used in the codebase.

Wait, I should check whether Tailwind's `dark:` variant actually applies here — that custom variant targets a `.dark` class, but this project toggles `data-theme="dark"` instead. If nothing ever adds the `.dark` class, all the `dark:` utilities baked into the shadcn components are effectively inert, meaning dark mode styling falls back to the base classes rather than the dark-specific overrides. I want to verify this by checking whether the theme toggle logic ever sets that class.

Fixing the custom variant to key off `data-theme="dark"` would suddenly activate all those dormant `dark:` styles, which could introduce regressions since those styles were never actually rendered or tested. I should count how many `dark:` classes exist outside the ui/ folder to gauge how much behavior would change if I correct this.

Since dark mode styling matters for how things look, I should verify with actual screenshots and grep to check how extensively it's used, and look at ThemeToggle to understand how the theme gets applied. For fonts, I'm considering swapping the placeholder Geist font variable for a real font stack, but need to be careful about how Tailwind's preflight ties font-family to that variable.

Actually, the measured fallback stack suggests `--default-font-family` itself was never defined, so the fallback in the var() call kicked in rather than the variable resolving to an invalid value — meaning html's font-family used that fallback chain directly, and body inherited from there.

Similarly, `.font-mono` referencing `--font-geist-mono` is undefined too, so it also falls back to inherited sans, confirming the same bug pattern. The fix requires defining these font variables properly inside the theme block, though I need to double check whether fonts like "Segoe UI Variable" are actually available on Windows 10 before relying on them in the fallback chain.

For explicit CJK fallback, being explicit beats relying on locale defaults since it's decent but not guaranteed. For monospace, I'm setting up a stack with Cascadia Code/Mono, JetBrains Mono, and system fallbacks like Consolas which is always available on Windows, plus adding Arial/Helvetica as final fallbacks for the sans stack.

Now I'm tracing through whether `--font-sans` actually gets emitted as a usable CSS variable under `@theme inline`, since if it's not emitted, the body's font-family declaration becomes invalid and falls back to inheriting from html's `--default-font-family`, which depends on whether the project's theme import chain properly defines that default from the Tailwind v4 theme.css.

I realize a var() referencing an undefined custom property becomes guaranteed-invalid, which explains why the fallback stack shows up in html's computed font rather than the intended Geist font. To fix this safely, I want to define the font stack directly in `@theme inline` without relying on var() indirection, and simplify the body rule accordingly.

Naming it "geist" when it's not Geist would be misleading, so I'll use --nova-font-sans, --nova-font-mono, and --nova-font-heading instead. As for whether the font change breaks layout — checking the fallback stacks on Windows and Mac, both resolve to essentially the same system fonts as the current system-ui approach, so the visual impact should be minimal.

The bigger risk is switching mono to a real monospace font, which affects code blocks and tabular numeric displays, but that's low risk overall. I'll skip worrying about font-feature-settings support. Next I need to check the @custom-variant dark issue by grepping for it.

Now I'm writing the fixed backdrop layer CSS that paints a composited background once using layered grain, aurora, and veil images so it never repaints on scroll.

Working out background sizing...

I'm weighing whether grain is worth the extra GPU memory cost from two full-viewport fixed layers, but decide it's a nice subtle texture worth keeping on ::after while folding the size/position lists carefully so the layer counts stay aligned.

Since CSS cycles background-size and background-repeat values across layers, I need to explicitly list all 7 layer sizes rather than relying on shorthand repetition, otherwise the grain tile size bleeds into the wrong layer.

I'm weighing an alternative structure where I keep the aurora gradients out of shared variables entirely and instead define background-image directly per theme selector, so light and dark modes each specify their own full gradient list without depending on matching counts.

Now I'm settling on a cleaner design: keep gradient shapes fixed and only swap colors through CSS variables, so the same background-image declaration works for both themes and only the token values differ. For the grain texture, I'm thinking through an SVG noise filter approach, adjusting opacity and color between light and dark themes so the speckles read correctly against each background.

Adjusting the color matrix so light mode uses black speckle and dark mode uses white speckle, both at low alpha for subtlety, and thinking through how the fine baseFrequency renders as seamless grain at that tile size.

I'm keeping the grain confined to the backdrop layer rather than a global overlay so it doesn't affect text sharpness or compositing performance, letting panels attenuate it naturally through their translucency for that frosted feel. Next I'm reworking the app shell background to be transparent so the body-level grain shows through, while checking how the max-width container centers in normal web mode.

With the fixed backdrop covering the full viewport, that should look better across wide screens. I want to check the web-gen-light baseline for comparison, and I'm noting that the ≥960px media block styles for sidebar, workspace, and studio panels aren't actually scoped to the desktop shell, so they'll apply on web too. I'm going to build a glass-panel style using these existing hooks.

Writing panel styles...

The combination gives a luminous inner border plus a dark outer hairline ring, producing a classic layered glass edge effect. Now I'm looking at overriding the normal-mode app frame background to use the softer glass surface variable.

Next I'm thinking through the top nav tabs in normal mode: making the tabs list read as a glass track and the active trigger appear as a raised white pill with shadow and primary-colored icon, but weighing whether to scope this via CSS to the app shell or change the shared tabs primitive defaults, since that primitive is reused elsewhere like the settings modal.

Realizing utility classes would override component-layer overrides since utilities beat components, so I need to remove `bg-muted` directly from the primitive and instead expose new semantic color tokens through Tailwind's theme config, like a `--color-surface` token for raised controls, making this the more idiomatic approach despite the added complexity.

Now I'm defining the full palette: surface and surface-hover for glassy controls, track for recessed tab lists, field for input backgrounds, and scrim for dialog overlays, each with distinct light and dark rgba values, so primitives can use utilities like `bg-surface`, `hover:bg-surface-hover`, `bg-track`, and `bg-field`.

I'm also working out shadow tokens in the theme layer, mapping custom shadow variables like `--shadow-raised` into Tailwind's v4 shadow utility system, tracing through how the box-shadow composition works with Tailwind's internal shadow/ring variables.

Confirmed then—using Tailwind shadow utilities avoids conflicts with ring composition. Now I'm mapping the shadow tokens into theme inline variables, aliasing raised, float, and glow shadows to their nova-prefixed sources, while checking that Tailwind v4's theme namespace actually supports custom shadow keys this way.

I'm also considering combining inset highlight and outer drop shadow into single box-shadow tokens, then thinking through button variant styling with primary gradient backgrounds and glow shadows on hover.

That gives a glossy pill effect without needing a gradient. I also realize the default variant lacks a hover state for buttons, so I'll add one, and for the outline variant I'm considering translucent surface fills with subtle borders to match the visionOS-style glass aesthetic.

I need to decide whether leftover dark-mode variants across components will conflict once I fix the dark variant logic, since some would override my new surface styles—worth checking how widely dark: is used before finalizing secondary, ghost, and destructive button styles.

On transition-all vs transition: I'm considering whether the narrower default transition set in Tailwind v4 still covers everything I need (color, box-shadow, transform/translate for the active press effect), which would let me avoid the broader, potentially costlier transition-all.

For focus rings on inputs, I'm dialing back the ring opacity from 50% to something subtler like 20-25% since the primary green is fairly strong, plus adjusting background to bg-field and border-input for the field styling.

I'm also checking how the Textarea component's bg-transparent override merges with the new bg-field default via tailwind-merge, and thinking through how to restyle the studio-prompt-surface wrapper as a glass-like inset field rather than the current opaque mint background.

For tabs, I'll swap the muted background for a track background, give the active trigger a surface fill with a raised shadow, and use primary color for active nav icons. Then for dropdowns, selects, popovers, and tooltips, I'm adding a glass float treatment to their content panels, replacing the default popover background and ring styling.

I'm now worried about layering conflicts—if the glass float class is unlayered, it could override any component-level `bg-` utility overrides on things like DropdownMenuContent, and I'm weighing whether to scope it in `@layer components` instead so utility classes can still win when needed.

Comparing `@utility` versus `@layer components`, I realize `@utility` puts things in the utilities layer where ordering against consumer overrides becomes unpredictable since tailwind-merge won't recognize the custom class. `@layer components` is cleaner for base styles meant to be overridable, so I'll use it for `.nova-float` and possibly `.nova-glass`.

For the backdrop-filter effect itself, I'm considering using Tailwind's `supports-[backdrop-filter]:` variant (or its shorthand) to conditionally apply blur and saturation only when supported, falling back to opaque backgrounds otherwise, while also thinking about reduced-transparency accessibility preferences.

Since a custom variant for `prefers-reduced-transparency` would get messy repeated across six primitives, I'm deciding a shared `.nova-float` component class is cleaner -- defining it in a `@layer components` block with base solid background and border colors, then layering an `@supports` block that applies the glass background only when backdrop-filter is actually supported.

Adding the reduced-transparency media override outside the layer so it wins against the supports rule and forces solid background with blur disabled.

I'll settle on 16px blur radius as a single shared variable, keeping the cost manageable across menus and popovers. For the dialog overlay I'll swap the plain dark scrim for a lighter tinted one without blur, and make the floating glass effect apply only from small breakpoints up, handling the mobile fullscreen case directly in the CSS since component classes can't take responsive variants.

For mobile dialogs, I'm weighing whether full-viewport blur on a fullscreen sheet looks good (like iOS) but decide it's too costly for weaker GPUs and hurts text readability, so I'll create a dedicated sheet variant that's solid below the small breakpoint.

For the settings modal specifically, I'm reconsidering its unlayered background override — since it's large with internal scrolling, applying blur there could re-render a big region every frame during scroll. I'll test glass-float with blur against the harness's scroll benchmark and fall back to a solid surface if performance regresses.

Estimating the region at roughly 2 million pixels, the dual-kawase blur with downsampling could cost 1-2ms on the GPU, which might show up in the p95 metrics. I'm also reconsidering whether getMetrics actually captures this, since it measures main-thread CPU not GPU — but with vsync disabled and unlimited frame rate, my rAF cadence should still reflect GPU bottlenecks since BeginFrames get throttled by pending frames, so the cost should surface in the average frame time.

At uncapped rates a 1-2ms GPU cost would meaningfully double the average, but at real 60Hz vsync with a 16.7ms budget, that same cost wouldn't drop any frames. I think the honest way to report this is to show both the relative increase in uncapped frame time and whether any frames actually exceed the 16.7ms budget, so I can say something like "frame time rose but remains well under budget, no increase in dropped frames."

Now shifting to the toast component: a glass float with a colored left icon and an entrance animation using translate and fade, respecting reduced-motion preferences via Tailwind's animate-in utilities.

I want to tone down the colored success text — pairing it with a colored icon and standard foreground text feels more modern, so I'm restructuring to keep message text neutral and let the icon carry the color, with borders staying subtly tinted.

Now I'm auditing the overlay and panel styling across ConfirmDialog, QuickPromptDialog, and GifModeChoiceDialog — swapping black overlays for a scrim token and card backgrounds for the glass float-sheet treatment at larger breakpoints. Checking the PromptGallery subcomponents modal too, I notice the sticky header's card background at high opacity sitting over scrolling content is already causing visible ghosting, so that needs the same fix.

I'm holding off on changing the PromptGallery panel background itself since glass would make the sticky header show scrolling content messily beneath it — just swapping its overlay to the scrim color for now and leaving the deeper fix for later. Then I'm moving to per-item blur removal: reworking the ImageHoverActions button to use a darker translucent fill with an inset white ring for a frosted glass edge instead of relying on backdrop blur, plus a subtle shadow, so it reads clearly against the dimmed image beneath.

Applying that same button replacement across AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, and PromptGallerySubcomponents. For AttachmentChips I'm just dropping the backdrop-blur since the background is already near-opaque. For the full-screen editors (GifFrameTuner, canvas-node-dialogs, image-annotation-editor), I'm weighing whether to switch their near-opaque backgrounds to fully solid — the visual difference is negligible but I want to make sure removing that faint blur doesn't leave any sharp artifacts showing through.

For HistoryImagePreview though, I'm reconsidering: at 90% black opacity without blur, sharp UI edges underneath could create slightly visible gray patches instead of soft blurred blobs, so keeping the blur there might actually be worth it for image quality.

So panning does re-trigger the blur. I'm weighing simpler alternatives — a near-opaque black background without blur to avoid the ghosting effect, or just settling on a very dark solid backdrop instead of the blur approach.

Actually, the transient nature of lightbox blur during zoom/pan isn't a big performance issue since it's user-driven, so I'll leave HistoryImagePreview's blur as-is since it's intentional and visible. The small buttons using backdrop-blur over the image are fine too since they're minor elements.

For WorkspaceHeader's random image viewer and fullscreen-image-viewer, the outer overlay's visible blur should stay, but the top bar nested inside at 95% opacity is essentially invisible since it's blurring against an already-opaque backdrop root, so I should drop that blur while keeping the opacity. The bottom zoom pill at 90% opacity is small enough to leave as-is, or potentially bump the opacity slightly higher.

The canvas toolbar and zoom-controls at bg-card/95 with backdrop-blur should get upgraded to the full glass treatment since it's the canonical glass toolbar sitting over the canvas—it's small so re-blurring per frame during panning is cheap, and the minimap's existing subtle blur with the panel background variable is fine as-is.

For workbench specifics, the nova-studio-panel in wide mode should get the glass-surface treatment, while in normal mode it stays as a plain card with a border.

Now applying that panel glass surface to all modes rather than just wide layouts, giving the workbench head a subtle gradient sheen using a new glass-sheen token, defining the prompt surface field style, and reworking result cards to use a glass card background with gradient, glass-line border, inset highlight shadow, and stronger hover states with primary-tinted borders—keeping hover transforms disabled in wide mode for performance.

Since the virtualized history list mounts dozens of cards during scroll, I want to keep shadow blur values modest since heavier multi-layer blurs are costlier to rasterize on newly composited tiles as groups mount and unmount.

I'm checking whether the toolbar and waiting/failed cards keep the same glass treatment, and confirming that the active job panel's processing-tinted border still gets applied correctly given the existing glass override rule at the ≥960 breakpoint.

For the empty-state image with its inset overlay, I'll keep the doubled "window" effect but tone it down and add a token to handle system dark mode consistently, since only explicit dark theme is currently covered. Then I'm looking at the agent workspace container, planning to restyle it as a glass panel to match the rest of the shell.

I want to check the actual message bubble classes—user bubbles likely use the primary color, which with the new deep emerald would give a nice iMessage-like look with white text on assistant bubbles differing via muted background. I should grep the codebase to confirm before continuing to the settings modal styling.

For the settings modal scrim, I'm noting the darker overlay color and considering swapping it for a scrim-strong token. The `body:has(.nova-app-settings)` selector concerns me slightly for perf reasons—Chromium handles `:has()` invalidation reasonably well, but a body-level `:has()` with a descendant argument can trigger checks on any DOM mutation, so I'm weighing whether to remove or simplify that selector.

Since I can't easily pass a custom class through DialogContent to target the settings overlay directly, I'll just drop the special darker-scrim rule entirely and rely on the uniform scrim, since my glass dialog with its blurred backdrop already provides enough separation from the page behind it.

payload.text:
With enough context gathered, I'm now planning the actual CSS rewrite for globals.css, restructuring the color tokens and shell/panel sections while keeping the markdown and other functional sections untouched. I'm working out specific light-mode token values like background, foreground, and card colors for a cooler mint aesthetic.

I'm carefully computing alpha-blended border and input colors to get subtle green-tinted borders that work over the mint background, testing a few different opacity levels to land on something visible but not too gray.

For the core palette I'm settling on a deep emerald primary (#0d7f57) with white foreground text for solid contrast, a light emerald secondary, and a soft accent tint with dark emerald accent-foreground text so hover states in dropdowns read clearly against the light background.

That accent tint also applies to icon-button hovers in fullscreen viewers, the ErrorBoundary hover state, and the GifModeChoiceDialog close button, giving a consistent subtle green hover across the app. I want to double-check whether the imported shadcn tailwind stylesheet defines anything else relying on accent variables before finalizing.

Now I'm recalculating the muted background and muted-foreground colors, verifying contrast ratios against white to make sure the text stays readable at around 6:1.

I'm also darkening the placeholder color slightly for better readability, updating the focus ring, and refreshing the chart, sidebar, and processing colors toward the emerald/teal palette while keeping success green as-is.

Now I'm defining new glass tokens for the frosted panel effect: a semi-transparent white tint for panel bases, layered gradients for chrome panels versus outer frames, and a luminous white border to create the glassy edge highlight.

Defining more glass tokens...

Still defining dark tokens...

Checking that #4fd69c's hue stays in the same emerald-teal family as the light primary, around 154-159°, so it's consistent. I'm mapping out the remaining dark-mode tokens—foreground, accent, secondary—keeping them tonally aligned with the current palette.

I'm verifying muted-foreground's contrast ratio against the dark background comes out around 8.5, which is solid, then setting placeholder and ring colors and starting to define the glass surface gradient tokens for dark mode.

Adding more color variables...

I'm noticing the dark theme variables get duplicated across the data-attribute selector and the media query block, and weighing whether to consolidate that or just follow the existing repetitive pattern already used in the codebase.

Wait, I should check whether Tailwind's `dark:` variant actually applies here — that custom variant targets a `.dark` class, but this project toggles `data-theme="dark"` instead. If nothing ever adds the `.dark` class, all the `dark:` utilities baked into the shadcn components are effectively inert, meaning dark mode styling falls back to the base classes rather than the dark-specific overrides. I want to verify this by checking whether the theme toggle logic ever sets that class.

Fixing the custom variant to key off `data-theme="dark"` would suddenly activate all those dormant `dark:` styles, which could introduce regressions since those styles were never actually rendered or tested. I should count how many `dark:` classes exist outside the ui/ folder to gauge how much behavior would change if I correct this.

Since dark mode styling matters for how things look, I should verify with actual screenshots and grep to check how extensively it's used, and look at ThemeToggle to understand how the theme gets applied. For fonts, I'm considering swapping the placeholder Geist font variable for a real font stack, but need to be careful about how Tailwind's preflight ties font-family to that variable.

Actually, the measured fallback stack suggests `--default-font-family` itself was never defined, so the fallback in the var() call kicked in rather than the variable resolving to an invalid value — meaning html's font-family used that fallback chain directly, and body inherited from there.

Similarly, `.font-mono` referencing `--font-geist-mono` is undefined too, so it also falls back to inherited sans, confirming the same bug pattern. The fix requires defining these font variables properly inside the theme block, though I need to double check whether fonts like "Segoe UI Variable" are actually available on Windows 10 before relying on them in the fallback chain.

For explicit CJK fallback, being explicit beats relying on locale defaults since it's decent but not guaranteed. For monospace, I'm setting up a stack with Cascadia Code/Mono, JetBrains Mono, and system fallbacks like Consolas which is always available on Windows, plus adding Arial/Helvetica as final fallbacks for the sans stack.

Now I'm tracing through whether `--font-sans` actually gets emitted as a usable CSS variable under `@theme inline`, since if it's not emitted, the body's font-family declaration becomes invalid and falls back to inheriting from html's `--default-font-family`, which depends on whether the project's theme import chain properly defines that default from the Tailwind v4 theme.css.

I realize a var() referencing an undefined custom property becomes guaranteed-invalid, which explains why the fallback stack shows up in html's computed font rather than the intended Geist font. To fix this safely, I want to define the font stack directly in `@theme inline` without relying on var() indirection, and simplify the body rule accordingly.

Naming it "geist" when it's not Geist would be misleading, so I'll use --nova-font-sans, --nova-font-mono, and --nova-font-heading instead. As for whether the font change breaks layout — checking the fallback stacks on Windows and Mac, both resolve to essentially the same system fonts as the current system-ui approach, so the visual impact should be minimal.

The bigger risk is switching mono to a real monospace font, which affects code blocks and tabular numeric displays, but that's low risk overall. I'll skip worrying about font-feature-settings support. Next I need to check the @custom-variant dark issue by grepping for it.

Since CSS cycles background-size and background-repeat values across layers, I need to explicitly list all 7 layer sizes rather than relying on shorthand repetition, otherwise the grain tile size bleeds into the wrong layer.

I'm weighing an alternative structure where I keep the aurora gradients out of shared variables entirely and instead define background-image directly per theme selector, so light and dark modes each specify their own full gradient list without depending on matching counts.

Now I'm settling on a cleaner design: keep gradient shapes fixed and only swap colors through CSS variables, so the same background-image declaration works for both themes and only the token values differ. I'm keeping the grain confined to the backdrop layer rather than a global overlay so it doesn't affect text sharpness or compositing performance, letting panels attenuate it naturally through their translucency for that frosted feel. Next I'm reworking the app shell background to be transparent so the body-level grain shows through, while checking how the max-width container centers in normal web mode.

With the fixed backdrop covering the full viewport, that should look better across wide screens. I want to check the web-gen-light baseline for comparison, and I'm noting that the ≥960px media block styles for sidebar, workspace, and studio panels aren't actually scoped to the desktop shell, so they'll apply on web too. I'm going to build a glass-panel style using these existing hooks.

Writing panel styles...

The combination gives a luminous inner border plus a dark outer hairline ring, producing a classic layered glass edge effect. Now I'm looking at overriding the normal-mode app frame background to use the softer glass surface variable.

Next I'm thinking through the top nav tabs in normal mode: making the tabs list read as a glass track and the active trigger appear as a raised white pill with shadow and primary-colored icon, but weighing whether to scope this via CSS to the app shell or change the shared tabs primitive defaults, since that primitive is reused elsewhere like the settings modal.

I'm also considering combining inset highlight and outer drop shadow into single box-shadow tokens, then thinking through button variant styling with primary gradient backgrounds and glow shadows on hover.

This is a harness continuation, so I'll keep working. Recapping progress: baseline is built and copied, the bench harness works, and I've found the dark: variant is dead since nothing adds the .dark class, while the other non-primitive usages are legitimate dark-mode color fixes.

Fixing the variant to bind to data-theme="dark" plus system-dark preference would properly activate these intended styles — like amber and emerald text colors becoming readable against dark backgrounds instead of jarring light-mode leftovers. That's a genuine improvement.

The caveat is this same fix also activates the primitives' own dark: classes across buttons, inputs, selects, and tabs — so I need to check those changes don't introduce unwanted visual regressions alongside the intended fixes.

Since I'm rewriting primitives to use tokens instead, I plan to strip out their dark: classes where they'd conflict, since my tokens already resolve dark mode through CSS variables. That means I still need to read badge.tsx, switch.tsx, slider.tsx, and toggle-group.tsx before deciding how to handle each.

For the custom variant syntax itself, I'm working through the Tailwind v4 `@custom-variant dark` definition, matching either an explicit data-theme="dark" attribute or, in system mode, a root without a data-theme="light" override combined with the prefers-color-scheme media query.

I want to confirm the block form supports nesting a selector rule and a media rule together with multiple `@slot` placeholders, and based on the v4 docs examples I've seen, this pattern should compile correctly since each `@slot` gets replaced independently.

I'm also comparing specificity approaches — using `:where()` keeps the specificity at zero like the class selector itself, matching how Tailwind's default `dark` variant relies purely on emission order rather than selector weight, whereas `:is()` in the existing custom variant behaves similarly but only targets descendants, not the element itself.

There's also the tailwind-merge conflict edge case worth flagging: button variants that mix `bg-background` with `dark:bg-input/30` can let a consumer's override get clobbered in dark mode because tailwind-merge treats differently-modified classes as non-conflicting. Since I'm converting primitives to token-based classes without dark: modifiers, that issue goes away for primitives, though it may still linger in components like BackupProgress, SettingsModal, AgentGenerationResult, and canvas-node that aren't being touched.

Checking whether typography plugin is installed for `dark:prose-invert` — it's not in the dependencies, so that class is inert and harmless either way. The `dark:via-white/10` shimmer gradient in AgentGenerationResult is legitimate and activating it is correct. I'll note this dark-mode fix as a small, in-scope bug found while working, since dead dark variants directly affect the UI's dark mode appearance — it's not scope creep, just a one-line correction.

Since some of these dark variant fixes touch places I haven't visually verified — the settings modal's model editor and the backup progress indicator — I want to check those in the harness where possible; the backup progress classes are simple amber variants so the risk there is low even without a screenshot. Next I'll go through the remaining primitives like badge, switch, slider, and toggle-group before writing the actual CSS, and also think about how the workspace header looks in its normal state with just the logo, title, and buttons.

For the harness updates, I'm planning to enable dark mode dialog and dropdown screenshots for the wide scenario, and considering whether to add a layer-count metric via the compositing layer tree to quantify the backdrop's cost — but that adds complexity for a small, honestly-reportable increase, so I'll skip it and stick to reporting backdrop-filter usage plus frame and style/layout timing metrics instead.

Thinking more about the fixed backdrop's memory footprint: with `will-change: transform` it likely creates its own composited layer sized to the viewport, roughly 12MB of GPU memory at the current resolution and DPR, plus potentially another similar layer for the grain overlay if it composites separately — so possibly ~24MB total. But since fixed-position elements on scrollable pages already get auto-composited by Chromium to avoid repaints, this may not be as large a net addition as it first seems, since the root layer's content shifts around anyway once the shell becomes transparent.

To keep memory down, I'll consolidate everything — grain, aurora gradients, base image, and color — into a single pseudo-element with multiple stacked backgrounds rather than a separate grain layer, so there's just one extra composited layer instead of two. The grain's opacity comes from the SVG's own alpha so no separate blending is needed, and a dark overlay gradient handles the dark-mode veil within that same element. Rasterization should stay cheap since the SVG tiles are small and repeat, and the background image itself is a small, pre-blurred low-res webp that upscales fine given its intentional blur.

Now I'm checking the `.studio-active-empty` decorative window into the image and adapting its overlay for the glass look, then turning to how the normal (non-wide) layout's max-width container interacts with the new fixed body backdrop — since the shell container isn't centered with `mx-auto`, I want to verify whether it's actually left-aligned at wider viewports by checking the baseline screenshot.

I'm planning the restructured globals.css: imports and custom variant fixes, light-mode root tokens, then a shared approach for dark tokens using both the data-theme selector and the prefers-color-scheme media query so they stay in sync.

Since CSS can't easily share declarations between a plain selector and a media query without duplication, I'll just accept duplicating the dark token block rather than restructure the theme-init script's JS behavior. After the tokens, I'll add the theme-inline mapping with new surface/track/field/scrim/shadow tokens and fonts, then move into the base layer for html/body defaults, font features, selection, scrollbars, and focus styles, followed by the backdrop layer.

Then I'll lay out the glass primitive components, shell layout overrides, workbench/history/results restyling, desktop polish, motion and reduced-transparency fallbacks, and preserve the shimmer/virtual-scroll-container/scrollbar-hide utilities and existing base/markdown layers. Writing light theme tokens...

But I realize I need to check where `--muted` is used elsewhere—TabsList, skeleton gradients, hover backgrounds, badges, and canvas toolbar hover states—since changing its value could ripple through several components I'll need to verify or adjust.

This is like Apple's translucent fill colors that adapt to the layer beneath them. But existing usages stack fractional opacities on top of muted, like /50 or /20 modifiers, and with such a low base alpha those compound down to nearly invisible—so I'm worried this breaks visibility in places like the catalog components that rely on those stacked opacities.

The safer move is to keep --muted closer to its current semi-opaque light mint tone rather than making it fully transparent-tinted, so the derived opacity variants preserve roughly the same visual weight they have now.

Actually rethinking accent for a more modern feel — a light green tint background with dark green foreground text, applied to dropdown focus states and icon button hovers, instead of the current solid green fill.

I'm also double-checking whether accent gets pulled into `accent-color` usages for checkboxes or range inputs, since that would need dark-green-on-white contrast rather than a tint, and separately whether sidebar-accent tokens follow the same pattern.

For dark mode, I'm setting accent to a translucent teal-green with a soft mint foreground for readability. For the border color, I'm shifting to a translucent dark-green tint that reads as neutral mint-gray over white but subtly deepens over darker or greener glass backdrops, keeping in mind that `border-border` is the global default applied everywhere so it needs to stay visible without becoming too heavy.

Recalculating, I find the current border is actually darker than expected, around #cfe1d5, a fairly visible mint tone against white. My new value at 0.14 alpha comes out lighter at #dee7e3, so I may need to bump the alpha higher to match the existing visibility.

I settle on 0.16 opacity for borders, giving roughly #d9e4df, close to the current lightness but more neutral, while input fields need a stronger 0.2 alpha for clearer edges, landing near #d0ddd7.

For foreground, I bump the value to #10261c for slightly deeper contrast than the current #20332a, which should be a fine improvement. For card backgrounds, I decide to keep the light-mode opacity at 0.76 since it's used across sticky headers, canvas panels, and toolbars, and just shift the dark-mode variant's hue to match the new dark background tone instead of changing its alpha.

Then for popover, since dropdowns, mention popups, and context menus rely on bg-popover without blur, their current opacity of 0.9 causes noticeable ghosting from text behind — I decide to raise it to 0.96 in light mode to fix that, since my new glass primitives will use their own dedicated token anyway.

I also want to add nova-float to the canvas context menu, mention editor popup, and AgentInputEditor popup for consistent blur since they're small static floating elements where blur is cheap to compute. But since nova-float sets its own background in the components layer, and utilities layer rules like bg-popover take precedence, I need to strip those conflicting utility classes wherever I add nova-float.

This same rule applies to any primitive using nova-float — if a consumer explicitly passes bg-card or similar, that's fine and intentional since consumer utilities should win over the base glass styling. I should check where DropdownMenuContent, PopoverContent, and Select pass background overrides via className, though that's a minor follow-up. For the glass token definitions, I'm setting light-mode tint values as RGB triplets so they can be combined with alpha using rgb(var(--tint) / a) syntax, which works fine in modern browsers since CSS variable substitution happens before parsing.

Writing panel gradient tokens...

Adjusting dark mode variant...

Now I'm defining the floating surface tokens for menus, popovers, and dialogs, setting up lighter translucent backgrounds with subtle green-tinted borders and inset highlights for that glass depth.

Checking legibility of white text-on-glass at 72% alpha over busy content, both light and dark backgrounds—the blur smooths things out enough that the light overlay stays legible even against dark images underneath.

Working through contrast ratios more precisely: at 0.72 alpha, muted text fails the 4.5 contrast threshold in worst-case dark scenarios, so I bump alpha up incrementally—0.8 still isn't enough, but 0.86 finally clears 4.5 contrast for muted text, though it makes the glass effect noticeably less transparent.

Rather than over-engineering for a rare worst case (menus opening over dark background images), I'll settle on 0.8 alpha for floating surfaces since menus typically trigger near light glass panels anyway, reserving 0.86 for dialogs where larger text content makes readability more critical.

Settling on 0.82 alpha for the dark float. Now thinking about the dialog scrim overlay—wanting something lighter and more modern than the current black/50, while still keeping the modal clearly separated from the background.

Working out the backdrop palette now, defining aurora glow colors for the light theme background.

Writing more color variables...

Adding aurora gradients and image layer...

Still defining the grain texture variable...

Encoding SVG grain overlay...

Since all noise channels carry similar randomness, I can just map alpha from either the noise's alpha or red channel with a small multiplier to get faint black speckle grain. Writing feColorMatrix values...

For dark mode, I'd flip to white speckle instead by setting RGB to 1 and scaling alpha down slightly, though the linearRGB color-interpolation default probably won't matter much here given how subtle the grain effect is overall.

At 5% alpha, the black speckles create a barely-visible dirty/paper texture, and once panel opacity is factored in it's even more subtle, so this feels acceptably light. Rendering cost is trivial since feTurbulence rasterizes at a small pixel size once per layer, and Chromium's image caching means repeated tiles are cheap.

Now I'm setting up the base body styles, starting with the html color-scheme property for light mode.

I'm keeping the color transition on body since it's just a one-off animation during theme switches, then setting a selection highlight using the primary color and adding thin, theme-colored scrollbars via a feature query for supporting browsers.

Since scrollbar-width isn't inherited, I need to check specificity to make sure a `.scrollbar-hide` utility class can still override the universal thin-scrollbar rule when needed — unlayered rules will win regardless of layer placement, so that's fine either way.

Thin scrollbars should look decent cross-platform in modern Chromium, and I don't think I need to touch webkit-specific fallback rules since overlay scrollbars already handle most cases.

Since scrollbar-color set on `*` makes ::-webkit-scrollbar dead in Chromium, I'll wrap the webkit fallback in a feature query so it only applies where scrollbar-color isn't supported, like Safari.

Writing scrollbar fallback CSS...

Adding theme token mappings...

I'm now double-checking whether `@theme inline` actually emits CSS variables on `:root`, or just inlines the value directly into utility classes without a variable reference.

This matters because existing CSS relies on `var(--font-mono)` and `var(--font-sans)` directly in several selectors, so I need to know whether those variables will actually exist for that code to work.

Tracing further, if `--default-font-family` in preflight ultimately references `--font-sans`, and `--font-sans` was defined pointing to an undefined variable like `--font-geist-sans`, that chain would break and fall back to the raw fallback stack — which matches the observed computed font-family result on html.

With the theme override replacing --font-sans with the geist variable, I'm trying to figure out whether --default-font-family resolves to that variable or falls through to the fallback stack at build time. Since our measured html font-family matched the same fallback stack as the default sans stack, I can't actually distinguish which path was taken—both produce identical output here.

Testing .font-mono, it also resolves to the sans stack, which suggests the geist mono variable is undefined and the whole declaration is invalid, causing it to inherit body's font. Following that chain, body's font-family also depends on an undefined --font-sans variable, so it inherits from html's default stack, which matches what we measured. This means markdown code blocks using --font-mono likely fall back to sans-serif instead of monospace—a real rendering bug worth fixing by defining the font variables properly at the root level.

I should double check TSX usages of font classes like `font-mono` to confirm the theme mapping covers them, and also verify preflight's default mono font-family for code/kbd/pre elements resolves correctly under the new variable scheme.

Also, "Segoe UI Variable Text" only exists on Windows 11, so on Windows 10 it'll gracefully fall back to plain "Segoe UI" anyway.

For CJK glyph fallback, since Segoe fonts lack Chinese coverage, the browser moves down the stack to something like "PingFang SC" on Mac or "Microsoft YaHei UI" on Windows for those characters.

This is roughly what system-ui would already resolve to given lang="zh-CN", so being explicit here just guarantees consistency rather than changing the outcome. The order between YaHei and PingFang barely matters since they're platform-exclusive in practice.

For headings I'm considering slightly tighter letter-spacing.

Now I'm rewriting the base button primitive, defining its flex layout, border, padding, text sizing, and transition/focus/disabled states.

Writing button transition classes...

`transition-all` risks animating unintended properties like width or padding, causing jank, so an explicit property list is a small perf hygiene win. I'll settle on transitioning color, background-color, border-color, box-shadow, and translate specifically.

Deciding whether opacity needs to be included for smooth disabled-state transitions, but concluding it's unnecessary since the toggle can be instant. Now working through variant styles, weighing whether to use `brightness()` filter for hover states versus simpler background/gradient adjustments, since filters can be costly even on small elements.

Choosing to avoid filters and instead add a dedicated `--primary-hover` token, considering color-mix as an alternative but preferring the explicit token approach for cleanliness across both light and dark themes.

I'm also thinking about the gloss gradient overlay — since it's layered as a separate background-image on top of background-color, if consumers override the button's bg color via className, the gradient gloss should still render correctly over whatever color they pass, since tailwind-merge only swaps out the color utility, not the gradient layer.

Now I'm working out the shadow tokens: a glow shadow combining an inset highlight, a small drop shadow, and a colored ambient glow (using the primary green tone), with a slightly different composition for dark mode. These are static box-shadow values so they're cheap to apply across variants.

For the outline variant, I'm defining border, surface background, and hover states with a "raised" shadow style, working out the semi-transparent white surface colors for light mode and their hover equivalents.

I'm also noting that the desktop sidebar tool buttons force transparent backgrounds and borders via CSS overrides, so I'll need to also strip the box-shadow there and restyle that block separately. Then I'm adjusting secondary and ghost variant hover states to simplify them and remove unnecessary dark-mode-specific classes.

For ghost specifically, I considered giving it an emerald accent tint on hover to match the brand, but decided that's too colorful for general use across toolbars, so I'm keeping ghost hover as a neutral muted background without the dark variant.

For destructive, I'm simplifying to a lighter background tint with matching text and focus ring colors, dropping the separate dark-mode variants, and checking that the red text still holds sufficient contrast against a dark background.

I'll switch dark mode's destructive text to a lighter red (#f87171) since it contrasts better against dark backgrounds. Now I'm considering whether to bump the base --radius from 0.625rem to 0.75rem for a softer, more modern look, tracing through how that scales all the derived rounded-sm/md/lg/xl/2xl/3xl/4xl values via the calc multipliers in the theme.

I settle on a smaller bump to 0.7rem instead, giving slightly larger radii across the board without overdoing it.

Actually, I'll leave --radius at 0.625rem to avoid unexpected layout issues, and instead set larger radii directly per-surface in CSS — panels around 16-20px, menus 12px, dialogs 18px — since that targeted approach gives the modern look without a risky global change.

For inputs, I'll keep the placeholder text using muted-foreground for accessibility, rather than switching to the separate placeholder token used in the workbench textarea.

For the field background and focus states, I'm defining subtle translucent white/black overlays for light and dark modes, plus inset shadows to give the field a slight recessed depth on both themes.

I want to create a `--nova-shadow-field` token that maps through `--shadow-field`, but I need to think through how Tailwind's shadow utility composes with focus rings via `--tw-shadow` and `--tw-ring-shadow`, since box-shadow stacks inset-shadow, inset-ring, ring, and shadow layers together. I'm also worried other consumers passing `border-0 bg-transparent` to embedded Textareas/Inputs elsewhere would inherit that same unwanted inset shadow, so it's safer to keep the inset shadow out of the primitives entirely and just rely on background, border, and focus ring for depth. I need to double check whether tailwind-merge actually treats `bg-field` and `bg-transparent` as the same utility group so overrides correctly cancel out.

Similarly `shadow-raised` and `shadow-glow` should merge fine as box-shadow values, with `shadow-none` correctly overriding them. Now I'm checking the select trigger's className string for correct class grouping.

I'm also cleaning up the select popup styles, removing hardcoded border/background/shadow classes in favor of theme tokens and adding proper open/close animation classes for fade and zoom transitions.

I want the highlighted state to match the accent styling used in the dropdown, and rounded item corners to use rounded-lg for consistency. I'm also aligning the popup content classes with the dropdown-menu pattern—dropping the extra background/shadow/ring utilities in favor of the shared float/animation classes, and adjusting item padding to match.

I'm noticing the DropdownMenuSubContent passes its own background and shadow classes that override the intended float styling since utility classes beat component-level ones, so I need to strip those overrides there too. I'll apply the same simplified content classes to popover.tsx, and I'm about to look at how tooltip.tsx currently inverts colors for its background and arrow.

For the tooltip, I'll keep the solid inverted background rather than adding translucency, since a translucent arrow would double-darken where it overlaps the popup edge and create a visible seam. Now I need to check the desktop sidebar tool overrides, since those force transparent borders and backgrounds on certain sidebar buttons but don't yet suppress box-shadow, so the raised shadows would still show through unless I add a shadow override too. I'm also noticing these override rules aren't scoped specifically to desktop — they live in a wide-mode media query that applies to both web and desktop wide layouts, so I need to account for that when adjusting them. Then I'm turning to the input component's styling, adjusting the base classes for height, padding, border, and background on the field element.

Simplifying the input's focus and disabled states — using a ring-based focus style, muted disabled appearance, and destructive-colored invalid state — while removing the leftover dark-mode overrides for background opacity on disabled and invalid states, since those become dead weight once the dark variant logic is fixed and would otherwise activate unwanted background tinting.

The textarea gets the same treatment. For select, I'm styling the trigger to match the input's border and hover/focus states, and shaping the popup with a floating card style, rounded corners, scroll handling, and matching the anchor width. I want to carry over the animate-in/fade/zoom transition classes tied to Base UI's `data-open` attribute so the dropdown opens with the same entrance animation as other primitives.

Highlighted items get an accent background with rounded corners. Now moving to dropdown-menu.tsx, swapping its content styling to the same floating rounded card treatment used elsewhere for consistency.

Reconsidering the destructive focus style in dark mode, I'll keep it since it's a sensible tweak once the variant is fixed. Moving to the separator styling now.

For popover.tsx, I'm applying a floating rounded style with padding and removing the border/background/shadow in favor of the nova-float treatment. For tooltip.tsx, I'm evaluating whether the float shadow's inset white highlight still makes sense against a dark tooltip background.

I'm deciding a plain drop shadow like `shadow-lg` works better on dark tooltips than the light-surface float shadow, keeping the solid foreground background and rounded arrow. Now I'm moving to dialog.tsx and defining the overlay styling.

I'm moving the background color into the components layer so it applies without the utility class, using a solid background on mobile and glass/blur at larger breakpoints with a border added at sm+. For the footer, I'm deciding to keep the muted background and border mostly as is since overflow-y-auto still respects the rounded corners for clipping. Now moving on to tabs.tsx.

Adjusting more Tailwind classes...

I'm working through the CSS specificity comparison, figuring out how Tailwind's group-data variant selector's `:is()`/`:where()` structure resolves compared to the plain data-active selector, to determine which style wins when both apply.

For badge.tsx, I'm checking the dark-mode variant classes for destructive/invalid states and muted hover — they look like sensible existing tweaks, so I'm deciding to leave badge.tsx untouched rather than modify it further.

For switch.tsx, I'm calculating that once the variant fix activates, the unchecked dark track color becomes too faint (input/50 on a dark input opacity yields a near-invisible track), so I'll remove that dark class override and look at improving the checked-state background too.

Also checking the thumb contrast: keeping `bg-background` for the thumb creates decent visibility against the primary track when checked, but in the unchecked dark state the dark thumb on a faint track might lack contrast, so I'm considering switching to a white thumb consistently across themes for better visibility.

Now moving on to the slider component styling.

For slider, I want the track to be subtle and the thumb to stay white with a light primary border and soft shadow. Then for the segmented toggle group, I'm adjusting the root background to use the track color with a softer border, and updating pressed items to use a stronger surface color with a raised shadow effect.

Now I need to check the merge extension in utils.ts, then move on to the shell TSX changes: updating WorkspaceShell's outer padding and wide frame classes, glass styling for error portals, WorkspaceModeTabs list classes, Toast glass/icon tones, dialog overlays for ConfirmDialog and QuickPromptDialog, gallery scrims and chips across several components, and hover overlays for job cards.

Beyond that, I need to strip the extra blur from 95% overlays in GifFrameTuner, canvas-node-dialogs, and the image annotation editor, remove the nested top-bar blur in WorkspaceHeader and the fullscreen viewer, keep HistoryImagePreview as is, and apply the nova-float treatment to the canvas toolbar, zoom controls, context menu, mention editor, and input editor popup. AgentChatWorkspace doesn't need TSX changes since the CSS hook already exists. It's a lot of small class edits across many files, but each one is simple -- before diving in I want to double check lib/utils.ts, the HistoryImagePreview portal, and grep for existing glass- classes.

I've gathered exact grep matches for most target lines across PromptGallerySubcomponents, AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, AttachmentChips, QuickPromptDialog, GifModeChoiceDialog, and the various canvas components, so I can edit these directly using the unique single-line class strings rather than reading whole files. I'm just checking that canvas-node-dialogs doesn't have duplicate class strings at lines 153 and 387 that would break a unique-match edit.

Before making these edits, I still want to check remaining glass-token usage, HistoryImagePreview, and bg-destructive/bg-error/text-warning references to batch everything together.

The normal (non-wide) web layout has a visible flaw: the main frame is `max-w-5xl` but never centered, so on a 1440px screen the right side is a strip of flat background, and the frame sits flush against the top-left of the viewport. I'll fix that in the redesign too. Before writing styles I'll check the `cn()` merge rules and where tokens are used.
