payload.text:
Looking at the baseline screenshot, I notice the normal-mode web shell is capped at 1024px and left-aligned, leaving a large empty mint region on the right side rather than centering the content. The background image only fills that shell area while the rest of the page shows the flat body background, creating a visible seam between the two.

I traced this to the shell's className applying `max-w-5xl` without `mx-auto`, and confirmed neither the body nor main element adds any centering. Since nothing intentionally left-aligns it, this looks like an unpolished layout bug I should fix by centering the shell as part of modernizing the design.

Beyond centering, I'm noticing the frame sits flush against the top-left viewport edge with no outer margin, which looks unpolished — adding padding around it so it floats like a glass card would feel more modern, though I need to check how that interacts with the existing `px-0 py-0` styling.

In wide mode, I recall the frame also uses tight inner padding, so the same flush-edge issue likely applies there too and needs the same treatment for consistency.

I could target wide mode via a synced html attribute selector so the frame goes transparent there too. In normal mode the frame stays as one glass card wrapping header, tabs, and content; in desktop normal mode there's no frame at all, just content sitting directly on the backdrop with the topnav, header, and studio panel as separate glass pieces.

Now I'm noticing the history list layout — cards centered in a 760px column with their own scrollbar — and that the tall media area with big empty space above/below images isn't something I need to fix. What I do need to fix is the low-contrast primary button (current green with white text) and the active state of the segmented control, both of which my new deep emerald color should resolve.

I've done enough analysis; time to write the actual CSS changes. Given the file is 1121 lines with a markdown section from 781–1121 I need to preserve untouched, I'll avoid a full rewrite and instead use targeted edits to replace the relevant chunks safely.

Reproducing that much old text verbatim is heavy and error-prone, so instead I'll write a new head section as its own file and use a shell command to splice it together with the untouched markdown tail from the original, avoiding the need to match old text exactly.

A better verification approach: extract and diff the markdown tail section from HEAD against the new file to confirm it's byte-identical, since I'm rewriting the studio/nova-queue/keyframes/scrollbar sections anyway. Now I'm drafting the complete new globals.css section by section.

Writing CSS sections...

I'm verifying the logic covers all combinations of explicit theme attributes versus OS preference correctly, and confirming that complex selectors work properly nested inside `:where()`. I'm also checking whether Tailwind v4's `@custom-variant` syntax actually supports nesting a `@media` block with `&` selectors inside it, referencing how the docs structure similar variants.

Now I'm defining the Aurora Glass color tokens...

Adding destructive and ring colors, then double-checking the secondary token—shifting it to a translucent green tint keeps its light minty look consistent with how it renders over white for buttons and badges.

For destructive, the current red fails AA contrast on white, so switching to #dc2626 raises it to a passing 4.83 ratio while keeping the dark-mode variant (#f87171) unchanged, and I'm now verifying its luminance against the dark background color.

I'll also align `--error` with the same red values, using #dc2626 for light and #f87171 for dark to keep things consistent.

I'm checking the dark-mode `bg-error`/`bg-destructive` combos with white text—#f87171 on white text has poor contrast (2.8), so I want to keep dark `--error` at #ef4444 unchanged and only touch destructive, pending a quick grep for solid `bg-destructive`/`bg-error` usages.

Now looking at `--success`: light mode's #22c55e for `text-success` has weak contrast on white (2.3), so I'm considering bumping light success to something like #15803d for better readability.

For solid success badges, #15803d gives 5.0 contrast with white text versus #22c55e's 2.3, but since success is often used as an icon-only indicator (like the copy-confirmed state), I settle on #16a34a in light mode—3.3:1 satisfies the icon/non-text 3:1 threshold even though it wouldn't pass for small text—while leaving dark mode's #22c55e as is.

Now I'm checking the warning color: #f59e0b as text on light backgrounds only hits 2.15 contrast, too poor for readability in dialog messages. I'm switching light-mode warning to amber-700 (#b45309), which reaches 5.0 contrast against white for both text and solid badge use, and keeping dark mode's #f59e0b since it already contrasts well there.

I'm also finding the processing color (#32a979) fails as text at only 2.96 contrast, so I'm testing a darker teal like #0e8a7c to improve legibility while keeping the same hue family.

For chart tokens I'll just keep a coherent emerald/teal palette rather than overthinking distinctness. The sidebar tokens seem unused by any actual component but I'll update their values anyway for consistency. Now I'm defining the glass system variables for light mode, starting with the inner edge highlight color for luminous panel borders.

Adding more glass tokens...

Still defining color variables...

I'm checking whether the existing glass shadow token names are referenced elsewhere in the TSX components before renaming them, and thinking through how the Tailwind theme namespace resolves shadow utility names so I pick source variable names that won't collide.

I'm working out how v4's shadow utility generates the box-shadow variables, and whether a var()-referenced theme value breaks the color-replacement logic Tailwind normally applies to shadow colors.

Since a raw var() value can't be parsed for colors, I'm confirming it just passes through unchanged, and that mixing inset and outer shadows in the same shadow slot works fine since box-shadow supports both in one list — plus checking how focus ring utilities compose with the shadow variable. Now I'm sketching the backdrop styling with a background color, image, and veil overlay.

I'm defining aurora glow colors—emerald, sky, sun, teal tints—plus a grain texture overlay, and thinking through whether the aurora glow should sit above the bokeh image to tint it, with different colored glows positioned at different corners of the scene.

For dark mode, I'm scaling back the aurora opacities and layering a deep dark veil over the base image so the mint/leafy tones read as muted rather than saturated underneath.

Adding backdrop gradients...

I'm verifying that this radial-gradient syntax with implicit ellipse sizing is valid CSS. Then I'm tracing through the stacking context implications—since body's background propagates to the root canvas when html has no background, this affects how the negative z-index pseudo-element layers relative to body's own background.

I'm also checking whether this holds even when ConfirmDialog forces body into a stacking context via `position: fixed`, confirming the pseudo-element still stays behind the actual content. Now I'm checking if html itself ever gets a background applied through the tailwind preflight styles.

With `overflow-x: hidden` on both html and body, the html's overflow governs the viewport while body's own overflow-x hidden combined with an auto overflow-y makes body a scroll container in principle — though since body's height is auto and grows with content, it's really the viewport that scrolls, not body itself. I'm confirming that this overflow setup doesn't change the containing block for the fixed pseudo-element, since only transform, filter, contain, or will-change would do that — though I still need to check whether `overflow: hidden` clips it.

Since a fixed element's containing block is the viewport rather than body, body's overflow-hidden won't clip it, so that's fine. I'm also confirming other properties like the transition on body, the will-change on the pseudo-element, and the boot loader background are all irrelevant to the backdrop issue.

Now I'm thinking about removing the background image from the app shell itself since it's transparent, while keeping a refined decorative background just for the empty-state panel inside the active jobs section, using a layered gradient veil plus the nature image with different opacity values for light and dark themes.

I'm setting up matching dark-mode token declarations for both the data-theme attribute selector and the system media query, trying to avoid duplicating the same values twice.

Actually, Tailwind's `@variant` directive could solve this elegantly—I can nest my custom dark variant inside `:root` so it expands to the same selector pattern automatically, avoiding manual duplication entirely.

Same specificity as the existing dark selector, so source order still decides the winner. I'm a little unsure whether Tailwind's `@variant dark` expansion inside `:root` behaves exactly as I expect, but the verification harness should catch it — if dark tokens fail to apply, the dark screenshots would visibly look wrong, so I can confirm correctness that way rather than reasoning it out fully.

Since everything now routes through tokens, I can drop the scattered `[data-theme="dark"]` overrides elsewhere and consolidate them into the token block, adding `color-scheme: dark` there too so native form controls and scrollbars pick up sensible defaults automatically.

Adding more theme tokens...

Now I'm tracing how the font-sans variable flows through preflight's default font family reference to confirm the mapping resolves correctly.

That explains the earlier fallback behavior: when `--default-font-family` references an undefined var without its own fallback, it computes to the guaranteed-invalid value, so the outer var() falls back to the default list — matching what I observed on the html element.

My fix defines `--nova-font-sans` directly, resolving that issue, and I also need to map `--font-heading` to my sans stack since dialog titles use `font-heading`. I'm sketching the base layer styles for borders, tap highlight, background/foreground colors, and reconsidering whether font-feature-settings like cv11/ss01 even apply here since Segoe doesn't support them — probably skip that. I'm also adding a `::selection` rule with a color-mix based on the primary color.

Color-mix should be fine given browser support targets, and I'm confirming the default text color behavior for selection highlights stays sane without explicit color overrides. I'm updating the existing body rule's font-family to use my new variable while keeping the background-color and transition properties intact, then moving on to scrollbar styling with feature queries for scrollbar-color support and a fallback for webkit scrollbar pseudo-elements.

Now I'm working through a specificity conflict: `* { scrollbar-width: thin }` is unlayered and could override `.scrollbar-hide` if that class is also unlayered plain CSS, so I need to check the specificity ordering carefully.

I realize Tailwind arbitrary properties like `[scrollbar-width:none]` compile into `@layer utilities`, meaning any unlayered `*` rule I write would override them since unlayered CSS beats layered CSS regardless of specificity. So I should wrap the `*` scrollbar rule inside `@layer base` to keep it below utilities in priority, while `.scrollbar-hide` staying unlayered still wins over base.

I'm also checking that other unlayered selectors like `.studio-params-bar` and `.virtual-scroll-container` correctly override the layered rule, and defining color tokens for the scrollbar thumb in both light and dark modes, along with confirming `scrollbar-width: thin` renders properly with custom colors on Windows Chromium.

Now I'm setting up `.nova-float` styles with a fallback border, solid background, and shadow, then layering a `@supports` block that adds backdrop blur and saturation when the browser supports it — but I'm noticing this border rule might conflict with existing ring/border styles already used on dropdowns and selects.

Adding a border shifts sizing by 2px for the dropdown, which had no border before, though that's minor since utility classes still control radius and destructive-tinted borders correctly. I'm now weighing whether to switch to a box-shadow ring instead of a real border to avoid layout shifts, but that would break my plan to give toasts a colored border per type.

I'll stick with a real border since it's cleaner and easier to override; I just need to strip conflicting `border-border` classes from components like the ConfirmDialog panel when adding the nova-float style. I'm also considering saturate(1.6) for that Apple-style vibrancy behind the blur — it's a relatively cheap color matrix operation compared to blur, and should work fine in both light and dark mode.

For accessibility, I need to handle prefers-reduced-transparency by swapping the glass background for a solid one and disabling the backdrop-filter, making sure this rule sits after the @supports block in the same layer so it wins via source order rather than needing extra specificity. I should also override the glass token variables to more opaque values in that same media query so all glass panels become genuinely solid, not just the float bar.

Extending overrides to soft, card, and surface variants too, with concrete opaque hex values for light and dark. Chrome 118+ supports this media feature, mapping to Windows transparency settings, which is good news. Now I'm thinking through the float sheet component for dialogs—applying blur and saturation effects only at sm+ breakpoints via feature queries, though I'm wary of scroll performance on the settings modal with such a large blur radius.

I'm considering dropping blur specifically on the app settings dialog if performance suffers, while keeping it on smaller dialogs, and swapping out the primitive's default ring styling for the float sheet's border. For big static panels I'm defining a glass class with edge border, panel background, and layered shadow/highlight effects, but I realize I don't actually need this as a standalone class since I'm already overriding component utilities through existing unlayered semantic hook selectors—those naturally win over layered Tailwind utilities like border and background classes on the same elements, which is exactly the override mechanism already used elsewhere in the codebase.

Now I'm working out per-mode layout rules, starting with normal web mode: adjusting the shell's max-width and centering, restyling the app frame hook to use a softer glass surface and shadow at larger breakpoints, and considering adding padding around the frame so agent tab content still fits within the viewport height. I'm second-guessing whether adjusting this padding counts as a legitimate style change or scope creep.

I'll make the wide-mode frame transparent using a data attribute to strip border, background, and shadow so the sidebar and panels float directly on the backdrop, though I need to account for the attribute being set before hydration while wideMode state is still false during boot.

Actually, I think it's cleaner to add a distinct `nova-app-frame-wide` class directly in the TSX conditional rather than relying on the html attribute, since the frame's className doesn't currently have a wide-specific class. The desktop frame's existing transparent rules can stay as-is.

For the sidebar in wide mode, I'm restyling `.nova-app-sidebar` at ≥960px with a fixed width, glass surface, and rounded corners, updating the tabs list to remove its default border/background since the sidebar itself provides the surface. But since wide mode actually only activates at ≥1280px, I realize the ≥960px breakpoint for this rule doesn't line up correctly and needs reconsideration.

For the active nav item, instead of the current left-accent-bar style, I'm considering a raised white pill with a primary-colored icon, possibly dropping the left bar entirely or replacing it with a small rounded indicator using a `::before` pseudo-element since that's unused by the tabs primitive.

Writing indicator CSS...

But I should check spacing—the trigger's left padding is 10px, so I need to make sure this indicator doesn't overlap the icon.

Now for the horizontal tabs in top nav mode, I'm swapping the muted background for the track color and reconsidering whether border-glass-edge is even a valid Tailwind class before applying it.

Buttons get restyled by the primitive itself. I briefly consider giving the title gradient text, but that's a common AI-cliche flourish, so I'll skip it and keep things simple.

Now I'm thinking through the workbench panel glass styling: I want it applied outside the media query so it works in both normal and desktop modes, layering panel glass over frame glass over backdrop. I'm also checking that history cards sitting directly in the frame (without the panel) still look right, then moving on to restyle the studio-workbench-head with a sheen effect.

For the prompt surface, I'm setting the field background with a transparent textarea and muted toolbar, updating the focus glow to a subtle primary ring with border. For the params bar buttons, I'm simplifying by removing the old transparent background override since outline buttons now use the surface color, possibly keeping just a light primary hover tint.

I'm reviewing the result card, history toolbar, and active jobs panel styling — the processing tint gets overridden by the unlayered rule at wider breakpoints, and the waiting/failed cards keep their existing card background, which seems fine.

For the result and waiting/failed cards I'm adding a glass background with a subtle highlight shadow, but I want to preserve the failed card's destructive border tint and only apply the glass edge border color to the result card specifically.

I'm deciding to unify the wide-mode result card's opaque background with the same glass-card treatment since both are static and the cost is equivalent. The loading sweep animation already uses a composited transform so that's fine as-is.

For the queue metric I'm restyling it with a surface background, edge border, and 10px radius. For the agent workspace panel, I'm unifying the glass panel styling across all modes by overriding the border color, background, and shadow to use the glass tokens, and removing the separate desktop-specific override that had different radius and background values.

I'm settling on a consistent 20px panel radius for major surfaces like the sidebar, workspace, studio panels, and history panel. I'm giving the agent toolbar a sheen gradient with a glass-edge bottom border, keeping the messages area's scrollbar gutter behavior, and simplifying the composer background to a translucent surface tint. For the settings modal, I'm noting that since it now inherits the float-sheet dialog primitive with glass blur, its existing opaque-ish glass-surface background override may need reconciling.

For dense settings forms, readability matters more than showing the blurred backdrop, so I'm leaning toward a higher opacity like 0.9 so the frosted blur only contributes subtly underneath.

Actually, I'll settle on a clearer rule: large scrolling surfaces like the settings modal skip live backdrop blur entirely and use a near-opaque static glass gradient instead, avoiding performance risk, while smaller dialogs like confirmations and quick prompts keep the real frosted blur effect.

I'll measure with it on, then disable if regression shows. Though the headless GPU here (Intel UHD 770 at DPR 1.5) is a decent modern iGPU, so it's plausibly close to the user's actual device rather than a weaker or stronger stand-in.

For the dialog overlay, I'm considering removing the settings-specific darker scrim rule since it uses `:has()` which has perf cost, favoring a uniform scrim instead. The toast and error portal both get glass-float styling with the nova-float treatment, and the CompletedJobCard hover gets a gradient plus glass chip overlay. I'm now writing a CSS keyframe animation for a subtle rise effect, fading in while translating upward slightly.

I need to double check whether applying transform during this animation to the workspace container creates a containing block issue for any fixed-position descendants — since portals render to body they're unaffected, but I want to verify the fill-mode behavior resolves to `transform: none` cleanly after the animation completes so it doesn't accidentally trap fixed elements during the brief transition.

Also I'm now noticing the desktop shell has its own entry animation with a translateY transform and fill-mode both — I need to check that its final keyframe state doesn't leave a lingering transform that would create an unintended containing block for the whole app.

I'm checking whether full-screen fixed overlays like the GifFrameTuner editor are portaled or trapped inside the shell's stacking context — since the shell covers the viewport this mostly works fine either way, and a static translateY(0) shouldn't force compositing. This is existing behavior I don't need to fix; for my new rise animations I'll just define the end state with opacity change.

Actually, I realize `transform: translateY(0)` still establishes a containing block for fixed/absolute descendants even as an identity transform, so I should fix both my new animation and the existing nova-desktop-enter to use `transform: none` instead for correctness — low risk change. I also want to check whether studio-history-enter's retained `translateY(0)` end state causes the same containing-block issue for history job elements.

I need to check whether HistoryImagePreview uses createPortal — if it's rendered inline inside the fragment sibling to the transformed `.studio-history-job` div rather than portaled, a fixed overlay would end up positioned relative to that transformed ancestor instead of the viewport, which would be a real bug worth checking directly in the source.

I'm also reconsidering some smaller details: hover transforms on result cards briefly create their own containing blocks (harmless), reduced-motion preferences should disable the rise and toast animations, and the body's color transition during theme switches looks fine since panels and backdrops swap instantly while just the base color eases.

I should also update the theme-color metadata in layout.tsx to match the new backdrop color for mobile browser chrome consistency.

Now I'm defining the button component's variant classes...

Adding more button variants...

I'm also checking whether Tailwind v4's `bg-(image:--gloss)` syntax for referencing custom properties will merge correctly with `bg-primary` without conflicts in tailwind-merge.

I'm considering an alternative to avoid twMerge ambiguity: defining an actual utility class for the gloss background rather than relying on arbitrary value syntax, then working through how twMerge's bg-color grouping logic would treat that unknown class.

Actually, I realize this custom bg-gloss utility is risky since twMerge would group it with other bg-color classes and could override bg-primary unintentionally. I'm now checking whether my other custom colors and shadow utilities are correctly categorized so they conflict only with their intended counterparts.

Since both classes would coexist in the DOM, the actual visual outcome depends on unpredictable CSS ordering from Tailwind's utility sort. To resolve this reliably, I'll need to extend the tailwind-merge config in the utils file to properly recognize these custom shadow classes as part of the same conflict group.

Confirming that v3's theme keys align with Tailwind v4 namespaces, so extending the shadow scale with custom names should work fine. I'm also weighing whether arbitrary value syntax like shadow-(--var) could be ambiguous with color utilities in the merge logic.

I'm not fully certain twMerge's default shadow matcher accepts unlabeled arbitrary variables, so the safer path is to just extend the twMerge config explicitly inside the cn() utility rather than rely on defaults — I should check lib/utils.ts to see what's there now, and also confirm the bg-image group handles arbitrary variables similarly.

Since bg-image is listed before bg-color in the config's backgrounds section, it should be checked first and win the match. I'm checking the line ending situation across files: the repo stores LF but the working tree has CRLF for button.tsx and Toast.tsx, while globals.css shows a mixed pattern with some CRLF and some LF lines. This matters because writing changes back could normalize things unexpectedly.

With core.autocrlf enabled, git converts CRLF to LF on add, so the index stays consistent regardless of what ending style I write with, meaning line-ending differences won't falsely appear as diffs. Still, I plan to run git diff --stat afterward to confirm the untouched markdown tail region shows no unexpected changes. I'm also checking where scrollbars are hidden across the codebase, looking at the various scrollbar-width and utility class implementations used.

All the scrollbar-hiding rules already set the standard `scrollbar-width: none` in ways that override my global thin-scrollbar layer rule, whether through the unlayered `.scrollbar-hide` class, inline styles, or the unlayered `.nova-image-workspace .studio-params-bar` selector — so applying thin scrollbars globally won't break anything. I'll also swap out the existing desktop-shell thin scrollbar rule for the new global one. Now I'm shifting from planning into execution: I'm marking the baseline task complete since the build, screenshots, and perf smoke-test are done, and moving on to the tokens-backdrop step.

My plan is to write a new head section for globals.css to a temp file, then splice it together with the original markdown-related tail of the file before writing the combined result back into the actual globals.css. I need to double check that `--font-mono` will resolve correctly for the markdown styles once I define it in `:root`, which means reasoning through how Tailwind v4's `@theme inline` directive interacts with runtime CSS variables and whether it actually emits usable theme variables in this case.

I recall that the theme variable output logic only skips variables marked as `REFERENCE`, meaning `INLINE` variables would still get emitted to `:root` unless there's separate pruning for unused ones elsewhere in the codebase.

I'm now thinking about how optimization removes unused variables unless marked `STATIC`—since inline utilities inject values directly, the variable itself may not register as "used" and could get pruned, unless something else in the CSS references it via `var()`. Tailwind's optimizer seems to track `var(--...)` usages stylesheet-wide and preserve any theme variable referenced anywhere, so I'm checking the baseline evidence where `.font-mono` resolves to the sans stack instead of the expected mono variable, suggesting the inline utility reference might be invalid.

So my fix is to define the sans and mono font stacks explicitly as new custom properties in an unlayered `:root` block, listing out fallback fonts for both.

Both resolve to the same thing anyway, so it's fine either way. Actually, simplifying further, I'll just define `--font-sans` and `--font-mono` directly in `:root` with the stacks, skipping the indirection, and reference those in `@theme inline`.

I need to avoid mapping `--font-sans: var(--font-sans)` inside the theme block since that's circular — Tailwind might not resolve self-references correctly. I'll keep using the `--nova-font-*` source variables to avoid that issue, and I'm double-checking how Tailwind's preflight resolves `--default-font-family` through `--theme(--font-sans, initial)` to make sure my override still takes effect properly.

To be safe, I'll add an explicit `html { font-family: var(--nova-font-sans); }` rule inside my own base layer, since it will come after preflight's rules within the same `@layer base` due to source order.

I also need to update the existing unlayered body rule to use `var(--nova-font-sans)` directly, and confirm `.font-mono`/`.font-heading` utilities will correctly resolve since their underlying CSS variables are defined in `:root`.

Now I'm checking font fallback behavior on Chinese Windows — Tailwind's default sans stack resolves `system-ui` to Microsoft YaHei UI, whereas my custom stack prioritizes Segoe UI for Latin text with CJK fallbacks like PingFang SC that don't exist on Windows, so I need to verify the fallback chain actually lands on a real CJK font there.

YaHei UI, whose different ascent/descent ratios shift the baseline within the line box even when line-height is fixed by Tailwind's explicit values. Since mixed Latin/CJK text uses separate font metrics per glyph run, each run's inline box gets centered independently via the half-leading model, causing subtle pixel-level vertical misalignment between scripts on the same line.

With fixed line-height, only the primary font's metrics drive the half-leading calculation, so switching from YaHei UI to Segoe UI as primary shifts the baseline position slightly—maybe a pixel—and CJK glyphs sitting on that shared baseline could look subtly off-center vertically in tight buttons since their ideographic em box extends asymmetrically above and below the baseline.

Checking YaHei UI's metrics confirms it was actually designed to match Segoe UI, so the difference is negligible—meaning the font stack swap should be visually near-neutral for CJK on Windows while fixing the mono stack to be truly monospace, with Consolas as the reliable fallback since Cascadia isn't guaranteed present.

Segoe UI Variable Text only exists on Windows 11, gracefully skipped on Windows 10, and its metrics are close enough to standard Segoe UI to be a safe modern touch. I'm also confirming the Mac/Windows split works correctly—PingFang SC handles CJK after SF on Mac, while YaHei UI takes over on Windows since Apple's system fonts aren't present there. Now I'm ready to write out the complete new head of globals.css.

I recall Tailwind v4's docs supporting nested `@media`/`&` structures inside `@custom-variant` with `@slot` for the variant body, which confirms this pattern should work fine here.

The `substituteAtSlot` function walks the AST and swaps in the nodes for every `@slot` occurrence, confirming multiple slots work correctly. Now I'm drafting the design notes for an "Aurora Glass" aesthetic — using pre-blurred static backdrops for large panels while reserving real backdrop-filter effects for small, transient floating elements.

Keeping the dark green secondary-foreground text and chart/sidebar tokens mostly as-is, just updating them to the new palette.

This skill guides creation of distinctive, production-grade frontend interfaces that avoid generic "AI slop" aesthetics. Implement real working code with exceptional attention to aesthetic details and creative choices.

The user provides frontend requirements: a component, page, application, or interface to build. They may include context about the purpose, audience, or technical constraints.

## Design Thinking

Before coding, understand the context and commit to a BOLD aesthetic direction:
- **Purpose**: What problem does this interface solve? Who uses it?
- **Tone**: Pick an extreme: brutally minimal, maximalist chaos, retro-futuristic, organic/natural, luxury/refined, playful/toy-like, editorial/magazine, brutalist/raw, art deco/geometric, soft/pastel, industrial/utilitarian, etc. There are so many flavors to choose from. Use these for inspiration but design one that is true to the aesthetic direction.
- **Constraints**: Technical requirements (framework, performance, accessibility).
- **Differentiation**: What makes this UNFORGETTABLE? What's the one thing someone will remember?

**CRITICAL**: Choose a clear conceptual direction and execute it with precision. Bold maximalism and refined minimalism both work - the key is intentionality, not intensity.

Then implement working code (HTML/CSS/JS, React, Vue, etc.) that is:
- Production-grade and functional
- Visually striking and memorable
- Cohesive with a clear aesthetic point-of-view
- Meticulously refined in every detail

## Frontend Aesthetics Guidelines

Focus on:
- **Typography**: Choose fonts that are beautiful, unique, and interesting. Avoid generic fonts like Arial and Inter; opt instead for distinctive choices that elevate the frontend's aesthetics; unexpected, characterful font choices. Pair a distinctive display font with a refined body font.
- **Color & Theme**: Commit to a cohesive aesthetic. Use CSS variables for consistency. Dominant colors with sharp accents outperform timid, evenly-distributed palettes.
- **Motion**: Use animations for effects and micro-interactions. Prioritize CSS-only solutions for HTML. Use Motion library for React when available. Focus on high-impact moments: one well-orchestrated page load with staggered reveals (animation-delay) creates more delight than scattered micro-interactions. Use scroll-triggering and hover states that surprise.
- **Spatial Composition**: Unexpected layouts. Asymmetry. Overlap. Diagonal flow. Grid-breaking elements. Generous negative space OR controlled density.
- **Backgrounds & Visual Details**: Create atmosphere and depth rather than defaulting to solid colors. Add contextual effects and textures that match the overall aesthetic. Apply creative forms like gradient meshes, noise textures, geometric patterns, layered transparencies, dramatic shadows, decorative borders, custom cursors, and grain overlays.

NEVER use generic AI-generated aesthetics like overused font families (Inter, Roboto, Arial, system fonts), cliched color schemes (particularly purple gradients on white backgrounds), predictable layouts and component patterns, and cookie-cutter design that lacks context-specific character.

Interpret creatively and make unexpected choices that feel genuinely designed for the context. No design should be the same. Vary between light and dark themes, different fonts, different aesthetics. NEVER converge on common choices (Space Grotesk, for example) across generations.

**IMPORTANT**: Match implementation complexity to the aesthetic vision. Maximalist designs need elaborate code with extensive animations and effects. Minimalist or refined designs need restraint, precision, and careful attention to spacing, typography, and subtle details. Elegance comes from executing the vision well.

Remember: Claude is capable of extraordinary creative work. Don't hold back, show what can truly be created when thinking outside the box and committing fully to a distinctive vision.

My strategy is to keep that static pre-blurred background for the app shell while being careful that any glass panels containing scrolling content don't reintroduce the same performance cost.

That confirms the current fake-glass technique is the right performance tradeoff, so I should reserve real backdrop-filter for small transient elements like popovers, tooltips, and toasts, while keeping large panels on the pre-blurred layered approach. I also noticed layout.tsx never actually loads the Geist font despite referencing `--font-geist-sans`, so that variable resolves to nothing and the typography silently falls back to Arial/Helvetica -- worth checking if that's intentional or a bug affecting the modern look.

If that variable is undefined, the whole font-family declaration becomes invalid at computed-value time, so it falls back to the inherited value—meaning it inherits whatever the html element's font-family resolves to, which under Tailwind's preflight is the default sans stack rather than the browser's serif default.

Rather than guess further, I really need to just check the actual rendered output. Let me see if Playwright is set up so I can run the app and take screenshots to verify.

That's just a tool-result placeholder, not a real instruction, so I'll keep going with the task. I've reviewed the UI primitives, and now I need to check the actual current state with a screenshot, seeing whether playwright-cli is available for that.

I also want to read through WorkspaceHeader, WorkspaceModeTabs, Toast, and key workbench components to see how classes are used across the app. Given the file sizes, I might delegate some exploration to subagents to save context, but I still need enough understanding to make consistent design changes — mainly through globals.css, UI primitives, and a few shell components, since deep components already rely on token-based Tailwind classes.

Now I'm thinking through the performance implications of glassmorphism, particularly how backdrop-filter blur cost scales with element area and blur radius, and how it forces re-renders whenever content behind or the element itself changes.

Chromium may cache backdrop-filter results if the backdrop is unchanged, but in practice large backdrop-filter surfaces with scrolling content still cause jank on weaker GPUs, especially in Electron on high-DPI Windows. The existing pre-blurred bitmap comment confirms the codebase already hit this problem and deliberately avoided live backdrop-filter, so I should stick with a "faux glass" approach: keep the pre-blurred background image and layer cheap static gradients on top rather than adding real blur.

I'm now realizing the shell's scrollable height in normal mode could stretch the cover background awkwardly for long content, so a better fix is moving the background image onto a fixed-position pseudo-element behind the shell so it composites as its own layer and doesn't repaint on scroll.

For the surfaces, I'm planning semi-transparent gradient fills with a subtle inset highlight, gradient border, and layered shadow to simulate frosted glass without actual blur, since the fixed backdrop is already blurred underneath. I'm also considering a cheap static noise texture, like a tiny SVG with turbulence, to add real frosting grain.

I think it's best to apply that grain only to the fixed background layer as a low-opacity overlay, since it paints once and composites for free during scroll—rather than repainting it on interactive panels.

For real backdrop-filter usage, popovers, dropdown menus, and tooltips are ideal candidates: blur plus saturation on a translucent background, with an `@supports` fallback for browsers lacking support, since these are small and short-lived. Full-screen dialog overlays are trickier though—animating the fade-in of a blurred overlay might force the browser to recompute the blur every frame even though only opacity changes, which could get costly on large 4K viewports.

Modal dialogs with internal scrolling (like a large settings panel) raise a related question: since the overlay's blurred backdrop derives from static content behind it, I'm not sure scrolling inside the dialog itself should force recomputation, but Chromium's damage-rect based compositing might still redraw the overlay if the scrolled region overlaps it.

I'll keep the overlay blur modest, around 6px, to stay safe on performance, and lean on automatic fallbacks instead of a manual toggle: reduced-transparency preferences fall back to solid surfaces, reduced-motion disables animations, and a feature-support check handles browsers without backdrop-filter support.

I should also check cross-browser support since the web version needs to run on Firefox and Safari, not just Electron's Chromium, and Tailwind v4's Lightning CSS should handle the vendor prefixing for backdrop-blur utilities automatically.

For toolbars floating over the canvas, panning triggers backdrop blur recomputation on every frame since the content behind constantly shifts, though the affected areas are small.

Toast notifications are a good candidate since they're small and transient. For image hover actions, the blur is limited to small hover-triggered chips over images, though I need to check whether always-rendered but hidden elements still create layer overhead at opacity 0.

With something like a history list of 100 cards each carrying hover chips using backdrop-filter, that could still allocate 100+ render surfaces even when invisible, hurting scroll performance—so I should use solid translucent dark backgrounds instead of blur for repeated per-item elements. I also want to avoid nesting backdrop-filter elements inside other backdrop-filter elements, since Chromium's backdrop root behavior compounds cost there.

If a popover is portaled to the document body, its backdrop root becomes the page root, so it correctly blurs everything behind it—that's the desired outcome, and animating the popup's own opacity during fade-in is fine since opacity applies to the filtered backdrop result per spec.

Checking a few more edge cases—the scale-based zoom-in animation on the popup works fine with backdrop-filter, and overflow/border-radius on ancestors doesn't cause issues either.

Now I'm checking whether the Geist font is actually loading properly, since the layout doesn't seem to import it via next/font, meaning the CSS variable might just be falling back to the default sans-serif stack.

Since `--default-font-family` resolves to the guaranteed-invalid `var(--font-geist-sans)`, the property itself becomes invalid, so the fallback chain kicks in and html actually falls back to `ui-sans-serif` and the rest of the default stack.

Given this ends up cascading to system-ui, that's reasonably fine for a Chinese UI on Windows since it resolves to Segoe UI with Microsoft YaHei UI as backup. But loading custom web fonts for CJK is impractical due to file size, so I'm leaning toward deliberately defining a proper system font stack instead of relying on a web font for Chinese text.

I could self-host a display font for Latin headings via next/font/local, but that requires bundling a font file or adding a new dependency like fontsource, and since the app runs offline in Electron, relying on next/font/google's build-time fetch is risky if the build machine lacks internet. Given the modest visual payoff versus the build risk, this isn't worth pursuing.

I'll skip custom fonts and stick with a curated system stack using font-feature-settings for stylistic sets and tabular-nums for metrics, which is secondary to the main goal of a more modern frosted-glass style. On color, the current mint green (#43b957) is tied to the nature background image, so I'll keep that green identity but refine it to feel more sophisticated rather than replacing the brand color entirely.

I'm leaning toward a deeper emerald primary with a teal/cyan secondary tint for gradients, creating a green-teal aurora effect that fits a "nature glass" theme better than the overused purple gradients. I want to check the actual background image and old PWA screenshots to confirm the vibe matches, and I'm thinking about increasing surface translucency with a specular top highlight to let more of the background show through.

For gradient borders, I'm considering using a masked pseudo-element trick, but I'm weighing whether masks force extra GPU layers in Chromium and whether that's affordable for just a handful of large panels versus something used repeatedly on cards.

A cheaper alternative is stacking box-shadows for highlight, rim, and ambient depth effects—these are painted once for static elements, though large blurred shadows still cost something to paint initially. I'm also thinking about how scrolling content inside a panel interacts with compositing, since Chromium tends to composite scrollers automatically in many cases.

So my plan is to build the glass effect with layered translucent gradients, inset highlights, and soft shadows rather than blur on large panels—leaning on a pre-blurred backdrop image to sell the frosted look. I want to add subtle aurora-style radial gradients baked into the fixed background layer, and possibly consider a slow drifting animation on a separate composited blob layer since animating transform there stays cheap on the GPU.

Given that a constantly animating background is distracting and drains battery in a productivity app, I'll skip continuous motion and maybe only animate briefly on load. For interaction polish I'm planning glass-pill buttons with gradient fills and inner highlights, hover lift via composited transforms, and focus rings—tightening up the transition properties instead of using a blanket transition-all. I also want glass-pill active tabs, translucent inputs with inner shadows and focus glow, and thin rounded translucent scrollbars applied more broadly.

For dialogs, I'm avoiding double backdrop-filter cost by having the overlay do the blurring while the dialog content itself stays a high-opacity translucent surface without its own backdrop-filter, since it reads as frosted against the already-blurred backdrop.

But even though the dialog's own content scrolls independently, the backdrop filter still gets recomputed whenever that render pass is damaged, since the blur is applied as part of drawing that layer. So scrolling inside the dialog would trigger the blur to reapply for the damaged area each frame, though GPU-side this is generally cheap enough for a single element.

I should also account for the overlay tint sitting behind the frosted dialog — since the backdrop includes the dark overlay plus the page, a light frosted panel would end up looking grayish, so I might want to lighten the overlay tint for light themes.

I'll go with a hybrid approach: keep the overlay as a cheap flat tint without blur, and put the actual backdrop blur only on the dialog surface itself, giving that Apple-style frosted glass effect where the dialog shows the blurred page behind it. I could also make the dialog surface fairly opaque so the blur reads as a subtle accent rather than a dominant effect.

On mobile, since dialogs go fullscreen and cover the entire viewport, blurring is pointless since nothing behind is visible—so I'll just fall back to a solid background below the `sm` breakpoint as a performance win. I also want to add a `@supports` guard for browsers lacking `backdrop-filter`.

For accessibility, I should respect `prefers-reduced-transparency` (supported in Chrome 118+, mapping to Windows' transparency toggle) to switch glass surfaces to opaque, and `prefers-reduced-motion` to strip transitions and animations.

On performance, I'm avoiding `transition: all` on big elements and only animating transform/opacity for hover effects, and being careful with `will-change` — only applying it to the fixed background layer since Chromium's compositing behavior for fixed elements can vary based on display DPI and LCD text preferences.

I'm also checking the history card hover shadows for repaint cost during transitions and considering whether the history list is already virtualized, since `content-visibility: auto` could help performance but risks scroll-position issues if not handled carefully.

For validating my changes, my plan is to run the frontend build, lint, and vitest test suite, then do a visual check by serving the app and comparing screenshots before/after with Playwright, since it looks like the project already has some Playwright CLI tooling set up.

For performance, I'm thinking of scripting a scroll through the history list and measuring frame timings via requestAnimationFrame deltas or CDP tracing, tracking long frames and compositing layer counts (via LayerTree domain) before and after my change to give concrete evidence there's no regression.

But headless Chromium's rendering path complicates this — it may use software GL rather than a real GPU, so frame timing there might not reflect real-world performance. Running headed to get GPU-accelerated numbers is more representative but pops up a visible browser window, which feels intrusive for a brief check.

I should also check the environment first — Node version, Playwright setup, whether frontend dependencies are installed, and if a dev server is already running. Since the backend build process bundles the frontend, I'm weighing whether serving the frontend alone (via dev server or static export) is sufficient for capturing UI screenshots, even if some backend API calls fail silently in the background.

A `frontend/out` directory already exists, which could serve as a "before" baseline, but it might be stale from an older build. Instead, I think the cleanest approach is starting `next dev` in the background now, capturing baseline screenshots, then letting HMR pick up my changes and capturing "after" screenshots from the same running server.

But the app relies heavily on localStorage state for jobs, settings, and API keys, so empty states will dominate unless I seed fake data — which feels overly complex for just visual evaluation. Screenshots of empty states, the agent chat, settings dialog, and dropdowns should be sufficient; I'll check the existing screenshot-wide.png first to understand the current UI before deciding if I need to explore the prompt gallery for a populated view.

I also want to check the Electron main process for window options like backgroundColor and vibrancy. Windows 11 supports `backgroundMaterial` for native acrylic/mica blur via the OS compositor, but since this user's on Windows 10, that option would be ignored — I could still add it as an opt-in for Windows 11 users, though that requires making the desktop background transparent.

There's no AGENTS.md anywhere in the workspace, so nothing to worry about there. MEMORY.md is still just a blank template, so nothing needs updating unless something new comes up. Next I want to look at the background image, screenshots, and the desktop main.js window settings, and check if playwright is available.

payload.text:
I'm scanning the codebase for backdrop-blur usage and finding it applied repeatedly on a per-item basis in components like hover action chips, image galleries, message bubbles, and attachment chips—flagging these as places where the effect is duplicated per-card rather than applied once.

There's also a pattern of full-screen overlays combining near-opaque backgrounds (95%) with backdrop-blur, which is mostly wasted since the blur is barely visible through such low transparency, yet it still costs a full-viewport render. These appear in canvas-based editors like the image-annotation-editor, GifFrameTuner, and canvas-node-dialogs, where the blurred backdrop sits behind interactive editing content.

Removing that faint blur is a minor edit though, so I'll weigh whether it's worth the risk of touching many files versus leaving those transient full-screen modes alone as a lower-priority cleanup item. Next I want to check the custom overlay dialogs like ConfirmDialog, QuickPromptDialog, GifModeChoiceDialog, and PromptGallery, since they use raw black overlays instead of the shared dialog component and need consistent styling, then move on to reviewing WorkspaceHeader, WorkspaceModeTabs, and Toast for appearance.

I'm now weighing whether to make these changes mostly at the CSS layer—redefining tokens, adding glass utility classes, and updating shared semantic hooks and UI primitives like dialog, dropdown, popover, select, tooltip, tabs, button, input, and textarea—versus touching individual components directly.

Restyling every component individually feels too risky given the scope, so the token-and-primitives approach is the better path. Before diving in, I want baseline screenshots of the current UI, which means getting the dev server running first to see what I'm actually changing.

Using `next dev --webpack` gives me hot reload for quick iteration, though it's slower for perf measurements due to unminified React dev-mode code. But for scroll performance specifically, JS overhead shouldn't matter much unless there are scroll listeners triggering re-renders, like with virtualized lists using @tanstack/react-virtual.

That virtualization concern makes me reconsider — I should use production builds for fair before/after comparisons. I'm thinking of building the current baseline with `npm run build`, copying the output to a temp directory, then rebuilding after changes to compare. I need to check whether the `out` folder is gitignored before I rely on that workflow.

Actually, rebuilding is a normal dev action since the root `npm run dev` already does this, but I should flag it as medium-risk since it could regenerate service worker files like `sw.js` and `workbox-*.js` in the tracked `public` directory, potentially creating git diffs I need to watch for.

I should build with `NOVA_DESKTOP_BUILD=1` to disable PWA generation, avoiding the sw.js issue and matching the actual target since the user is running the Electron desktop app on Windows. I'll first check if `public/sw.js` and `out/` are tracked in git before proceeding, then set up a performance testing harness by launching Chromium with remote debugging enabled at a specific window size.

I'm also weighing headless vs headed mode: with `--headless=new`, rendering may fall back to software (SwiftShader) rather than GPU acceleration, which would make paint/raster-heavy effects like backdrop-filter blur appear far more expensive than they'd be with real GPU compositing. That actually makes software rendering a more sensitive stress test for catching regressions—if the numbers hold up under software rendering, they should be fine on real hardware too.

I'll stick with headless to avoid disturbing the user's desktop, and plan to capture metrics via CDP's Performance.getMetrics along with a rAF-based frame-time sampler during a scripted scroll.

For the sampler, I'll scroll a container programmatically for a few seconds, recording frame deltas to compute average FPS, p95 frame time, and slow-frame counts—headless rAF still runs at 60Hz, so slowdowns will show up as increased deltas. Since Node 24 has a stable global WebSocket, I can write the CDP client as a dependency-free script.

I'm planning to fetch the debugger URL from the DevTools JSON endpoint, connect via WebSocket, and either attach to an existing target or create a new page directly to get its ws URL. I'll keep this script in a temp directory outside the repo to avoid polluting the workspace and clean it up afterward.

Now I'm thinking about where scrollable content with real data would come from, since jobs are stored in local IndexedDB and mostly empty by default — the prompt gallery has static bundled data that might also pull from a remote source.

I'm weighing options for a scroll-performance test: seeding IndexedDB with fake jobs versus a hacky DOM-cloning trick via CDP to stress-test card rendering. Seeding the job store directly seems cleaner, so I want to check how `job-store.ts` persists data to see if I can inject fake completed jobs through `page.evaluate` using the app's own storage format.

Before diving deeper into the perf harness, I should keep it lean and focus on the actual design work as the main deliverable, though verifying performance impact matters given the user's concern. Now I want to look through the key visible components -- WorkspaceHeader, WorkspaceModeTabs, Toast, and ConfirmDialog -- to understand the current look and feel.

Given the codebase size (~1MB of TSX), I can't read everything directly, so I'll read the shell-level components fully and grep for recurring patterns in the rest, like usage of rounded/border/shadow/bg-muted classes to understand how surfaces are constructed.

I'm also looking for the semantic naming hooks like "nova-*" and "studio-*" used throughout to identify styling entry points. Thinking about what "modern" should mean here — the current mint-green translucent card aesthetic feels flat, so I'm planning to layer in a richer atmospheric background with aurora-style gradient blobs and subtle noise grain as a single fixed backdrop layer, separate from the existing pre-blurred nature image applied to the shell.

Since the shell scrolls with the document, its background currently repaints as part of the scrolling contents layer, and stretching a tall element with `background-size: cover` causes zoom/blur artifacts. Moving to a fixed, separately composited pseudo-element avoids that repaint cost — a real improvement over the naive `background-attachment: fixed` approach, which is known to hurt scroll performance.

I'm now considering placement: attaching the fixed pseudo-element to the shell itself, but I need to check whether any ancestor has a transform, filter, or containment property that would create its own containing block, since that would break the fixed positioning relative to the viewport — and the desktop shell's enter animation does apply a transform, which is a concern.

I realize since this app is essentially single-page, putting the backdrop on `body::before` works fine. I need to check the stacking context carefully though: since body itself has no positioning, its background propagates to the root canvas and paints below everything, including negative z-index elements, so a fixed pseudo-element on body with `z-index: -1` should still render correctly above that canvas background.

Now I need to make sure `.nova-app-shell` becomes transparent since I'm moving its background image into this fixed layer, and check whether the boot loader and `.studio-active-empty` styles need adjustment too. I'm also wondering whether to force compositing on the fixed layer with `transform: translateZ(0)` or `will-change` for smoother rendering.

In wide mode the document itself doesn't scroll since panels scroll internally, so the fixed layer never needs repainting there anyway; only normal mode matters. I'll settle on `will-change: transform` over `translateZ(0)`, and consider whether a simple pseudo-element on body versus an actual backdrop div in the layout is cleaner for adding the aurora effect.

For the layered background I'll combine gradients, the image, and a grain texture from an SVG feTurbulence filter into one composited element painted once, tiling the grain at a small size like 160px so rasterization stays cheap on resize.

Grain is worth keeping for that frosted, tactile refinement, but I'll keep opacity low around 0.035–0.05 since translucent glass panels will attenuate it further. Now I'm thinking through the glass panel styling itself—sidebar, workspace frame, studio panels, cards—making them more translucent with a subtle diagonal gradient so the color beneath shows through more.

Since the backdrop is already soft and pre-blurred, translucency alone reads as frosted without needing real blur, except where panels overlap scrolling content (like sticky headers)—those need actual blur or higher opacity to avoid messy overlap. I'm also adding a soft white border, a faint outer hairline shadow for definition, and an inset specular highlight along the top edge to give it that glassy sheen.

For depth, I'm layering multiple soft shadows at increasing blur radii and opacity to create a sense of elevation. Since these shadows are painted once per panel's layer and don't repaint during inner scrolling, performance stays fine—but for hover elevation transitions, I should animate opacity of a pseudo-element carrying the bigger shadow rather than transitioning the shadow property directly, since that avoids repainting the whole card every frame.

Now I'm planning where to apply real backdrop-filter blur: dropdown menus, select popups, tooltips, dialog content, toasts, and canvas toolbar controls, using a semi-transparent color-mix background paired with backdrop-filter for that frosted glass effect.

For buttons, I'm designing a primary style with an emerald-to-teal gradient, inner highlight, and colored glow shadow, plus outline buttons redesigned as glass pills with translucent backgrounds and hairline borders. I'm also considering whether to replace the generic `transition-all` in the shared button component with an explicit property list, since it's a shadcn file I'm free to modify.

I'm mapping out remaining touches: translucent inputs with inset shadows and emerald focus rings, frosted segmented tabs with raised glass pills for active states, thin translucent scrollbars app-wide, refined typography with font-feature settings and letter-spacing, and minimal staggered entrance motion building on the existing `nova-desktop-enter` animation.

Now I'm designing dark mode with a deep forest/ink background and emerald-teal aurora glows, using subtle white-alpha glass surfaces and borders rather than just darkening the existing image. I'm also adding accessibility fallbacks for reduced transparency, missing backdrop-filter support, and reduced motion.

Then I'm checking contrast ratios for text over translucent surfaces—confirming dark text on light backgrounds works, but muted text needs to be darkened slightly (to something like #5a6d62) to reliably maintain WCAG AA when surfaces get more translucent or backdrops darken.

I'm also weighing whether to add automatic performance detection—like checking hardwareConcurrency or deviceMemory to disable backdrop-filters on low-end devices—but that heuristic adds complexity. A user-facing toggle for effects intensity would be nice but requires touching the large SettingsModal and persistence logic, which feels like scope creep beyond what was actually requested.

Actually, there's a cleaner path: Windows' OS-level "transparency effects" setting maps to the `prefers-reduced-transparency` media query, which Chromium supports starting around version 118, and since Electron 43 ships Chromium 140+, this should just work natively for users who've disabled transparency in their system settings.

Now I'm scanning for existing performance hazards that conflict with the goal — several components use per-item backdrop blur (ImageHoverActions, AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, PromptGallerySubcomponents, AttachmentChips), and the prompt gallery in particular could render dozens or hundreds of blurred hover buttons, which risks scroll jank if they're always mounted rather than conditionally rendered.

Even elements with opacity 0 can still trigger compositing when backdrop-filter is applied, since Chromium creates a render surface per backdrop-filter element regardless of visible opacity, and each surface adds an offscreen texture and draw pass whenever content shifts. In a scrolling list, this means many render surfaces get redrawn every frame, so swapping those per-item blurs for a solid translucent fallback would meaningfully cut GPU cost.

For the full-screen editor overlays using heavy blur, I want to check whether they sit above actively repainting canvases -- since those cases would damage the backdrop-filter render pass on every canvas update, making the blur costly precisely where content changes most.

I'll remove those invisible blurs since they're a low-risk, targeted change that frees up performance budget for the more visible glass effects elsewhere — it directly serves the "no performance impact" goal. That said, I should reconsider full-screen overlays like the fullscreen image viewer and WorkspaceHeader's image viewer separately, since backdrop-blur there might actually be visible and worth keeping.

I should also flag the 95% opacity editors as clear waste to address. Next I want to go through the actual component files—WorkspaceHeader, WorkspaceModeTabs, Toast, ConfirmDialog—plus the workbench and history card JSX to check their class usage, and check useWideMode to see which mode is default so I know what most users see.

The picture is clear enough to set direction. Live `backdrop-blur-sm` is already on repeated list items: the hover buttons on every history card, gallery card and chat image. That hurts scrolling on long lists. Several full-screen editors also pair `bg-background/95` with a blur, which costs performance while the 95%-opaque background hides nearly all of it. I'll check the shell components, the wide-mode default and build side effects next.
