payload.text:
I'm taking stock of what I've reviewed so far in this Next.js/Tailwind/shadcn Electron project—the globals.css file and several UI primitive components—and figuring out what to check next.

WorkspaceShell, Toast, ConfirmDialog, WorkspaceModeTabs, and useWideMode are done. I've noted the build output is gitignored, found the Chromium binary path for testing, and confirmed wide mode defaults to false with desktop runtime detection in place.

Now I'm planning to review WorkspaceHeader, CompletedJobCard, HistoryJobList, and ImageGenerationWorkbench to understand class usage patterns, since AgentChatWorkspace is the default tab and these components will shape the visual design decisions I need to make before building a baseline.

Given the size of these files, I'm leaning toward grepping for className patterns rather than reading them fully, and thinking that taking baseline screenshots first would give me faster visual context than combing through 50KB of source. That means I need to decide how to serve the app for screenshots -- either spin up a lightweight static server against the existing build output, or run a fresh build with the desktop flag to get current source reflected.

Running the actual backend feels risky since it could spin up polling jobs, websockets, or outbound calls to configured providers on startup, so I'd rather avoid touching `.env` or launching the full server and just stick with a plain static server for now.

For a realistic populated view, I'm thinking about seeding IndexedDB with job data, and I should check job-store.ts for the storage format, plus look into whether the prompt gallery pulls remote data or needs a password. Then I'll spin up a Next dev server on a spare port in the background so HMR picks up CSS changes while I iterate on screenshots.

For the actual perf comparison, I want to build production baseline and after versions rather than relying on dev mode. I need to use NOVA_DESKTOP_BUILD=1 when building to skip PWA/service worker generation — otherwise a registered service worker could cache stale assets and contaminate the before/after comparison between runs.

Since `out` is gitignored and rebuilding it just reflects current source, I'll copy the baseline `out` to temp storage, then rebuild again after my changes, accepting the extra build time as a cost of accurate benchmarking.

Now I'm planning a Node-based CDP harness stored outside the repo that launches headless Chrome with a fixed debugging port, opens the page, sets a device metrics override for a fixed viewport, and toggles wide mode via localStorage before capturing screenshots across several states — default agent tab, image-generation tab, wide mode, dark theme, and open dialogs or dropdowns.

I'm also weighing a scroll performance test and a lightweight static server to serve the built output directory. I'd rather avoid installing Playwright since Node already has a stable global WebSocket, so the raw CDP approach keeps things dependency-free — I still need to check runtime-storage.ts and job-store.ts for proper state seeding, and confirm how desktop-bridge detects the desktop runtime via window.novaDesktop.

For desktop-specific styling, I could inject a fake window.novaDesktop object before page load so isDesktopRuntime resolves true, since the project supports both a web (Docker) build and an Electron desktop build and I want both to render correctly. I should read through desktop-bridge.ts and runtime-storage.ts next, then move into concretely designing the solution now that I understand the structure well enough.

I'm leaning toward a "Mint Aurora Glass" direction — preserving the brand's green identity but styled like modern OS glass (visionOS/macOS Sonoma-ish), with a composited background of a blurred nature image plus soft aurora glows and grain, three tiers of glass surfaces (chrome, panels, floating elements) defined through CSS variables with increasing opacity and blur, and subtle inner highlights along the top edges for depth.

I'm also considering layered soft shadows tinted green-gray instead of pure black, an emerald gradient accent for primary buttons with a glow effect, and a slight bump to the base radius token from 0.625rem to 0.75rem to soften the overall look, weighing how that uniform change would cascade through all the rounded-* utility classes.

Now I'm setting performance guardrails: real backdrop-filter blur should only apply to floating layers like popovers, menus, tooltips, dialogs, and toasts, plus fixed toolbars—never on repeated list items or large scrolling panels, which should instead use a faux-glass effect over a pre-blurred fixed background for efficiency.

I'm also making sure hover effects only animate transform and opacity, shadows fade via pseudo-element opacity, and adding fallbacks for browsers without backdrop-filter support and for reduced-transparency or reduced-motion preferences. For the per-item hover chips, I'm swapping the blurred white overlay for a more opaque black background so the chips stay legible over images without needing per-item blur.

But before finalizing, I want to check whether these hover chips are actually always present in the DOM (with opacity toggled) or only rendered conditionally on hover — that changes whether there's a real performance concern, so I should look at the ImageHoverActions code to confirm.

So the blur cost during hover is likely small, though I should check whether always-visible elements like AttachmentChips labels actually need blur given their near-opaque background already masks most of it. I want to look at the actual files before deciding, keeping changes minimal but thorough since the user wants a careful pass without hurting performance—my plan is to standardize glass usage so real blur is only applied where it visually matters.

Now I'm checking the full-screen overlay editors using near-opaque backdrop blur—since the background is mostly static while these editors are open, the blur there is largely wasted, though I need to confirm nothing behind them keeps animating.

But if something behind the overlay, like a shimmering loading card, is animating infinitely, the backdrop damage gets recomputed every frame even though it's mostly invisible under the near-opaque overlay. I'm trying to trace how Chromium's compositor expands damage regions for backdrop filters in that case—whether the whole element bounds get reprocessed or just the damaged rect clipped to the blur radius.

So dropping the blur from those 95%-opaque overlays is a clear win with essentially no visual downside, since removing blur just means the tiny 5% show-through becomes sharp instead of blurred, which shouldn't matter much on typical backgrounds.

For the full-screen image viewers with 80% opacity and blur, the frosted look is intentional and part of the glass language, so I'll keep it even though it costs a per-frame blur when animated content sits behind it. For HistoryImagePreview's near-black 90% overlay, the blur is basically invisible at that opacity, so I'm weighing whether it's even worth keeping there.

I'll leave the image preview overlay as-is rather than over-engineering it, and shift focus to the dialog overlay — considering whether to keep it flat black or add a subtle blur so the frosted popup reads well against it.

I'm not certain whether the browser caches the blurred backdrop texture across those few frames, but even without caching, six frames of full-screen blur during the fade-in is negligible on GPU rendering. The real performance risk would be continuous backdrop-filter use, like scrolling content behind a blurred element.

Actually, I recall that in Chromium's compositor, any damage from animated content behind a backdrop-filter (like a spinner or sweep animation on a waiting card) forces the entire blurred region to redraw each frame, not just the small changed area, because damage gets expanded to the backdrop-filter bounds. So a tiny spinner behind a full-screen blur could trigger 60fps full-screen re-blurring, which is the real perf trap—though at typical resolutions this is still likely under half a millisecond per frame on a discrete GPU.

Given the performance concern, I'm leaning toward a flat, unblurred scrim for the overlay and reserving real backdrop blur for the dialog itself, since it covers a much smaller area than the viewport. Any animated content behind it would only trigger re-blur within that smaller popup region, which is a reasonable compromise, and on mobile the popup can just use an opaque background instead of blur since it goes full-screen there.

I'm also thinking about the settings modal specifically — it's a large component with internal scrolling, and I need to consider whether scrolling content inside the popup forces the backdrop-filter render pass to recompute, since the blurred backdrop and the element's contents are composited together.

Since Chromium doesn't cache the filtered backdrop separately, every scroll frame likely re-blurs the visible area behind the dialog. For a ~900x700 scroll area at high DPR with a 16px blur, that could add a few milliseconds of GPU work per frame on weaker integrated graphics, risking occasional dropped frames during scroll.

So the safer approach is to differentiate by dialog type: settings-style dialogs with internal scrolling should stick with a high-opacity faux-glass surface rather than real blur, while smaller dialogs like confirmations or quick prompts can afford real blur since their content rarely scrolls. I should check how `DialogContent` is actually used across the app and whether large dialogs override its width, since a shared component serving both cases needs a consistent rule -- perhaps defaulting to a high-opacity glass tint (around 90-92%) with only a modest blur radius, so the opacity itself does most of the visual work and the blur cost stays low.

Dialogs get real blur with ~84-88% opacity since higher opacity offsets legibility concerns for larger surfaces. For the settings modal with scrolling content, I'm weighing whether continuous backdrop recalculation is actually a problem — precedent from Linear's command palette and Apple's sticky nav suggests scrolling backdrop-filter is acceptable on modern hardware even in the worst case.

Given the explicit performance concern, the safest approach is a high-opacity glass surface with no blur for large scrolling dialogs, and a flat tinted scrim for the overlay, though I need another way to preserve the frosted feel without blur.

Since the overlay's backdrop hasn't changed and the overlay itself has zero damage, Chromium shouldn't need to redraw it — the root pass just recomposites the cached overlay texture with the dialog on top, though I'm second-guessing whether render pass textures actually persist across frames without explicit caching, since viz's damage-based skipping still needs that texture available to composite into the dirty region.

There's likely a `CanSkipRenderPass()` check that skips drawing when a pass has no damage and was cached, tied to cc's `cache_render_surface` flag, but I'm not confident where that flag actually gets set. Since I can't resolve this through reasoning alone, I should just measure it directly with the harness — checking frame times with a dialog open versus closed.

Let me settle on a conservative design instead: overlays get a flat tinted scrim with zero blur, while dialog popups use a high-opacity background plus real backdrop blur and saturation. The tricky part is how that interacts with scrolling content behind or inside the popup, which might force per-frame reblurring.

To decide, I want actual measurements rather than guessing—build both versions and compare scroll-in-dialog frame times with and without blur, dropping it if there's a real regression. Since headless software rendering isn't representative of real GPU performance, I'm considering running headed Chromium with GPU enabled, possibly positioned off-screen, to get numbers that actually reflect the user's machine.

That renderer string would tell me whether it's SwiftShader or real hardware GPU. I'm also weighing the Chromium version behind chromium-1228 and Electron 43, and thinking about how Tailwind v4's font stack renders with the Geist font variable through preflight defaults.

I'm tracing whether an undefined CSS variable reference cascades as invalid all the way up through the fallback chain, which determines whether the body actually inherits a broken font-family or falls back to the default sans-serif stack.

If it falls back, `ui-sans-serif` isn't supported in Chromium so it drops to `system-ui`, which on Windows resolves to Segoe UI for Latin text but pulls in Microsoft YaHei UI for CJK glyphs depending on locale.

Since body's own font-family declaration references the same invalid custom property with no fallback, the whole rule becomes invalid at computed-value time, so body's font-family unsets and inherits the system-ui stack from html — meaning the current rendering effectively defaults to system fonts. I'm now considering whether to define an explicit fallback font stack rather than relying on this inheritance behavior, since there's no bundled variable font to use as a stronger default.

This means code blocks might actually render in the sans font instead of monospace, since if Tailwind's `@theme inline` never emits `--font-mono` as a real property, `var(--font-mono)` resolves to nothing and the whole font-family declaration falls back to inheriting the surrounding text style.

Fixing this globally by defining real font stacks for `--font-sans` and `--font-mono` in `@theme` seems like a solid, verifiable improvement — I can confirm the bug via `getComputedStyle` in a test harness. Beyond that, I'm noting other polish items: keeping lucide icons, adding subtle press/hover micro-interactions with transform-based lifts, glowing focus rings, and a custom `::selection` color.

Now I'm working through smaller theming details — setting a caret color tied to the primary color, applying thin overlay-style scrollbars globally using the standard `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` properties (well-supported in modern Chromium), and refining the color palette itself. I'm reconsidering the light theme's background, foreground, and primary green tones to improve contrast while keeping the brand feel.

I'm checking actual contrast ratios for the green primary against white text — the current #43b957 fails WCAG AA badly at ~2.6:1, so I'm testing darker candidates like #1f9d55, #15803d, and #16a34a, along with a possible gradient option, to find something that hits at least 4.5:1 for button labels while still feeling modern and on-brand.

Finishing the luminance calculation gives contrast ratio of 3.92 against white—short of the 4.5 target, so I need to try a darker candidate like #0f8a.

Working through #0f8a53's luminance, I get contrast around 4.39, which is very close but still not quite 4.5, so I'm testing another variant, #0d8450.

Its contrast comes out to 4.74, which passes. But this deep emerald shade is darker than the current brand green #43b957.

I'm also checking whether using dark text like #0c2416 on the lighter brand green button would give sufficient contrast, working through the luminance calculation for each channel of #43b957.

That passes, good. Dark mode already handles this fine with dark text on the primary color. For light mode, I'm leaning toward a deeper emerald with white text for primary buttons, matching the modern high-contrast style of apps like Linear or Vercel, while keeping the brand mint green for backgrounds and accents. A deeper green would also improve link text contrast when used for text/icons on light backgrounds.

That gives ~4.36 against white, just under the 4.5 threshold, so I'm testing a slightly darker variant #0c8259 to see if it clears the bar.

Both contrast checks pass, confirming #0b7a54 works as the primary emerald tone. I'm now checking whether the button gradient's lighter endpoint, #12935f, still holds sufficient white-text contrast — coming out around 3.91, a bit lower but likely acceptable for larger button text.

Rather than obsess further, I'll settle on a gradient from #0c8259 to #096b4c, since the lighter stop clears 4.5 contrast comfortably, giving a clean deep emerald-teal look, paired with a soft mint glow shadow at low opacity. I'm also mapping out everywhere `--primary` gets applied — buttons, icons, rings, borders, tab indicators, sliders, switches, badges, and tint variants — to make sure the new color choice holds up across all these uses.

Now I'm thinking about `--accent`, which currently renders as a saturated green fill with white text for hover states in dropdowns. That feels dated compared to the subtler tint-based highlight style modern UIs use, so I'm weighing whether to shift it to a soft mint tint with dark text instead, and checking where else `bg-accent` gets used before committing to that change.

For dark mode, I'm double-checking contrast ratios for a fresher emerald-mint primary color against dark text to make sure readability holds up.

Now I'm turning to the glass surfaces in light mode—checking whether a semi-transparent white overlay on the mint bokeh backdrop still gives enough contrast for text, since the background image has both light bokeh areas and some darker green leaves.

Checking contrast ratio for the current muted color against the light surface gives about 4.37, which falls short of the 4.5 threshold I need.

So I'm darkening the muted tone slightly to something like #56695e to fix that. For the dark mode glass panels, I'm designing a darkened backdrop with a multiply blend and layering translucent gradient panels with soft borders and inset highlights, plus planning aurora-style radial glows in both light and dark modes using mint, aqua, and warm accent colors positioned at the corners over the background image.

Now I'm generating the SVG grain overlay code...

Rasterization cost is trivial for such a small tile, so I'm placing the noise backdrop on a fixed, pointer-events-none pseudo-element behind body content, making sure the app shell's own background becomes transparent so this layer shows through while the glass frame keeps its own translucent surface.

One concern: ConfirmDialog locks scroll by setting body position to fixed, and since position:fixed always creates a new stacking context regardless of z-index, that means once the dialog opens, body itself becomes a stacking context — I need to check whether the backdrop pseudo-element still renders correctly behind everything in that scenario.

I'm also checking whether the desktop shell's entrance animation, which uses a transform, creates a containing block issue for fixed descendants — but since the backdrop isn't nested inside the shell, that's not a problem. Now I'm looking at how overflow-x hidden on both html and body interacts with the implicit overflow-y auto behavior, since setting only one axis to hidden can force the other axis into a scrollable state and potentially turn body into its own scroll container.

This shouldn't disrupt the fixed backdrop element though, since only transform, filter, contain, or will-change actually create new containing blocks for fixed positioning — a scrollable ancestor alone doesn't matter. I'm also considering whether the browser will composite this fixed pseudo-element into its own layer, especially since will-change: transform essentially guarantees that treatment, sized to the full viewport.

The pseudo-element backdrop approach is safest cross-browser, so I'll go with that. Now I'm checking the wide-mode desktop layout classes—sidebar and workspace glass surfaces, plus the studio panel classes that need to be applied in the image generation workbench and history components—and working through how the card background opacity interacts with the `bg-card/95` utility.

I realize translucent cards nested on already-translucent panels create that layered glass effect intentionally, but I need to check for a ghosting risk: absolute-positioned dropdowns using `bg-card` instead of `bg-popover` could let background text bleed through more visibly if I increase transparency further.

So rather than lowering `--card` alpha further, I'll keep it around 0.74-0.8 and apply richer glass styling specifically to top-level panels via semantic classes. I want to check WorkspaceHeader's normal-mode variant and the ImageGenerationWorkbench wrapper, and grep for `nova-`/`studio-` class hooks in the TSX files to see what's already available before writing the implementation plan with TodoWrite covering baseline screenshots, perf numbers, and the token/backdrop/glass rollout.

My plan is to update primitives like button, input, dropdown, dialog, tabs, badge and similar components, then move to shell components—Toast, ConfirmDialog, WorkspaceModeTabs, header—cleaning up wasted blur usage for performance, then verify everything with a full build, lint, tests, and screenshot comparisons across light/dark/wide/desktop modes. Before that, let me grep for `bg-accent` and `text-accent` usage alongside the earlier searches.
继续摸底：先确认高频样式钩子（`nova-*`/`studio-*`）在组件里的分布、`accent` 色的用途，以及桌面端检测逻辑，这决定改 token 时的影响面。

payload.text:
Continuing from where I left off - I've done enough exploration, so now I should organize a plan: build a todo list, capture a baseline production build with screenshots and performance metrics, implement the changes, rebuild and capture after-metrics, then run lint and tests. Let me start by writing out the todo list.

Some key issues I've noticed: the stack is Next.js 16 static export with Tailwind v4 and shadcn using base-nova style, running in an Electron desktop shell. The globals.css defines a "fresh glass" mint palette, and there's a pre-blurred background image on the app shell that scrolls with content and may be stretched incorrectly. I also spotted that `--font-geist-sans` is never defined, so the font falls back to an inherited value, and `--font-mono` is likely broken too, meaning code blocks may not render as monospace. Additionally, the per-item hover action overlays always mount their backdrop-blur elements in the DOM even at opacity 0 on medium+ screens, which means every history or gallery card carries several always-rendered backdrop-filter elements — a real performance cost since each one creates its own render surface, even if the parent's opacity is zero.

Actually, thinking through Chromium's rendering pipeline more carefully — when a parent has opacity 0 and no active animation, Chromium's compositor typically skips drawing that subtree entirely via the "is_drawn" optimization in the effect tree, so the backdrop-filter render surfaces inside wouldn't actually be drawn at rest. Since there's no running animation on the overlay when idle, just a `transition-all`, this suggests the hover buttons aren't a significant performance issue while at rest, though the composited layers still add some paint cost overall.

With virtualization, mounted card count stays bounded, though I'm unsure whether the prompt gallery is virtualized too. The cleanest fix is swapping the per-item hover blur chips for a solid translucent dark chip with a ring instead — same glassy look without layers or blur cost, and I'll just edit the class strings directly rather than introducing a shared class.

Revisiting the user's ask: modernize the UI with glassmorphism where possible, without hurting performance. Since the background is already pre-blurred and static, a translucent panel layered on top looks visually identical to real backdrop-filter blur but is much cheaper, so faking the frosted effect on the main panels is the right call.

Real backdrop-filter should only go on floating elements like menus, tooltips, and dialogs where there's actual content behind them to blur. I'm also considering native Windows acrylic via Electron's backgroundMaterial, but since the target is likely Windows 10, it wouldn't apply and would complicate the design, so I'll skip it or just mention it briefly as an optional future enhancement.

I'm also reconsidering the shell's `background-size: cover` — on tall pages it forces the pre-blurred image to scale enormously, which wastes raster work as the user scrolls. Moving that background to a fixed, separately composited layer would let it raster once and just composite on scroll, which is more efficient.

Now I'm setting up a way to measure the actual performance impact. I want to build a baseline first, but I need to be careful about whether the build includes the service worker registration, since a stale cached bundle could skew before/after comparisons.

To avoid that, I'll use a fresh browser profile directory for each test run so there's no cache carryover, and build with the desktop flag set to skip touching the PWA service worker files. Since the build itself takes a couple minutes, I'll run it in the background and poll for completion rather than blocking synchronously.

Once built, I'll copy the exported output into a temp directory and spin up a lightweight static file server on separate ports for baseline versus after screenshots. The app's API calls to Nova endpoints will simply 404 against the static server, which matches how earlier testing was done, though I'm now wondering whether I should stub out JSON responses for the config endpoint so the UI doesn't show error banners that could throw off the screenshot comparison.

For the harness itself, I'm weighing whether to launch headless Chrome with remote debugging enabled at a fixed window size, versus running headed but positioned off-screen so it uses real GPU rendering instead of software rendering — headless mode on Windows typically falls back to SwiftShader, which would skew performance numbers for a fair stress test.

I'm also considering that Windows' native window occlusion tracking might throttle an off-screen headed window as if it were covered, so I'd need flags like `--disable-features=CalculateNativeWinOcclusion` plus `--disable-backgrounding-occluded-windows` to keep it rendering normally. That's probably overkill though — I'll start with the simpler headless approach first.

Actually, thinking about what's most useful to the user, since they care about their actual Electron app on their real machine with their GPU, a headed Chromium instance is the closest match to real conditions. I'll try running it off-screen with occlusion disabled, and fall back to headless with GPU flags if rAF throttling turns out to be an issue — a brief taskbar flash for ~30 seconds is a minor tradeoff worth mentioning.

I should also verify whether new headless mode actually enables hardware GPU rendering with the right flags, or if it defaults to software rendering via SwiftShader unless explicitly overridden — I'll check `SystemInfo.getInfo` output to confirm.

For metrics, I'm planning to capture frame timing during a smooth scroll (fps, dropped frames), count of live blur/backdrop-filter surfaces via DOM scan, and layout/style/task/script duration from `Performance.getMetrics`.

I'm also considering paint timing but deciding rAF-based frame timing plus CPU task duration is sufficient, along with first-contentful-paint and boot time via `performance.getEntriesByType('paint')` and rough CSS bundle size comparisons.

Now I'm sketching test scenarios: wide mode with a seeded history of ~60 completed image jobs to scroll through, and possibly a prompt-gallery scenario if it's easy to enable.

I also want to check the agent tab (not scroll-heavy by default), settings dialog scrolling, and dropdown/select screenshots. For seeding history data, I need to dig into job-store.ts and useWorkspaceJobs to understand how jobs and images are persisted—likely IndexedDB via localforage—so I should read job-store.ts and image-db.ts to figure out the schema and whether I can generate and store fake images via canvas-to-blob in page.evaluate.

Since the day-group virtualization renders every job card in a group at once, spreading jobs across multiple days better tests that behavior than dumping them all on one day, so I'll seed around 80 jobs across roughly 10 days, about 8 per day, to mimic realistic usage while stressing the virtualization.

Now I'm building the benchmark harness script itself — a small static server that serves the app's files while returning 404s for API/WebSocket calls, keeping that behavior consistent with what the app already handles when there's no backend, and mapping URL paths to files including trailing-slash index resolution and content-type detection by extension.

I also need a Chrome launcher that spawns chrome.exe and connects to its DevTools endpoint, plus a minimal CDP client over WebSocket that flattens sessions via Target.createTarget/attachToTarget so I can send page-level commands with a sessionId. Then for the scenario runner I'm enabling Page and Runtime domains, overriding device metrics, and injecting scripts on new document load to preset localStorage theme values and stub any desktop bridge the app expects before its own scripts run.

For seeding, I navigate to the origin, evaluate a script that writes 'nova-jobs' to localStorage and populates the 'nova-image-db' IndexedDB store with generated images, then reload. The tricky part is that in desktop mode, storage goes through a fake bridge instead of localStorage directly, so I'm considering backing that fake config with localStorage and implementing records.list by reading from the same IndexedDB, or just keeping an in-memory seeded array for the fake bridge to serve.

I can implement records.list to pull entries from the same IDB store asynchronously, reusing the web-mode seeding for desktop mode too, so job saves go through the fake config backed by localStorage while image records come from that shared IDB read.

Now I need to figure out what else the desktop startup path calls—likely records.list for other namespaces, file reads, S3 config, and updater status/subscription methods. I'm building a fallback Proxy that returns sensible defaults for unknown calls, but explicit cases like onStatus need to return an actual unsubscribe function rather than a generic promise.

Still writing platform stubs...

Adding a stub for opening the data directory and finishing the fallback object. I'm noting that desktop runtime detection relies on the presence of window.novaDesktop, checked alongside a mounted state, and confirming this is fine—the desktop app's frontend calls the local backend API rather than routing through this stub.

Given the user is on Windows with desktop packaging, I should verify changes in desktop mode too, since desktop-specific shell CSS applies at wider viewports. I'll plan to capture screenshots for each scenario, save them to a bench directory, and view them as images—though I'm wary that viewing many large screenshots could eat up a lot of context.

For performance measurement per scenario, I need to wait for the app to be ready (boot loader gone, images loaded) and then identify the right scroll target—likely the studio history list element, since it has its own overflow behavior distinct from the window scroll.

For measuring, I'm setting up a rAF-driven loop that programmatically sets scrollTop each frame, tracking frame timing deltas over about 4 seconds to compute average FPS, p95 frame time, and jank counts. I realize this approach captures mostly main-thread cost since the scroll is driven synchronously rather than via native touch/wheel input.

A better approach would use CDP's `Input.synthesizeScrollGesture` to drive real compositor-threaded scrolling like an actual user gesture, paired with the in-page rAF recorder to still capture frame deltas without forcing main-thread work per frame.

But rAF only tracks main-thread frames, so compositor-dropped frames could slip past it—I'd really need trace events like `PipelineReporter` (with states like STATE_PRESENTED_ALL vs STATE_DROPPED) from categories such as `benchmark,cc,viz,gpu,devtools.timeline`, which is essentially what DevTools' own Frames track relies on.

Parsing these traces properly means grabbing `Tracing.dataCollected` events, isolating `PipelineReporter` entries with async-begin phase and checking the frame reporter state to compute a dropped-frame percentage—rigorous, but fragile across Chrome versions and potentially time-consuming to debug. A middle-ground approach might combine the rAF method during programmatic scrolling with deltas from `Performance.getMetrics` for things like layout duration.

I'm also considering counting live backdrop-filter elements in the DOM at rest for each scenario as a structural metric to include in the report—showing how many active blur surfaces exist, which is simpler and more directly useful than deep GPU profiling.

I should also compare CSS bundle sizes before and after to confirm the change didn't bloat the stylesheet, and figure out how to programmatically open the settings dialog, likely by searching for a button with the "设置" label via the DOM.

Once open, I'll find the scrollable element with the largest overflow inside `.nova-app-settings` and scroll it, though without an API key it may not be tall enough to scroll — so I'll just skip that step if it isn't scrollable, and still capture a screenshot of the settings dialog. Then I'll move on to opening the "随机图片" dropdown in the sidebar to grab another screenshot.

I could also hover a result card and capture a clipped screenshot to check the hover chip styling.

Now I'm sketching out the scenario list: each test runs twice, once as baseline and once after changes, covering things like the default web light-theme view, the wide-mode image-gen workbench with 80 seeded jobs (checking screenshots, hover states, scroll performance, and backdrop counts), and more variants to come.

I'm also planning dark-theme and normal-mode versions of the image-gen tab tests, a desktop-bridge wide-mode scenario checking dropdowns and settings dialogs, and at least one dark desktop screenshot. I'm noting that switching tabs requires a real click on the tab role element, and that wide mode depends on a localStorage flag plus viewport width, which I can set via an init script or the fake bridge config.

For theming, I'll set the 'theme' key in localStorage explicitly rather than relying on system preference, and also emulate prefers-color-scheme to stay consistent. I'm estimating each scenario takes 15-20 seconds with seeding, reload, image wait, screenshot, and two perf runs, totaling roughly two minutes for six scenarios.

I'll generate around 80 jobs spread across 10 days with 1-2 images each, mixing in a few failed jobs to render error cards while skipping waiting jobs since those without a serverTaskId become failed on reload anyway. For images, I'm planning to generate them in-page using canvas at a 512×384 resolution.

I'll stick with PNG since Chrome sniffs the actual format anyway, and go with 480×360 smooth gradients plus a few shapes to keep things simple. These gradient PNGs won't compress great since every pixel differs, so estimating around 200KB each across 120 images puts total storage near 24MB, which should still be manageable.

Actually, I'll reduce this to 12 distinct images reused round-robin across jobs, keeping generation fast while still representing realistic memory usage since real generated images can be 1-4MB PNGs anyway. Fairness between before/after comparisons doesn't depend on exact size, and since identical data URLs get cached by Chrome, reuse won't distort the benchmark.

Each job needs an id, alternating mode between text-to-image and image-to-image, a realistic bilingual prompt, output settings like size/temperature/aspect ratio/model, and a created date. I'll also mirror this into IndexedDB's images store, including reference thumbnails for image-to-image jobs, and set up localStorage's job list accordingly.

Since no API key exists, forms will render in a disabled state with a configure-key banner — that's consistent across runs, so I'll leave it as is rather than faking key storage. I also need to make sure the seeding script opens the IndexedDB at version 2 with the same schema the app uses, running after the app has already created the stores so I'm just appending records rather than upgrading.

For the desktop scenario, the fake bridge reads image records from the same IndexedDB, so I need to open that connection early enough in the init script, before the app's own scripts run. Since baseline and after runs use different ports (and thus different origins) with fresh user-data-dirs, each one needs its own seeding pass — storage won't carry over between them.

To reduce variance from thermal drift or timing, I think it's better to run both labels within a single browser session, alternating between them (A, B, A, B) and reporting the median across a few repeats. I'll design the harness to accept a list of labeled targets with their ports/roots, then run each scenario interleaved. Since the "after" build doesn't exist yet, the harness should support running just the baseline now to capture reference screenshots, then later support both baseline and after together for the real comparison.

Writing Chrome flags...

Actually, disabling frame rate limit and vsync gives an uncapped frame rate, which turns frame time into a direct measure of render cost — more sensitive for catching regressions than a vsync-capped 60fps that masks differences. I'll go with uncapped for sensitivity.

I'll drive the scroll position by elapsed time rather than frame count, so the path stays consistent regardless of frame rate, and report average frame time, p95, and the count of frames exceeding 16.7ms as a janky-frame proxy. I need to verify headless mode actually honors the unthrottled BeginFrameSource with these flags before relying on it.

For GPU detection I'll query SystemInfo.getInfo() to pull the device string and feature status flags like gpu_compositing. For the WebSocket client, Node 24's built-in browser-compatible WebSocket should handle large base64 screenshot payloads without hitting payload size limits.

I'm also weighing whether Chrome's DevTools protocol will reject connections due to Origin header checks — Chrome 111+ requires --remote-allow-origins=* for such connections, so I should add that flag. Since it's bound to 127.0.0.1 with a short-lived temporary profile, this seems acceptable security-wise, though I'm still thinking through the local-page-connection risk with wildcard origins allowed.

I'll simulate mouse events for clicks by dispatching moved, pressed, and released events through CDP. For readiness detection, I'll wait until the boot loader is gone, the document is complete, and all visible images finish loading, with timeouts guarding each wait so nothing hangs indefinitely. I also want to capture console errors and exceptions per scenario to catch any runtime issues like hydration errors introduced by my changes.

I'll count exceptions and console.error messages separately from expected 404 API errors, comparing baseline versus after runs, and write everything into a timestamped JSON report alongside per-target screenshots. I'll also print a summary table to stdout, use dedicated ports for the static servers and Chrome debugging, and stage temporary scripts in a scratch directory.

I'm weighing whether to clean up the bench directory afterward per the cleanup instructions, or preserve screenshots so the user can visually compare the redesign — maybe by embedding compact before/after thumbnails as base64 JPEGs in a small HTML viewer rather than full-size images, which would be too heavy.

I'll save before/after screenshots in a gitignored output folder as a deliverable for review, confirming backdrop-filter renders fine in headless CDP screenshots. Now I'm writing the benchmarking harness script for capturing these screenshots.

Setting up harness script...

Still writing server logic...

I want to make sure the path stays within root by checking that the resolved file path starts with the root directory, guarding against `..` traversal attempts, then falls back to trying a `.html` extension if the plain path doesn't exist, before serving the file with the correct MIME type and error handling wrapped around the whole request.

For launching Chrome, I'm locating the Playwright-bundled Chromium executable under the local app data directory and building a headless launch with a specific remote debugging port, isolated user data directory, and a set of flags to disable extensions, background networking, syncing, and other noise that could skew benchmark timing.

I'm then polling the `/json/version` endpoint after spawning the process to confirm Chrome is ready before proceeding, retrying for up to ten seconds. Now I'm writing a small CDP client class that wraps a WebSocket connection, tracking request IDs and pending promises so I can send commands and resolve them when matching responses arrive.

Adding the Page wrapper class...

Adding navigation and event-waiting logic...

Finishing the mouse event dispatch and adding a screenshot helper method. Now I'm defining scenario configurations for different viewport/theme/tab combinations to test.

I'm thinking through storage seeding strategy—since localStorage persists per origin across targets in the same browser context, I need each scenario's init script to run on its own new target page while sharing that underlying storage, but I have to watch out for scenarios that mutate stored state and affect later scenarios.

Writing seed generation script...

Adding gradient overlays...

Now I'm drafting the image prompts, starting with a misty bamboo path scene rendered with cinematic lighting.

Still generating benchmark job records...

Setting up IndexedDB storage...

I'm double-checking edge cases: undefined fields dropping correctly from JSON, the model name being valid, and how the desktop bridge variant reads jobs from runtime storage instead.

For theme initialization, I'm making sure the pre-page script sets localStorage theme and wide-mode flags before any page script runs, and defines the desktop bridge object when needed so the layout's theme-init logic picks up the right values consistently across scenarios.

Writing IndexedDB read logic...

Writing scroll performance script...

Computing frame timing stats...

I'm reconsidering the scroll animation parameters — with a fast single cycle over several seconds, peak speeds get quite extreme, which stresses rendering hard. I'll slow it down to a 6-second duration with one full down-and-up cycle, and also plan to capture performance metrics before and after the scroll test for comparison.

I also need to think about which element actually scrolls in normal (non-wide) mode — the window's scroll range might be small since content areas like the history panel have their own internal scroll container, so I should check the range first and skip if it's too small. There's also a subtlety with how `overflow-x: hidden` on html/body affects which element becomes the actual page scroller.

I'm writing a script to count elements currently visible in the viewport versus total elements on the page.

I'll check the font stack for body, html, and mono elements to confirm the font bug, and grab GPU info via SystemInfo at the browser level. For screenshots, I'll capture the full viewport at DPR 1, and for hover states I'll locate the media element, move the mouse to its center, wait briefly, then clip the screenshot to the card's bounding rect.

For the dropdown, I'll trigger it in wide mode, wait, then clip a screenshot around the popup content element with some padding before dismissing it with Escape. For settings, I'll click the '设置' button, screenshot the dialog, then find the scrollable container inside it to test scroll performance.

I'll skip tooltips, model-select dropdowns, and toasts since triggering them reliably is too fiddly, and I'll also skip the ConfirmDialog since it requires an extra step to open. For fairness in perf measurement, I'll interleave repeated runs across all targets rather than running them sequentially per target, capturing screenshots only on the first repetition, and I'm now thinking through the lifecycle of creating and attaching to each target with the right domains enabled.

I need to seed data once per origin before the first scenario runs there — spin up a page, navigate, seed, then close it. After that, each scenario run navigates, waits for readiness, optionally clicks a tab, waits for all images to finish loading plus a short settle delay for entrance animations, then screenshots and exercises hover/dropdown/settings before measuring perf and closing the target.

I'm also considering Chrome flags for consistent frame timing on perf runs, like disabling vsync and frame rate limiting, and thinking through GPU rendering backend choices (ANGLE vs SwiftShader) in headless mode along with window size and device pixel ratio settings that reflect realistic Windows display scaling, since backdrop-filter cost varies with DPR.

I'll keep screenshots at DPR 1 for smaller file sizes but bump DPR to 1.5 for perf stress testing, applying the metrics override after screenshots complete with a short wait before running perf. For output, I'm planning a simple summary table showing whether each scenario met its target.

I also need to sum the CSS file sizes under the static export directory, and I'm checking edge cases: default repeat count of 3, screenshot capture limited to viewport, and confirming the PWA/service worker registration is disabled so it won't interfere.

WebSocket connections to `/api/nova/ws` will just fail gracefully against my server since I'm not handling upgrade events, matching prior behavior. Now I'll write the harness file while polling the build progress in parallel.

While the build runs I'll write a dependency-free CDP benchmark script into a temp directory outside the repo. It starts a static server, drives the local Chromium, seeds 80 fake history jobs, takes screenshots, and measures scroll frame times and live `backdrop-filter` counts. The history list is virtualized per day group, so I spread the seeded jobs across 10 days to match real usage.

But mono font is the real bug: `.font-mono` resolves through `--font-mono` to `--font-geist-mono`, which is never defined, so the value is invalid and it inherits sans instead — meaning code blocks and metric text render in sans rather than monospace. I need to check whether `@theme inline` actually emits `--font-sans`/`--font-mono` as CSS variables on `:root`, or just inlines them directly into utilities, since that determines whether the fallback chain even makes sense.

But every scenario shows `errors=1` and a backdrop count of 0, so I'll check whether the history cards actually rendered.

I'm also puzzled by the backdrop count being 0/0 across scenarios—at rest there shouldn't be any backdrop-filter elements, but the hover chip buttons use backdrop-blur classes inside an overlay that becomes flex-displayed at this viewport width, so I'd expect a nonzero computed backdropFilter value even with opacity 0. I suspect this might be a quirk of how Tailwind v4's backdrop-blur utility computes its final value.

I notice the dropdown screenshot is missing from the list entirely, which suggests that click may have failed. The settings screenshot has an identical file size to the main screenshot, which strongly implies the settings dialog never actually opened. I want to check the report for any dropdown or settings errors and pull up a few screenshots to confirm—viewing images costs context, but it's necessary here, so I'll look at the wide gen light screenshots for web and desktop plus the agent light one.

I'm looking at the baseline hover and dropdown states: the history card uses its own gray overlay with expand icon rather than ImageHoverActions, plus a green border on hover, while the dropdown menu is currently a plain flat white popover. For the glass redesign, I'm planning to turn that dropdown into a frosted glass menu with blur applied.

Tracing where ImageHoverActions is actually used across the app (agent bubbles, gif review, image gallery, attachment chips, prompt gallery), its overlay is mounted in the DOM at rest for medium+ screens with opacity zero rather than being conditionally rendered, so its blurred buttons exist even when invisible. That explains why the gen tab's blur count came back at zero -- no messages or prompt gallery cards are currently on screen, even with keepMounted tabs -- and confirms this is expected given the empty state, not a bug. I'm now considering the real-world case where the prompt gallery has many cards, each mounting an always-present blurred overlay at opacity zero.

Rather than going deeper into cc internals, I realize I can just measure it empirically, but that requires deep data setup across galleries and messages. Since I'm planning to replace the per-item blur with a non-blur translucent chip anyway, removing backdrop-filter is strictly a reduction in cost, so I don't need to prove it's expensive to justify the change.

Over a dimmed image, a white/20 chip with a ring still reads as translucent even without blur — the icons stay legible since the black overlay dims the background enough. Blur just smooths the interior, so dropping it keeps the glass look while cutting cost, even though the user asked for more glass rather than less.

But I'm reconsidering scale: if the gallery has hundreds of cards and each renders up to five buttons, that's 500+ composited layers even hidden at opacity 0, which is real memory overhead worth avoiding for "不能影响整体使用性能."

That said, I want to actually measure this rather than assume — I could use the LayerTree domain to enable layer tracking and count composited layers directly, giving concrete evidence of compositing cost differences between designs.

This composited-layer count seems worth including as a concrete before/after signal for perf regression checks; I'll skip trying to test prompt gallery perf since that requires remote data, treating it as a pure reduction instead. Before writing CSS, I want to check a few more component pieces first—the hover overlay in CompletedJobCard, the header layout in WorkspaceHeader, the top panel in ImageGenerationWorkbench, the workspace wrapper in AgentChatWorkspace, and the header in HistoryJobList.

I'm weighing whether to delegate this reading to a subagent versus doing it myself, but decide reading targeted line ranges directly is safer to avoid losing detail through a summary. What I really need to pin down is the normal-mode, non-wide layout structure.

In normal mode, the shell is nested frame containers with rounded corners and a glass-surface-soft override, wrapping regular header/tabs/content with standard card backgrounds. In wide mode, there's a sidebar, workspace, and studio panels each using different glass-surface variants, with the workspace becoming transparent for the image workspace case — and I notice these wide-mode desktop-polish styles live inside a min-width media query block that may not be properly scoped.

Now I'm thinking through the desktop runtime shell/frame/inner structure, which are all transparent with minimal padding, and how the baseline light screenshot shows a mostly white, mint-tinted look from the nature background plus glass-surface-soft frame. I'm settling on calling the new direction "Aurora Glass" while keeping the mint/emerald identity, and starting to define the backdrop layer with a fixed, negative z-index pseudo-element on body.

I'm working through the CSS stacking order details — verifying whether body's background propagates to the canvas since html has no explicit background, and whether the fixed backdrop pseudo-element renders correctly relative to that canvas paint given it's not part of a positioned ancestor's stacking context.

But I realize when the scroll-lock code sets body's position to fixed, that changes things: fixed elements always create their own stacking context, so now body::before's negative z-index would only place it behind body's own content, not the canvas — this could break the intended layering while the dialog is open.

I confirm the fixed backdrop stays anchored to the viewport regardless of body's scroll offset, so there's no visual jump when scroll gets locked, and the boot loader already covers the screen during startup so this timing isn't an issue either way.

Now I'm mapping out the actual layers of the backdrop: a base background color, the existing pre-blurred nature image tinted darker in dark mode via multiply blending, a set of soft aurora-style radial gradient blobs in emerald/aqua/lime tones, and a subtle grain texture layered on top.

I'm figuring out how to combine these into a single element's background stack so it only needs to render once, and considering whether a faint vignette at the edges would help tie the composition together.

For dark mode, since opacity can't be applied per background layer, I'm using a darkening gradient overlay on top of the image, with aurora glows and grain layered above that, all controlled through CSS variables that swap per theme.

Now I'm defining the glass surface tokens — starting with the chrome-level glass for sidebars and nav panels, layering a translucent gradient with borders, inset highlights, and soft shadows to get that frosted depth effect.

I'm checking readability with nested translucency: cards sitting inside glass panels over the mint bokeh backdrop still resolve to mostly white, so text contrast holds. Now I'm defining a separate glass token for floating elements like menus, popovers, and toasts, with its own opacity and blur settings.

I'm worried that setting `--popover` itself to translucent could cause unintended ghosting anywhere `bg-popover` is used without the accompanying blur applied, so I want to check how widely that token is reused before committing — likely safer to keep `--popover` more opaque and apply the glass blur separately via targeted selectors.

I'll create a `.nova-glass-float` utility guarded by `@supports (backdrop-filter)`, applying it to dropdowns, selects, popovers, and dialog content rather than changing the base token globally. For tooltips, I'm leaning toward keeping the inverted dark style but making it a translucent dark glass with blur, since the surface area is small and cheap to render.

For dialogs specifically, I want the content panel to use glass-float with blur while keeping the overlay scrim flat and untinted for performance, though I'm considering tinting it slightly greener rather than pure black so the frosted panel reads more glass-like against it. I still need to check how the settings modal's existing desktop-only glass-surface background interacts with this new approach.

For mobile, since dialog content goes fullscreen below 640px, blur is wasteful there, so I'll gate the backdrop-filter behind a `sm:` breakpoint and fall back to an opaque popover color on small screens. Then I'll move on to reviewing the button variants, starting with the primary emerald gradient button.

For hover states I want to avoid expensive filter repaints, so swapping the background-image gradient on hover is cheap enough given the small button size, with a short transition on color/background/border/shadow/transform properties. Then I'm defining the outline variant as a glass pill with light/dark translucent backgrounds and subtle hover brightening, followed by secondary and ghost variants using simpler background treatments.

Since these are shadcn base classes written as cva strings, I'll edit them directly and trust tailwind-merge to resolve conflicts when components pass their own overrides like custom rounding or shadow-none. For elevation, I'm deciding against adding hover lift transforms since it could feel jittery in toolbars—keeping just color transitions plus the existing press-down effect on active state.

payload.text:
With enough context gathered, I'm now planning the actual CSS rewrite for globals.css, restructuring the color tokens and shell/panel sections while keeping the markdown and other functional sections untouched. I'm working out specific light-mode token values like background, foreground, and card colors for a cooler mint aesthetic.

I'm carefully computing alpha-blended border and input colors to get subtle green-tinted borders that work over the mint background, testing a few different opacity levels to land on something visible but not too gray.

For the core palette I'm settling on a deep emerald primary (#0d7f57) with white foreground text for solid contrast, a light emerald secondary, and a soft accent tint with dark emerald accent-foreground text so hover states in dropdowns read clearly against the light background.

That accent tint also applies to icon-button hovers in fullscreen viewers, the ErrorBoundary hover state, and the GifModeChoiceDialog close button, giving a consistent subtle green hover across the app. I want to double-check whether the imported shadcn tailwind stylesheet defines anything else relying on accent variables before finalizing.

Now I'm recalculating the muted background and muted-foreground colors, verifying contrast ratios against white to make sure the text stays readable at around 6:1.

I'm also darkening the placeholder color slightly for better readability, updating the focus ring, and refreshing the chart, sidebar, and processing colors toward the emerald/teal palette while keeping success green as-is.

Now I'm defining new glass tokens for the frosted panel effect: a semi-transparent white tint for panel bases, layered gradients for chrome panels versus outer frames, and a luminous white border to create the glassy edge highlight.

Defining more glass tokens...

Still defining dark tokens...

Checking that #4fd69c's hue stays in the same emerald-teal family as the light primary, around 154-159°, so it's consistent. I'm mapping out the remaining dark-mode tokens—foreground, accent, secondary—keeping them tonally aligned with the current palette.

I'm verifying muted-foreground's contrast ratio against the dark background comes out around 8.5, which is solid, then setting placeholder and ring colors and starting to define the glass surface gradient tokens for dark mode.

Adding more color variables...

I'm noticing the dark theme variables get duplicated across the data-attribute selector and the media query block, and weighing whether to consolidate that or just follow the existing repetitive pattern already used in the codebase.

Wait, I should check whether Tailwind's `dark:` variant actually applies here — that custom variant targets a `.dark` class, but this project toggles `data-theme="dark"` instead. If nothing ever adds the `.dark` class, all the `dark:` utilities baked into the shadcn components are effectively inert, meaning dark mode styling falls back to the base classes rather than the dark-specific overrides. I want to verify this by checking whether the theme toggle logic ever sets that class.

Fixing the custom variant to key off `data-theme="dark"` would suddenly activate all those dormant `dark:` styles, which could introduce regressions since those styles were never actually rendered or tested. I should count how many `dark:` classes exist outside the ui/ folder to gauge how much behavior would change if I correct this.

Since dark mode styling matters for how things look, I should verify with actual screenshots and grep to check how extensively it's used, and look at ThemeToggle to understand how the theme gets applied. For fonts, I'm considering swapping the placeholder Geist font variable for a real font stack, but need to be careful about how Tailwind's preflight ties font-family to that variable.

Actually, the measured fallback stack suggests `--default-font-family` itself was never defined, so the fallback in the var() call kicked in rather than the variable resolving to an invalid value — meaning html's font-family used that fallback chain directly, and body inherited from there.

Similarly, `.font-mono` referencing `--font-geist-mono` is undefined too, so it also falls back to inherited sans, confirming the same bug pattern. The fix requires defining these font variables properly inside the theme block, though I need to double check whether fonts like "Segoe UI Variable" are actually available on Windows 10 before relying on them in the fallback chain.

For explicit CJK fallback, being explicit beats relying on locale defaults since it's decent but not guaranteed. For monospace, I'm setting up a stack with Cascadia Code/Mono, JetBrains Mono, and system fallbacks like Consolas which is always available on Windows, plus adding Arial/Helvetica as final fallbacks for the sans stack.

Now I'm tracing through whether `--font-sans` actually gets emitted as a usable CSS variable under `@theme inline`, since if it's not emitted, the body's font-family declaration becomes invalid and falls back to inheriting from html's `--default-font-family`, which depends on whether the project's theme import chain properly defines that default from the Tailwind v4 theme.css.

I realize a var() referencing an undefined custom property becomes guaranteed-invalid, which explains why the fallback stack shows up in html's computed font rather than the intended Geist font. To fix this safely, I want to define the font stack directly in `@theme inline` without relying on var() indirection, and simplify the body rule accordingly.

Naming it "geist" when it's not Geist would be misleading, so I'll use --nova-font-sans, --nova-font-mono, and --nova-font-heading instead. As for whether the font change breaks layout — checking the fallback stacks on Windows and Mac, both resolve to essentially the same system fonts as the current system-ui approach, so the visual impact should be minimal.

The bigger risk is switching mono to a real monospace font, which affects code blocks and tabular numeric displays, but that's low risk overall. I'll skip worrying about font-feature-settings support. Next I need to check the @custom-variant dark issue by grepping for it.

Now I'm writing the fixed backdrop layer CSS that paints a composited background once using layered grain, aurora, and veil images so it never repaints on scroll.

Working out background sizing...

I'm weighing whether grain is worth the extra GPU memory cost from two full-viewport fixed layers, but decide it's a nice subtle texture worth keeping on ::after while folding the size/position lists carefully so the layer counts stay aligned.

Since CSS cycles background-size and background-repeat values across layers, I need to explicitly list all 7 layer sizes rather than relying on shorthand repetition, otherwise the grain tile size bleeds into the wrong layer.

I'm weighing an alternative structure where I keep the aurora gradients out of shared variables entirely and instead define background-image directly per theme selector, so light and dark modes each specify their own full gradient list without depending on matching counts.

Now I'm settling on a cleaner design: keep gradient shapes fixed and only swap colors through CSS variables, so the same background-image declaration works for both themes and only the token values differ. For the grain texture, I'm thinking through an SVG noise filter approach, adjusting opacity and color between light and dark themes so the speckles read correctly against each background.

Adjusting the color matrix so light mode uses black speckle and dark mode uses white speckle, both at low alpha for subtlety, and thinking through how the fine baseFrequency renders as seamless grain at that tile size.

I'm keeping the grain confined to the backdrop layer rather than a global overlay so it doesn't affect text sharpness or compositing performance, letting panels attenuate it naturally through their translucency for that frosted feel. Next I'm reworking the app shell background to be transparent so the body-level grain shows through, while checking how the max-width container centers in normal web mode.

With the fixed backdrop covering the full viewport, that should look better across wide screens. I want to check the web-gen-light baseline for comparison, and I'm noting that the ≥960px media block styles for sidebar, workspace, and studio panels aren't actually scoped to the desktop shell, so they'll apply on web too. I'm going to build a glass-panel style using these existing hooks.

Writing panel styles...

The combination gives a luminous inner border plus a dark outer hairline ring, producing a classic layered glass edge effect. Now I'm looking at overriding the normal-mode app frame background to use the softer glass surface variable.

Next I'm thinking through the top nav tabs in normal mode: making the tabs list read as a glass track and the active trigger appear as a raised white pill with shadow and primary-colored icon, but weighing whether to scope this via CSS to the app shell or change the shared tabs primitive defaults, since that primitive is reused elsewhere like the settings modal.

Realizing utility classes would override component-layer overrides since utilities beat components, so I need to remove `bg-muted` directly from the primitive and instead expose new semantic color tokens through Tailwind's theme config, like a `--color-surface` token for raised controls, making this the more idiomatic approach despite the added complexity.

Now I'm defining the full palette: surface and surface-hover for glassy controls, track for recessed tab lists, field for input backgrounds, and scrim for dialog overlays, each with distinct light and dark rgba values, so primitives can use utilities like `bg-surface`, `hover:bg-surface-hover`, `bg-track`, and `bg-field`.

I'm also working out shadow tokens in the theme layer, mapping custom shadow variables like `--shadow-raised` into Tailwind's v4 shadow utility system, tracing through how the box-shadow composition works with Tailwind's internal shadow/ring variables.

Confirmed then—using Tailwind shadow utilities avoids conflicts with ring composition. Now I'm mapping the shadow tokens into theme inline variables, aliasing raised, float, and glow shadows to their nova-prefixed sources, while checking that Tailwind v4's theme namespace actually supports custom shadow keys this way.

I'm also considering combining inset highlight and outer drop shadow into single box-shadow tokens, then thinking through button variant styling with primary gradient backgrounds and glow shadows on hover.

That gives a glossy pill effect without needing a gradient. I also realize the default variant lacks a hover state for buttons, so I'll add one, and for the outline variant I'm considering translucent surface fills with subtle borders to match the visionOS-style glass aesthetic.

I need to decide whether leftover dark-mode variants across components will conflict once I fix the dark variant logic, since some would override my new surface styles—worth checking how widely dark: is used before finalizing secondary, ghost, and destructive button styles.

On transition-all vs transition: I'm considering whether the narrower default transition set in Tailwind v4 still covers everything I need (color, box-shadow, transform/translate for the active press effect), which would let me avoid the broader, potentially costlier transition-all.

For focus rings on inputs, I'm dialing back the ring opacity from 50% to something subtler like 20-25% since the primary green is fairly strong, plus adjusting background to bg-field and border-input for the field styling.

I'm also checking how the Textarea component's bg-transparent override merges with the new bg-field default via tailwind-merge, and thinking through how to restyle the studio-prompt-surface wrapper as a glass-like inset field rather than the current opaque mint background.

For tabs, I'll swap the muted background for a track background, give the active trigger a surface fill with a raised shadow, and use primary color for active nav icons. Then for dropdowns, selects, popovers, and tooltips, I'm adding a glass float treatment to their content panels, replacing the default popover background and ring styling.

I'm now worried about layering conflicts—if the glass float class is unlayered, it could override any component-level `bg-` utility overrides on things like DropdownMenuContent, and I'm weighing whether to scope it in `@layer components` instead so utility classes can still win when needed.

Comparing `@utility` versus `@layer components`, I realize `@utility` puts things in the utilities layer where ordering against consumer overrides becomes unpredictable since tailwind-merge won't recognize the custom class. `@layer components` is cleaner for base styles meant to be overridable, so I'll use it for `.nova-float` and possibly `.nova-glass`.

For the backdrop-filter effect itself, I'm considering using Tailwind's `supports-[backdrop-filter]:` variant (or its shorthand) to conditionally apply blur and saturation only when supported, falling back to opaque backgrounds otherwise, while also thinking about reduced-transparency accessibility preferences.

Since a custom variant for `prefers-reduced-transparency` would get messy repeated across six primitives, I'm deciding a shared `.nova-float` component class is cleaner -- defining it in a `@layer components` block with base solid background and border colors, then layering an `@supports` block that applies the glass background only when backdrop-filter is actually supported.

Adding the reduced-transparency media override outside the layer so it wins against the supports rule and forces solid background with blur disabled.

I'll settle on 16px blur radius as a single shared variable, keeping the cost manageable across menus and popovers. For the dialog overlay I'll swap the plain dark scrim for a lighter tinted one without blur, and make the floating glass effect apply only from small breakpoints up, handling the mobile fullscreen case directly in the CSS since component classes can't take responsive variants.

For mobile dialogs, I'm weighing whether full-viewport blur on a fullscreen sheet looks good (like iOS) but decide it's too costly for weaker GPUs and hurts text readability, so I'll create a dedicated sheet variant that's solid below the small breakpoint.

For the settings modal specifically, I'm reconsidering its unlayered background override — since it's large with internal scrolling, applying blur there could re-render a big region every frame during scroll. I'll test glass-float with blur against the harness's scroll benchmark and fall back to a solid surface if performance regresses.

Estimating the region at roughly 2 million pixels, the dual-kawase blur with downsampling could cost 1-2ms on the GPU, which might show up in the p95 metrics. I'm also reconsidering whether getMetrics actually captures this, since it measures main-thread CPU not GPU — but with vsync disabled and unlimited frame rate, my rAF cadence should still reflect GPU bottlenecks since BeginFrames get throttled by pending frames, so the cost should surface in the average frame time.

At uncapped rates a 1-2ms GPU cost would meaningfully double the average, but at real 60Hz vsync with a 16.7ms budget, that same cost wouldn't drop any frames. I think the honest way to report this is to show both the relative increase in uncapped frame time and whether any frames actually exceed the 16.7ms budget, so I can say something like "frame time rose but remains well under budget, no increase in dropped frames."

Now shifting to the toast component: a glass float with a colored left icon and an entrance animation using translate and fade, respecting reduced-motion preferences via Tailwind's animate-in utilities.

I want to tone down the colored success text — pairing it with a colored icon and standard foreground text feels more modern, so I'm restructuring to keep message text neutral and let the icon carry the color, with borders staying subtly tinted.

Now I'm auditing the overlay and panel styling across ConfirmDialog, QuickPromptDialog, and GifModeChoiceDialog — swapping black overlays for a scrim token and card backgrounds for the glass float-sheet treatment at larger breakpoints. Checking the PromptGallery subcomponents modal too, I notice the sticky header's card background at high opacity sitting over scrolling content is already causing visible ghosting, so that needs the same fix.

I'm holding off on changing the PromptGallery panel background itself since glass would make the sticky header show scrolling content messily beneath it — just swapping its overlay to the scrim color for now and leaving the deeper fix for later. Then I'm moving to per-item blur removal: reworking the ImageHoverActions button to use a darker translucent fill with an inset white ring for a frosted glass edge instead of relying on backdrop blur, plus a subtle shadow, so it reads clearly against the dimmed image beneath.

Applying that same button replacement across AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, and PromptGallerySubcomponents. For AttachmentChips I'm just dropping the backdrop-blur since the background is already near-opaque. For the full-screen editors (GifFrameTuner, canvas-node-dialogs, image-annotation-editor), I'm weighing whether to switch their near-opaque backgrounds to fully solid — the visual difference is negligible but I want to make sure removing that faint blur doesn't leave any sharp artifacts showing through.

For HistoryImagePreview though, I'm reconsidering: at 90% black opacity without blur, sharp UI edges underneath could create slightly visible gray patches instead of soft blurred blobs, so keeping the blur there might actually be worth it for image quality.

So panning does re-trigger the blur. I'm weighing simpler alternatives — a near-opaque black background without blur to avoid the ghosting effect, or just settling on a very dark solid backdrop instead of the blur approach.

Actually, the transient nature of lightbox blur during zoom/pan isn't a big performance issue since it's user-driven, so I'll leave HistoryImagePreview's blur as-is since it's intentional and visible. The small buttons using backdrop-blur over the image are fine too since they're minor elements.

For WorkspaceHeader's random image viewer and fullscreen-image-viewer, the outer overlay's visible blur should stay, but the top bar nested inside at 95% opacity is essentially invisible since it's blurring against an already-opaque backdrop root, so I should drop that blur while keeping the opacity. The bottom zoom pill at 90% opacity is small enough to leave as-is, or potentially bump the opacity slightly higher.

The canvas toolbar and zoom-controls at bg-card/95 with backdrop-blur should get upgraded to the full glass treatment since it's the canonical glass toolbar sitting over the canvas—it's small so re-blurring per frame during panning is cheap, and the minimap's existing subtle blur with the panel background variable is fine as-is.

For workbench specifics, the nova-studio-panel in wide mode should get the glass-surface treatment, while in normal mode it stays as a plain card with a border.

Now applying that panel glass surface to all modes rather than just wide layouts, giving the workbench head a subtle gradient sheen using a new glass-sheen token, defining the prompt surface field style, and reworking result cards to use a glass card background with gradient, glass-line border, inset highlight shadow, and stronger hover states with primary-tinted borders—keeping hover transforms disabled in wide mode for performance.

Since the virtualized history list mounts dozens of cards during scroll, I want to keep shadow blur values modest since heavier multi-layer blurs are costlier to rasterize on newly composited tiles as groups mount and unmount.

I'm checking whether the toolbar and waiting/failed cards keep the same glass treatment, and confirming that the active job panel's processing-tinted border still gets applied correctly given the existing glass override rule at the ≥960 breakpoint.

For the empty-state image with its inset overlay, I'll keep the doubled "window" effect but tone it down and add a token to handle system dark mode consistently, since only explicit dark theme is currently covered. Then I'm looking at the agent workspace container, planning to restyle it as a glass panel to match the rest of the shell.

I want to check the actual message bubble classes—user bubbles likely use the primary color, which with the new deep emerald would give a nice iMessage-like look with white text on assistant bubbles differing via muted background. I should grep the codebase to confirm before continuing to the settings modal styling.

For the settings modal scrim, I'm noting the darker overlay color and considering swapping it for a scrim-strong token. The `body:has(.nova-app-settings)` selector concerns me slightly for perf reasons—Chromium handles `:has()` invalidation reasonably well, but a body-level `:has()` with a descendant argument can trigger checks on any DOM mutation, so I'm weighing whether to remove or simplify that selector.

Since I can't easily pass a custom class through DialogContent to target the settings overlay directly, I'll just drop the special darker-scrim rule entirely and rely on the uniform scrim, since my glass dialog with its blurred backdrop already provides enough separation from the page behind it.

Now I'm thinking about scrollbars — currently thin scrollbars only apply on desktop shell and settings at wider viewports, but I want to extend that globally so Windows users don't see the default chunky scrollbars everywhere. Setting `scrollbar-width` and `scrollbar-color` on the universal selector is cheap performance-wise, and since Chrome 121+ ignores the older `::-webkit-scrollbar` pseudo-rules once the standard properties are set, I need to check how that interacts with the existing desktop-specific webkit rules.

I'm also noticing the virtual-scroll-container's scrollbar-color uses an hsl() wrapping a hex custom property, which produces an invalid color and silently falls back—an existing bug I should fix with color-mix instead. I'll also strip out the now-dead webkit-scrollbar rules for desktop since Chromium 121+ ignores them when scrollbar-width is set.

Since Safari still lacks scrollbar-color, I'll keep the webkit rules but generalize them rather than removing them, so Safari retains styled scrollbars while modern Chromium relies on the standard properties.

Next I want to add entrance motion for panels, extending the existing desktop shell enter animation with a staggered rise effect for the sidebar and workspace.

Since keepMounted tabs don't remount on switch, this rise animation only fires once at app startup, which is fine — I'll use a subtle 260ms cubic-bezier motion for sidebar, workspace, and normal-mode frame. I'm also considering whether tab panel visibility changes (via the hidden attribute) should get their own fade transition.

A translateY on mount risks corrupting canvas measurements, so I should stick to opacity-only fade to avoid geometry side effects — 0 to 1 over 160ms is safer. I also need to account for `prefers-reduced-motion` disabling these entrance animations, and `prefers-reduced-transparency` making panels more opaque.
