This is a harness continuation, so I'll keep working. Recapping progress: baseline is built and copied, the bench harness works, and I've found the dark: variant is dead since nothing adds the .dark class, while the other non-primitive usages are legitimate dark-mode color fixes.

Fixing the variant to bind to data-theme="dark" plus system-dark preference would properly activate these intended styles — like amber and emerald text colors becoming readable against dark backgrounds instead of jarring light-mode leftovers. That's a genuine improvement.

The caveat is this same fix also activates the primitives' own dark: classes across buttons, inputs, selects, and tabs — so I need to check those changes don't introduce unwanted visual regressions alongside the intended fixes.

Since I'm rewriting primitives to use tokens instead, I plan to strip out their dark: classes where they'd conflict, since my tokens already resolve dark mode through CSS variables. That means I still need to read badge.tsx, switch.tsx, slider.tsx, and toggle-group.tsx before deciding how to handle each.

For the custom variant syntax itself, I'm working through the Tailwind v4 `@custom-variant dark` definition, matching either an explicit data-theme="dark" attribute or, in system mode, a root without a data-theme="light" override combined with the prefers-color-scheme media query.

I want to confirm the block form supports nesting a selector rule and a media rule together with multiple `@slot` placeholders, and based on the v4 docs examples I've seen, this pattern should compile correctly since each `@slot` gets replaced independently.

I'm also comparing specificity approaches — using `:where()` keeps the specificity at zero like the class selector itself, matching how Tailwind's default `dark` variant relies purely on emission order rather than selector weight, whereas `:is()` in the existing custom variant behaves similarly but only targets descendants, not the element itself.

There's also the tailwind-merge conflict edge case worth flagging: button variants that mix `bg-background` with `dark:bg-input/30` can let a consumer's override get clobbered in dark mode because tailwind-merge treats differently-modified classes as non-conflicting. Since I'm converting primitives to token-based classes without dark: modifiers, that issue goes away for primitives, though it may still linger in components like BackupProgress, SettingsModal, AgentGenerationResult, and canvas-node that aren't being touched.

Checking whether typography plugin is installed for `dark:prose-invert` — it's not in the dependencies, so that class is inert and harmless either way. The `dark:via-white/10` shimmer gradient in AgentGenerationResult is legitimate and activating it is correct. I'll note this dark-mode fix as a small, in-scope bug found while working, since dead dark variants directly affect the UI's dark mode appearance — it's not scope creep, just a one-line correction.

Since some of these dark variant fixes touch places I haven't visually verified — the settings modal's model editor and the backup progress indicator — I want to check those in the harness where possible; the backup progress classes are simple amber variants so the risk there is low even without a screenshot. Next I'll go through the remaining primitives like badge, switch, slider, and toggle-group before writing the actual CSS, and also think about how the workspace header looks in its normal state with just the logo, title, and buttons.

For the harness updates, I'm planning to enable dark mode dialog and dropdown screenshots for the wide scenario, and considering whether to add a layer-count metric via the compositing layer tree to quantify the backdrop's cost — but that adds complexity for a small, honestly-reportable increase, so I'll skip it and stick to reporting backdrop-filter usage plus frame and style/layout timing metrics instead.

Thinking more about the fixed backdrop's memory footprint: with `will-change: transform` it likely creates its own composited layer sized to the viewport, roughly 12MB of GPU memory at the current resolution and DPR, plus potentially another similar layer for the grain overlay if it composites separately — so possibly ~24MB total. But since fixed-position elements on scrollable pages already get auto-composited by Chromium to avoid repaints, this may not be as large a net addition as it first seems, since the root layer's content shifts around anyway once the shell becomes transparent.

To keep memory down, I'll consolidate everything — grain, aurora gradients, base image, and color — into a single pseudo-element with multiple stacked backgrounds rather than a separate grain layer, so there's just one extra composited layer instead of two. The grain's opacity comes from the SVG's own alpha so no separate blending is needed, and a dark overlay gradient handles the dark-mode veil within that same element. Rasterization should stay cheap since the SVG tiles are small and repeat, and the background image itself is a small, pre-blurred low-res webp that upscales fine given its intentional blur.

Now I'm checking the `.studio-active-empty` decorative window into the image and adapting its overlay for the glass look, then turning to how the normal (non-wide) layout's max-width container interacts with the new fixed body backdrop — since the shell container isn't centered with `mx-auto`, I want to verify whether it's actually left-aligned at wider viewports by checking the baseline screenshot.

I'm planning the restructured globals.css: imports and custom variant fixes, light-mode root tokens, then a shared approach for dark tokens using both the data-theme selector and the prefers-color-scheme media query so they stay in sync.

Since CSS can't easily share declarations between a plain selector and a media query without duplication, I'll just accept duplicating the dark token block rather than restructure the theme-init script's JS behavior. After the tokens, I'll add the theme-inline mapping with new surface/track/field/scrim/shadow tokens and fonts, then move into the base layer for html/body defaults, font features, selection, scrollbars, and focus styles, followed by the backdrop layer.

Then I'll lay out the glass primitive components, shell layout overrides, workbench/history/results restyling, desktop polish, motion and reduced-transparency fallbacks, and preserve the shimmer/virtual-scroll-container/scrollbar-hide utilities and existing base/markdown layers. Writing light theme tokens...

But I realize I need to check where `--muted` is used elsewhere—TabsList, skeleton gradients, hover backgrounds, badges, and canvas toolbar hover states—since changing its value could ripple through several components I'll need to verify or adjust.

This is like Apple's translucent fill colors that adapt to the layer beneath them. But existing usages stack fractional opacities on top of muted, like /50 or /20 modifiers, and with such a low base alpha those compound down to nearly invisible—so I'm worried this breaks visibility in places like the catalog components that rely on those stacked opacities.

The safer move is to keep --muted closer to its current semi-opaque light mint tone rather than making it fully transparent-tinted, so the derived opacity variants preserve roughly the same visual weight they have now.

Actually rethinking accent for a more modern feel — a light green tint background with dark green foreground text, applied to dropdown focus states and icon button hovers, instead of the current solid green fill.

I'm also double-checking whether accent gets pulled into `accent-color` usages for checkboxes or range inputs, since that would need dark-green-on-white contrast rather than a tint, and separately whether sidebar-accent tokens follow the same pattern.

For dark mode, I'm setting accent to a translucent teal-green with a soft mint foreground for readability. For the border color, I'm shifting to a translucent dark-green tint that reads as neutral mint-gray over white but subtly deepens over darker or greener glass backdrops, keeping in mind that `border-border` is the global default applied everywhere so it needs to stay visible without becoming too heavy.

Recalculating, I find the current border is actually darker than expected, around #cfe1d5, a fairly visible mint tone against white. My new value at 0.14 alpha comes out lighter at #dee7e3, so I may need to bump the alpha higher to match the existing visibility.

I settle on 0.16 opacity for borders, giving roughly #d9e4df, close to the current lightness but more neutral, while input fields need a stronger 0.2 alpha for clearer edges, landing near #d0ddd7.

For foreground, I bump the value to #10261c for slightly deeper contrast than the current #20332a, which should be a fine improvement. For card backgrounds, I decide to keep the light-mode opacity at 0.76 since it's used across sticky headers, canvas panels, and toolbars, and just shift the dark-mode variant's hue to match the new dark background tone instead of changing its alpha.

Then for popover, since dropdowns, mention popups, and context menus rely on bg-popover without blur, their current opacity of 0.9 causes noticeable ghosting from text behind — I decide to raise it to 0.96 in light mode to fix that, since my new glass primitives will use their own dedicated token anyway.

I also want to add nova-float to the canvas context menu, mention editor popup, and AgentInputEditor popup for consistent blur since they're small static floating elements where blur is cheap to compute. But since nova-float sets its own background in the components layer, and utilities layer rules like bg-popover take precedence, I need to strip those conflicting utility classes wherever I add nova-float.

This same rule applies to any primitive using nova-float — if a consumer explicitly passes bg-card or similar, that's fine and intentional since consumer utilities should win over the base glass styling. I should check where DropdownMenuContent, PopoverContent, and Select pass background overrides via className, though that's a minor follow-up. For the glass token definitions, I'm setting light-mode tint values as RGB triplets so they can be combined with alpha using rgb(var(--tint) / a) syntax, which works fine in modern browsers since CSS variable substitution happens before parsing.

Writing panel gradient tokens...

Adjusting dark mode variant...

Now I'm defining the floating surface tokens for menus, popovers, and dialogs, setting up lighter translucent backgrounds with subtle green-tinted borders and inset highlights for that glass depth.

Checking legibility of white text-on-glass at 72% alpha over busy content, both light and dark backgrounds—the blur smooths things out enough that the light overlay stays legible even against dark images underneath.

Working through contrast ratios more precisely: at 0.72 alpha, muted text fails the 4.5 contrast threshold in worst-case dark scenarios, so I bump alpha up incrementally—0.8 still isn't enough, but 0.86 finally clears 4.5 contrast for muted text, though it makes the glass effect noticeably less transparent.

Rather than over-engineering for a rare worst case (menus opening over dark background images), I'll settle on 0.8 alpha for floating surfaces since menus typically trigger near light glass panels anyway, reserving 0.86 for dialogs where larger text content makes readability more critical.

Settling on 0.82 alpha for the dark float. Now thinking about the dialog scrim overlay—wanting something lighter and more modern than the current black/50, while still keeping the modal clearly separated from the background.

Working out the backdrop palette now, defining aurora glow colors for the light theme background.

Writing more color variables...

Adding aurora gradients and image layer...

Still defining the grain texture variable...

Encoding SVG grain overlay...

Since all noise channels carry similar randomness, I can just map alpha from either the noise's alpha or red channel with a small multiplier to get faint black speckle grain. Writing feColorMatrix values...

For dark mode, I'd flip to white speckle instead by setting RGB to 1 and scaling alpha down slightly, though the linearRGB color-interpolation default probably won't matter much here given how subtle the grain effect is overall.

At 5% alpha, the black speckles create a barely-visible dirty/paper texture, and once panel opacity is factored in it's even more subtle, so this feels acceptably light. Rendering cost is trivial since feTurbulence rasterizes at a small pixel size once per layer, and Chromium's image caching means repeated tiles are cheap.

Now I'm setting up the base body styles, starting with the html color-scheme property for light mode.

I'm keeping the color transition on body since it's just a one-off animation during theme switches, then setting a selection highlight using the primary color and adding thin, theme-colored scrollbars via a feature query for supporting browsers.

Since scrollbar-width isn't inherited, I need to check specificity to make sure a `.scrollbar-hide` utility class can still override the universal thin-scrollbar rule when needed — unlayered rules will win regardless of layer placement, so that's fine either way.

Thin scrollbars should look decent cross-platform in modern Chromium, and I don't think I need to touch webkit-specific fallback rules since overlay scrollbars already handle most cases.

Since scrollbar-color set on `*` makes ::-webkit-scrollbar dead in Chromium, I'll wrap the webkit fallback in a feature query so it only applies where scrollbar-color isn't supported, like Safari.

Writing scrollbar fallback CSS...

Adding theme token mappings...

I'm now double-checking whether `@theme inline` actually emits CSS variables on `:root`, or just inlines the value directly into utility classes without a variable reference.

This matters because existing CSS relies on `var(--font-mono)` and `var(--font-sans)` directly in several selectors, so I need to know whether those variables will actually exist for that code to work.

Tracing further, if `--default-font-family` in preflight ultimately references `--font-sans`, and `--font-sans` was defined pointing to an undefined variable like `--font-geist-sans`, that chain would break and fall back to the raw fallback stack — which matches the observed computed font-family result on html.

With the theme override replacing --font-sans with the geist variable, I'm trying to figure out whether --default-font-family resolves to that variable or falls through to the fallback stack at build time. Since our measured html font-family matched the same fallback stack as the default sans stack, I can't actually distinguish which path was taken—both produce identical output here.

Testing .font-mono, it also resolves to the sans stack, which suggests the geist mono variable is undefined and the whole declaration is invalid, causing it to inherit body's font. Following that chain, body's font-family also depends on an undefined --font-sans variable, so it inherits from html's default stack, which matches what we measured. This means markdown code blocks using --font-mono likely fall back to sans-serif instead of monospace—a real rendering bug worth fixing by defining the font variables properly at the root level.

I should double check TSX usages of font classes like `font-mono` to confirm the theme mapping covers them, and also verify preflight's default mono font-family for code/kbd/pre elements resolves correctly under the new variable scheme.

Also, "Segoe UI Variable Text" only exists on Windows 11, so on Windows 10 it'll gracefully fall back to plain "Segoe UI" anyway.

For CJK glyph fallback, since Segoe fonts lack Chinese coverage, the browser moves down the stack to something like "PingFang SC" on Mac or "Microsoft YaHei UI" on Windows for those characters.

This is roughly what system-ui would already resolve to given lang="zh-CN", so being explicit here just guarantees consistency rather than changing the outcome. The order between YaHei and PingFang barely matters since they're platform-exclusive in practice.

For headings I'm considering slightly tighter letter-spacing.

Now I'm rewriting the base button primitive, defining its flex layout, border, padding, text sizing, and transition/focus/disabled states.

Writing button transition classes...

`transition-all` risks animating unintended properties like width or padding, causing jank, so an explicit property list is a small perf hygiene win. I'll settle on transitioning color, background-color, border-color, box-shadow, and translate specifically.

Deciding whether opacity needs to be included for smooth disabled-state transitions, but concluding it's unnecessary since the toggle can be instant. Now working through variant styles, weighing whether to use `brightness()` filter for hover states versus simpler background/gradient adjustments, since filters can be costly even on small elements.

Choosing to avoid filters and instead add a dedicated `--primary-hover` token, considering color-mix as an alternative but preferring the explicit token approach for cleanliness across both light and dark themes.

I'm also thinking about the gloss gradient overlay — since it's layered as a separate background-image on top of background-color, if consumers override the button's bg color via className, the gradient gloss should still render correctly over whatever color they pass, since tailwind-merge only swaps out the color utility, not the gradient layer.

Now I'm working out the shadow tokens: a glow shadow combining an inset highlight, a small drop shadow, and a colored ambient glow (using the primary green tone), with a slightly different composition for dark mode. These are static box-shadow values so they're cheap to apply across variants.

For the outline variant, I'm defining border, surface background, and hover states with a "raised" shadow style, working out the semi-transparent white surface colors for light mode and their hover equivalents.

I'm also noting that the desktop sidebar tool buttons force transparent backgrounds and borders via CSS overrides, so I'll need to also strip the box-shadow there and restyle that block separately. Then I'm adjusting secondary and ghost variant hover states to simplify them and remove unnecessary dark-mode-specific classes.

For ghost specifically, I considered giving it an emerald accent tint on hover to match the brand, but decided that's too colorful for general use across toolbars, so I'm keeping ghost hover as a neutral muted background without the dark variant.

For destructive, I'm simplifying to a lighter background tint with matching text and focus ring colors, dropping the separate dark-mode variants, and checking that the red text still holds sufficient contrast against a dark background.

I'll switch dark mode's destructive text to a lighter red (#f87171) since it contrasts better against dark backgrounds. Now I'm considering whether to bump the base --radius from 0.625rem to 0.75rem for a softer, more modern look, tracing through how that scales all the derived rounded-sm/md/lg/xl/2xl/3xl/4xl values via the calc multipliers in the theme.

I settle on a smaller bump to 0.7rem instead, giving slightly larger radii across the board without overdoing it.

Actually, I'll leave --radius at 0.625rem to avoid unexpected layout issues, and instead set larger radii directly per-surface in CSS — panels around 16-20px, menus 12px, dialogs 18px — since that targeted approach gives the modern look without a risky global change.

For inputs, I'll keep the placeholder text using muted-foreground for accessibility, rather than switching to the separate placeholder token used in the workbench textarea.

For the field background and focus states, I'm defining subtle translucent white/black overlays for light and dark modes, plus inset shadows to give the field a slight recessed depth on both themes.

I want to create a `--nova-shadow-field` token that maps through `--shadow-field`, but I need to think through how Tailwind's shadow utility composes with focus rings via `--tw-shadow` and `--tw-ring-shadow`, since box-shadow stacks inset-shadow, inset-ring, ring, and shadow layers together. To fix that, I should add a scoped override resetting the textarea's box-shadow to none within `.studio-prompt-surface`.

I'm also worried other consumers passing `border-0 bg-transparent` to embedded Textareas/Inputs elsewhere would inherit that same unwanted inset shadow, so it's safer to keep the inset shadow out of the primitives entirely and just rely on background, border, and focus ring for depth. I'll apply the same simplified content classes to popover.tsx, and I'm about to look at how tooltip.tsx currently inverts colors for its background and arrow.

For the tooltip, I'll keep the solid inverted background rather than adding translucency, since a translucent arrow would double-darken where it overlaps the popup edge and create a visible seam. I'll refine the styling with rounded corners, tighter padding, a floating shadow, and smaller medium-weight text while keeping it fully opaque for crispness.

Now moving to the dialog component: the overlay uses a fixed full-screen scrim with fade in/out transitions and no blur, and the content is set up as a full-screen sheet on mobile that transforms into a centered rounded card on larger screens, with scrollable overflow and adjusted padding for different breakpoints.

I'm adding a subtle border ring and thinking through how the sheet should look solid below the small breakpoint but glassy with blur above it, calculating the rounded corner radius to match the design scale. For the footer, I'm keeping the muted background band with top border and reversed flex column layout, just considering a slightly lighter opacity for the glass look. For the tab list, I'm considering an inset track shadow token but realize consumers like WorkspaceModeTabs override the background classes directly via tailwind-merge, so I need to update those call sites too rather than just the base component. I'm figuring out the best way to reconstruct globals.css—thinking I'll write the new head section separately and splice it together with the preserved markdown tail from the original file to avoid rewriting hundreds of lines unnecessarily.

Now I'm composing the head CSS, starting with the custom dark-mode variant definition.

Multiple @slot substitutions inside nested rules...

I'll verify by checking the compiled CSS output for the correct dark variant selectors. Since `&:where(...)` adds zero specificity, `dark:bg-x` ends up winning purely by source order over `bg-y`, which is what Tailwind relies on for variant precedence.

Now I'm finalizing the light-mode color tokens, defining values for background, foreground, card, popover, primary, secondary, and muted using a green-tinted palette with soft transparency layers.

I'm testing different opacity values for the border color against the light background, trying to match the visibility of the old greenish border while keeping the new value consistent, landing around 0.14-0.16 opacity for a good balance.

For the input border, I'm calculating a stronger opacity (0.22) since input fields typically need higher contrast to meet accessibility guidelines for UI component boundaries.

I'm keeping the muted background close to the original mint tone, just slightly adjusted, and now checking the muted-foreground color's contrast ratio against white by computing its relative luminance channel by channel.

Contrast comes out around 6.46 against white and 5.78 against the mint background, both comfortably passing accessibility standards, so I'm moving on to compute the luminance for the placeholder color.

I finish the placeholder calculation, getting a contrast ratio of about 3.42 against white — decent though not strictly required to meet WCAG for placeholder text. Now I'm checking the accent color, a low-opacity green used for dropdown focus backgrounds paired with a darker accent-foreground text color.

Reviewing sidebar and chart tokens next — these seem unused elsewhere so I'll keep them mostly as-is while updating the primary. Then I'm defining status colors: success in green, error in red, and warning in amber, each paired with white foreground text.

Adding processing status color and checking contrast on success green against white — it's a bit low but acceptable since it's mostly used for small icons and dots, not body text. Now I'm defining the glass overlay tokens for the light theme, setting up translucent edges, hairlines, and highlights...

Still writing glass tokens...

Still writing shadow variables...

Since --glass-shadow references --glass-hairline and --glass-highlight, I need to check how those resolve when the dark block redefines them, making sure the cascading works correctly.

Since dark mode needs black-based shadow colors, I'll redeclare --glass-shadow there anyway. I'm also defining the surface tokens—background fills, hover states, track colors, field backgrounds, scrim, and scrollbar thumb—checking that the subtle dark tint for --track still reads as a recessed groove against the mint glass surface.

Now I'm defining the utility shadow tokens for raised, lifted, and glowing elevation states, layering soft shadows with inset highlights to create depth.

Now I'm setting the resting-state button highlight to be subtle against the lighter surface, then defining the aurora backdrop palette with soft emerald, sky, sun, and teal tones layered as translucent gradients for the background veil.

Then I'm mapping the background color directly instead of duplicating a base variable, and starting to define dark mode color tokens for background, foreground, card, and popover surfaces.

Adding more dark theme colors...

Bumping it slightly to 7% white instead seems safer for visibility, though the skeleton gradient use of muted should still look fine either way. I'm also checking the dark muted-foreground contrast ratio to make sure text using it stays readable against the darker backgrounds.

Contrast ratio checks against the dark background 8.9:1, good enough for text. Checking the destructive red color next, computing its luminance against the dark background comes to about 6.8:1, which passes too.

Now I'm verifying which components actually use bg-error solid backgrounds versus tinted variants -- ConfirmDialog's destructive variant just tints the button, so no white-on-red contrast issue there. Checking the dark theme's success and error foreground colors, and searching for any solid bg-error usage with white text that could fail contrast.

Now I'm defining the dark theme's warning and processing color pairs, then setting up the glass surface variables (edge, hairline, highlight, chrome gradient) for the dark palette.

Still writing glass gradients...

Still defining glass theme variables...

Adding aurora gradient colors and backdrop veil variables...

I'm checking dark mode contrast for tab pills and buttons, then extending the theme mapping with more surface and track color tokens.

That resolves fine with color-mix opacity modifiers. Checking name collisions like primary-hover versus primary with Tailwind's longest-match lookup, those work correctly too, and I want to keep glass-edge defined for border usage in components like Toast even though most overrides use semantic colors directly.

Now setting up the font stack variables — defining sans and mono font families with proper fallback chains for cross-platform rendering, then mapping them to the standard font-sans/font-mono tokens.

I'm double-checking that defining --font-sans in :root won't conflict with Tailwind's @theme inline emission, since both resolve to the same value there's no actual clash.

Now I'm thinking about the font fallback chain for CJK glyph coverage — since the user's on Windows 10, "Segoe UI" is right but lacks CJK glyphs, so I need to check that the browser correctly skips macOS-only fonts and lands on a proper CJK fallback like "Microsoft YaHei UI" or "PingFang SC".

Interesting — on Chinese Windows, system-ui affects even Latin characters, since Microsoft YaHei UI's Latin glyphs are actually derived from Segoe UI's design. So switching to my explicit stack wouldn't change the visual glyph shapes much, but it could affect line-height metrics since YaHei UI's ascent/descent differ from Segoe UI's, and Tailwind's explicit line-heights might interact with that difference.

Given how minimal the practical visual benefit is against the risk of subtle mixed-font baseline shifts, I'm weighing whether this font change is really worth pursuing as part of the modernization pass.

Tabular numeral support should be fine with Segoe UI here. Now I'm building the fixed backdrop layer with a grain texture layered under multiple soft radial gradients positioned around the viewport corners to create an aurora-like glow effect.

I'm double-checking gradient syntax validity and confirming that transparent stops won't cause gray fringing in modern browsers. I'm also verifying the root-absolute webp URL resolves correctly from the stylesheet's location regardless of custom property indirection.

Since the app runs through Electron's local backend server, root-absolute paths like `/studio-nature-bg.webp` should resolve fine there too, matching the baseline behavior. I'm confirming that Next.js's webpack/css-loader pipeline leaves root-absolute URLs and data URIs untouched, so no bundling issues arise.

Now I'm generating the SVG markup for a subtle grain texture overlay.

With fractalNoise's alpha averaging around 0.5, applying the color matrix and rect opacity works out to roughly a 2.5% average darkening effect—a very subtle grain.

To get more visible paper-like texture, I'm bumping the rect opacity to .14 for the light theme, which pushes the variation closer to 3% in the gaps while staying under 1% where panels sit at higher opacity. For dark mode I'm considering swapping to a white speckle with lower opacity instead.

That amplitude might be too strong on a near-black background since dark backgrounds amplify contrast, so I'm dialing dark mode down to a lower opacity around .07 using a color matrix that maps everything to white. I'm also thinking through how to encode this as a data URI in CSS -- specifically whether characters like `#`, `<`, and `>` need escaping, since most browsers tolerate unencoded angle brackets inside quoted url() strings.

I'll play it safe and encode `<`, `>`, and `#` explicitly rather than relying on browser leniency, and I'll leave spaces unencoded since browsers generally accept them within quoted url() values. I'm also considering whether Lightning CSS might rewrite the quoting style when it minifies the stylesheet.

Then I think through the paint order: since `html` has no background class, the propagated `body` background paints on the canvas, and `body::before` with negative z-index paints above that canvas layer but still beneath all in-flow content, since it sits within the root stacking context created by `html`.

Now I'm looking at the base layer styles setting border colors, font family, tap highlight, and background/text colors on body.

I'm adding selection styling with a semi-transparent primary color, plus a scrollbar-color fallback using `@supports`. I'm also flagging that Chromium 121+ disables `::-webkit-scrollbar` pseudo-elements once `scrollbar-color` is applied globally, which could conflict with the `.scrollbar-hide` utility class.

I need to check whether other components rely solely on `::-webkit-scrollbar { display: none }` without pairing it with `scrollbar-width: none`, since my global `* { scrollbar-width: thin }` rule would override that and unexpectedly reveal scrollbars that were previously hidden. I should search the TSX files for `-webkit-scrollbar` and any Tailwind scrollbar-hiding utilities to catch this regression before it happens.

Now I'm reviewing the `.nova-float` component styles, which set borders, background/foreground colors, and shadow variables for popover-style elements, with a media query adding border and shadow to `.nova-float-sheet` above a certain breakpoint, plus a feature query checking backdrop-filter support.

Adding glass blur effects...

Actually I realize consumers passing utilities like `ring-1` or `shadow-lg` alongside `.nova-float` will conflict, since Tailwind's box-shadow utilities compose via CSS variables on the same property and will replace my float shadow entirely rather than combine with it. I need to remove those conflicting shadow utilities wherever I apply nova-float, like in ConfirmDialog's panel.

I'm also thinking through blur radius choices for glass effects—smaller elements like dropdowns can use a lighter blur (18px) while dialogs benefit from a heavier one (24px), since Chromium's downsampled blur implementation keeps larger radii affordable performance-wise.

For accessibility, I need a `prefers-reduced-transparency` media query that falls back glass surfaces to opaque backgrounds and disables backdrop-filter entirely, and this override has to sit unlayered so it takes priority over the layered component styles that gate backdrop-filter behind a supports check.

I need to override that dark translucent rule in the reduced-transparency block, so I have to carefully balance CSS specificity between the theme selectors so the reduced-transparency override always wins regardless of light/dark/system mode.

Working through the specificity logic for each theme case confirms the selector ordering resolves correctly. Now I'm thinking about the mobile frame styling — since the app frame is transparent below 640px per the TSX, my unlayered background rule needs to be wrapped in a min-width media query so it doesn't override that behavior.

Now I'm tokenizing the empty-state background with a layered gradient veil and nature image, using CSS variables for light/dark opacity values instead of the old inset box-shadow trick — equally cheap performance-wise. Moving on to reduced-motion handling next.

I'm defining a subtle rise-in keyframe animation applied to sidebar and workspace elements, using fill-mode both so opacity and transform hold their final state after completion — checking whether the finished animation still triggers compositing/containing-block side effects in Chromium, but concluding it should be fine since the fill just holds static values without an active animation running.

I'm now working out where to apply this rise effect without double-animating: the desktop shell already fades and translates in via its own enter animation, so animating children inside it too would stack transforms. I'm leaning toward keeping the shell-level animation and only applying the rise effect to sidebar/workspace children outside the desktop shell context, rather than disabling it selectively per child.

I'll keep desktop-enter on the shell as is but guard the sidebar rise animation with a `:not()` selector so it only applies outside desktop mode. Since the sidebar class only gets added after wideMode is set post-mount, the animation naturally triggers once the boot loader is gone. Next I'm setting up the toast animation with a short ease-out entrance.

With that in place, I need to extend the reduced-motion block, check existing scrollbar styling usage before adding a global rule, and adjust the settings dialog's backdrop and border styling for larger viewports.

I'm confirming that unlayered CSS rules override the component-layer utility classes without needing !important, so my border-radius override at desktop widths should win cleanly over the dialog primitive's rounded utility. I'm also double-checking that the desktop settings class stays reserved for scrollbar styling and isn't disrupted by the new global rule, then reviewing the overlay background rule tied to the settings modal.

Now I'm cleaning up unused workbench surface variables and figuring out how to target the ActiveJobList's studio panel styling, since I need a way to distinguish it from other panels without a dedicated class hook.

I'm checking the line ending situation across files: the repo stores LF but the working tree has CRLF for button.tsx and Toast.tsx, while globals.css shows a mixed pattern with some CRLF and some LF lines. This matters because writing changes back could normalize things unexpectedly.

With core.autocrlf enabled, git converts CRLF to LF on add, so the index stays consistent regardless of what ending style I write with, meaning line-ending differences won't falsely appear as diffs. Still, I plan to run git diff --stat afterward to confirm the untouched markdown tail region shows no unexpected changes. I'm also checking where scrollbars are hidden across the codebase, looking at the various scrollbar-width and utility class implementations used.

All the scrollbar-hiding rules already set the standard `scrollbar-width: none` in ways that override my global thin-scrollbar layer rule, whether through the unlayered `.scrollbar-hide` class, inline styles, or the unlayered `.nova-image-workspace .studio-params-bar` selector — so applying thin scrollbars globally won't break anything. I recall that the theme variable output logic only skips variables marked as `REFERENCE`, meaning `INLINE` variables would still get emitted to `:root` unless there's separate pruning for unused ones elsewhere in the codebase.

I'm now thinking about how optimization removes unused variables unless marked `STATIC`—since inline utilities inject values directly, the variable itself may not register as "used" and could get pruned, unless something else in the CSS references it via `var()`. Tailwind's optimizer seems to track `var(--...)` usages stylesheet-wide and preserve any theme variable referenced anywhere, so I'm checking the baseline evidence where `.font-mono` resolves to the sans stack instead of the expected mono variable, suggesting the inline utility reference might be invalid.

So my fix is to define the sans and mono font stacks explicitly as new custom properties in an unlayered `:root` block, listing out fallback fonts for both.

Both resolve to the same thing anyway, so it's fine either way. Actually, simplifying further, I'll just define `--font-sans` and `--font-mono` directly in `:root` with the stacks, skipping the indirection, and reference those in `@theme inline`.

I need to avoid mapping `--font-sans: var(--font-sans)` inside the theme block since that's circular — Tailwind might not resolve self-references correctly. I'll keep using the `--nova-font-*` source variables to avoid that issue, and I'm double-checking how Tailwind's preflight resolves `--default-font-family` through `--theme(--font-sans, initial)` to make sure my override still takes effect properly.

To be safe, I'll add an explicit `html { font-family: var(--nova-font-sans); }` rule inside my own base layer, since it will come after preflight's rules within the same `@layer base` due to source order.

I also need to update the existing unlayered body rule to use `var(--nova-font-sans)` directly, and confirm `.font-mono`/`.font-heading` utilities will correctly resolve since their underlying CSS variables are defined in `:root`.

Now I'm checking font fallback behavior on Chinese Windows — Tailwind's default sans stack resolves `system-ui` to Microsoft YaHei UI, whereas my custom stack prioritizes Segoe UI for Latin text with CJK fallbacks like PingFang SC that don't exist on Windows, so I need to verify the fallback chain actually lands on a real CJK font there.

YaHei UI, whose different ascent/descent ratios shift the baseline within the line box even when line-height is fixed by Tailwind's explicit values. Since mixed Latin/CJK text uses separate font metrics per glyph run, each run's inline box gets centered independently via the half-leading model, causing subtle pixel-level vertical misalignment between scripts on the same line.

With fixed line-height, only the primary font's metrics drive the half-leading calculation, so switching from YaHei UI to Segoe UI as primary shifts the baseline position slightly—maybe a pixel—and CJK glyphs sitting on that shared baseline could look subtly off-center vertically in tight buttons since their ideographic em box extends asymmetrically above and below the baseline.

Checking YaHei UI's metrics confirms it was actually designed to match Segoe UI, so the difference is negligible—meaning the font stack swap should be visually near-neutral for CJK on Windows while fixing the mono stack to be truly monospace, with Consolas as the reliable fallback since Cascadia isn't guaranteed present.

Segoe UI Variable Text only exists on Windows 11, gracefully skipped on Windows 10, and its metrics are close enough to standard Segoe UI to be a safe modern touch. I'm also confirming the Mac/Windows split works correctly—PingFang SC handles CJK after SF on Mac, while YaHei UI takes over on Windows since Apple's system fonts aren't present there. # DotCraft Error Diagnosis

Use persisted evidence to explain a DotCraft failure. Check operational logs first. For thread failures, treat rollout JSONL as the authority for thread history and use `state.db` for projections, runtime state, and traces.

## Safety

- Keep diagnosis read-only. Do not edit logs, `state.db`, or rollout files unless the user asks for repair.
- Read SQLite with `mode=ro`; copy evidence to a temporary directory before using a client that may write.
- Do not dump prompts, model output, tool arguments/results, provider history entries, credentials, or raw trace JSON. Use bounded sanitized previews only when necessary.
- Cite log timestamps/categories, rollout lines/items, or trace event IDs for each conclusion.

## Workflow

1. **Set the failure window.** Record the approximate local time, workspace, component, and any thread, Turn, request, process, or connection ID.
2. **Check operational logs.** Read the newest files around that window:
   - Hub: `~/.craft/logs/dotcraft-hub-*.log`
   - Workspace host: `<workspace>/.craft/logs/dotcraft-*.log`
   - Read the applicable `Logging.Directory` setting before assuming `logs`. `Logging.Enabled`, retention, or a custom directory can explain missing files.
   - For managed AppServer startup, inspect both the Hub log and the target workspace log.
   - Correlate timestamp, severity, PID, category, and scopes such as `Module`, `WorkspacePath`, `RequestMethod`, `RequestId`, `ThreadId`, and `TurnId`.
3. **Inspect thread evidence when relevant.** Run the bundled summarizer against the matching rollout and database:

```powershell
python path\to\dotcraft-error-diagnosis\scripts\analyze_dotcraft_thread.py `
  --state-db "D:\path\to\workspace\.craft\state.db" `
  --thread "D:\path\to\workspace\.craft\threads\active\thread_x.jsonl"
```

4. **Reconstruct current thread state.**
   - Apply `turn_state_replaced` by Turn ID and let it replace earlier incremental state for that Turn.
   - Apply `thread_rolled_back` before reporting Turns; ignore rolled-back tail Turns as current evidence.
   - Report model and provider history only as schema, boundary, count, source, reason, and validation metadata.
5. **Correlate state and traces.**
   - Read `trace_session_bindings` for `root_thread_id = thread_id`. The main session often has `binding_kind = threadMain`; subagents and maintenance forks may have different session keys.
   - Inspect `trace_sessions` counters, duration, finish reason, maintenance forks, and prompt drift.
   - Query `trace_events` by `session_key` and timestamp. Prioritize events with `type = 'Error'`, tool failures, unusual finish reasons, or a failed request immediately before the rollout `Error` item.
6. **Conclude from the strongest evidence.** Separate a confirmed root cause from an inference. Recommend the smallest durable fix and relevant regression test.

## Output

- **Finding**: root cause or most likely failure class.
- **Evidence**: 3-6 bullets with timestamps, rollout line/item IDs, trace event IDs, and table names.
- **Fix**: concrete remediation steps.
- **Residual risk**: what remains uncertain and what extra evidence would settle it.

+# Read-only, content-free inspection of one DotCraft thread's failure window.

+import json
+import pathlib
+import sqlite3
+import sys

+WS = pathlib.Path(r"F:\项目\nova-image-studio\.craft")
+THREAD = "thread_20260928_22oc7a"
+ROLLOUT = WS / "threads" / "active" / f"{THREAD}.jsonl"
+DB = WS / "state.db"
+LINE_LO, LINE_HI = 650, 676

+
+CONTENT_KEYS = {"text", "content", "arguments", "args", "result", "output", "reasoning", "summary", "message",
+                "prompt", "data", "image", "delta", "value", "input", "instructions", "preview", "body", "error",
+                "payload_text", "raw", "json"}
+META_HINTS = ("type", "kind", "status", "reason", "role", "_id", "id_", "turnid", "itemid", "time", "_at", "model",
+              "provider", "name", "source", "state", "phase", "boundary", "schema", "version", "mode", "code", "finish")
+
+
+def is_meta(key):
+    k = str(key or "").lower()
+    return k not in CONTENT_KEYS and (k == "id" or any(h in k for h in META_HINTS))
+
+
+def shape(v, key=None, depth=0):
+    if isinstance(v, dict):
+        return f"<dict {len(v)}>" if depth >= 6 else {k: shape(x, k, depth + 1) for k, x in v.items()}
+    if isinstance(v, list):
+        if depth >= 6:
+            return f"<list {len(v)}>"
+        out = [shape(x, key, depth + 1) for x in v[:6]]
+        return out + ([f"+{len(v) - 6} more"] if len(v) > 6 else [])
+    if isinstance(v, str):
+        s = v.strip()
+        if s[:1] in "{[" and len(s) > 1:
+            try:
+                return {"<json>": shape(json.loads(s), key, depth + 1)}
+            except ValueError:
+                pass
+        if is_meta(key) and len(v) <= 80 and "\n" not in v:
+            return v
+        return f"<str len={len(v)}>"
+    return v
+
+
+def dump(obj, limit=1400):
+    text = json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False, default=str)
+    return text if len(text) <= limit else text[:limit] + f" …(+{len(text) - limit})"
+
+
+print(f"== rollout lines {LINE_LO}-{LINE_HI} (structure only) ==")
+with ROLLOUT.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
+    for n, line in enumerate(fh, start=1):
+        if n < LINE_LO:
+            continue
+        if n > LINE_HI:
+            break
+        try:
+            print(n, f"bytes={len(line.encode('utf-8'))}", dump(shape(json.loads(line))))
+        except ValueError as error:
+            print(n, "unparseable", error)
+
+con = sqlite3.connect(DB.resolve().as_uri() + "?mode=ro", uri=True)
+con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
+
+
+def cols(table):
+    return [r[1] for r in con.execute(f"PRAGMA table_info({table})")]
+
+
+def row_view(row):
+    view = {}

Looking at the token usage data, request index 32 shows a big jump in output tokens (16156) compared to the prior request 31 (8344), while both usage events landed at nearly the same timestamp. I'm trying to reconcile the timing gaps between these usage reports — one shows 12.3 minutes since the previous usage while the other shows only about 51ms, suggesting there might be two usage reports emitted per response rather than a strict one-to-one mapping.

The 16156 output tokens with finish_reason "length" suggests the model hit its output cap, and since reasoning tokens show as 0 despite 36 thinking blocks being present, it seems the provider folds thinking tokens into the overall output count rather than reporting them separately.

I'm trying to piece together the timeline of requests around 07:20-07:32 to figure out which RequestIndex corresponds to which tool call and response, since the token usage entries at 31 and 32 could be tied to different calls in the sequence.

So it seems like the function call at 07:20:04 got a result back at 07:20:05, but then the next assistant response only came at 07:32:26 — a huge gap of over 12 minutes — with no function_call this time, just reasoning and text, which matches the failed retry pattern I'm suspecting.

That's likely just a measurement artifact from the diagnostic tool measuring gap between usage reports rather than actual cache expiry timing. The token count differences between cached inputs aren't the real issue here — just a secondary detail, not the root cause.

Reconsidering the two usage events again: one shows input 57965/output 8344, the next shows input 66138/output 16156, both timestamped together, with the difference roughly matching the prior output size. That suggests the usage reporting for one call may have gotten delayed or attributed to the wrong timestamp rather than reflecting an actual anomaly.

Actually, call 32's input of 66138 equals call 31's input plus its output, which suggests call 32's request included call 31's response as context — meaning call 31 finished normally at 07:20:04 with a long 8344-token output, and call 32 is the one that failed. Regardless of the exact accounting, what matters is that the failed request (RequestIndex 32) hit finish_reason "length" with 16156 output tokens, no tool call, essentially empty text, and a stream duration of about 740 seconds.

I checked whether 16156 aligns with a common max_tokens setting like 16384 and it's close but not exact, so the limit likely comes from a provider default rather than an explicit config value — I searched the workspace config for MaxOutputTokens or MaxTokens settings and found nothing, and even a recursive grep through the project's config directory turned up no matches, so I still need to check the global config file for where this limit is actually set.

I'm considering grepping the global config safely by searching only for specific key names like MaxTokens, ReasoningEffort, or Thinking, avoiding exposure of any secrets like API keys, since pinpointing where the setting lives would help me recommend the smallest concrete fix — whether that's raising the output token limit or lowering reasoning effort.

Actually I think I already have enough to form the diagnosis: the model exhausted its per-response output token budget (16156 tokens, mostly reasoning) before emitting any tool call, producing a "length" finish reason with essentially empty text, and DotCraft treated this truncated response as terminal rather than retrying or continuing the turn.

ReasoningOutputTokens is 0 since the provider doesn't separately track thinking tokens, so that 16K output covers the reasoning too. The diagnostic event shows a 12.3-minute duration on attempt 1 of 5, with visible output emitted and no failure kind — meaning the stream itself completed normally, so no retry logic kicked in. The rollout confirms the timeline: function_result at 07:20:05Z followed by the assistant's reasoning+text response at 07:32:26Z with no function call, and turn_001 is marked Failed while the session's error_count sits at 0.

Context compaction count is also 0, ruling that out, and context usage was only ~60.7K tokens — nowhere near the window limit, so this isn't an overflow issue either. Checking the hub log, the AppServer for this workspace started cleanly at 14:09:28 with no errors afterward; the only error logged belongs to a different workspace entirely.

So the real culprit is model output-length truncation: my prior response, meant to write globals.css, burned its entire output budget on reasoning about a large CSS rewrite and hit the length limit before ever emitting a tool call, which is why DotCraft marked the turn as Failed.

That's really on me for over-deliberating in a single response instead of writing the file incrementally. I also notice the rollout file is 12MB, likely from persisted base64 screenshot images, but since context usage was only ~60K tokens, that's unrelated to the failure — worth mentioning as a ruled-out red herring rather than the actual cause.

Actually the rollout size isn't relevant here — the real context usage was only about 60.7K tokens, and there was no compaction, so I shouldn't speculate further on where the 12MB went.

For the fix: nothing's actually broken, I just need to resume the UI work with smaller incremental steps — writing globals.css in chunks and editing files piece by piece rather than planning the whole rewrite in one shot. On the config side, I could consider raising the max output token ceiling or lowering reasoning effort for long implementation sessions, though I don't see MaxTokens or Model keys in the workspace config, so it's likely inherited from a global default I'd need to check.

I could offer to check the global config and adjust it rather than diagnosing further myself, per the skill's guidance to recommend the smallest durable fix. I'm also puzzling over whether 16156 is really the hard cap — it's not a round number, so maybe the configured limit is something like 16384 and the actual count reflects some dynamic calculation rather than a fixed ceiling.

Since I can't pin down the exact mechanism, I'll frame it more loosely as "roughly 16K output tokens" and note that finish_reason=length simply signals the per-response output cap was hit, without overclaiming the precise number. I'm also considering whether request 31's usage of 8344 output tokens relates to 32's 16156 — maybe the provider stream flushes cumulative usage at multiple points but only records them at the terminal event, which could explain the discrepancy.

That timing contradiction makes me doubt the continuation theory anyway. I'll not try to resolve the discrepancy and instead just report the RequestIndex 32 figures directly, noting the terminal timestamp shows 16,156 output tokens for that request.

For residual risk, I should keep it focused: the exact configured token cap isn't visible in the trace since there's no explicit MaxTokens in workspace config, so it likely falls back to a default. arguments.newString:
- For a Turn that ends with no tool call and little or no text, check `ResponseTerminal` events for `finish_reason = 'length'` with `MetadataJson.hasToolCall = false`. Then read the same `RequestIndex` in `TokenUsage` (`OutputTokens`; some providers report `ReasoningOutputTokens = 0` and count thinking inside `OutputTokens`) and the `ProviderResponseDiagnostic` `stream_attempt` (`durationMs`, `failureKind`, `attemptNumber`). A completed stream with `finish_reason = 'length'` is an output-cap truncation, not a provider or network failure.
   - On long threads the analyzer's Markdown report can exceed tool output limits and lose its beginning. `Runtime State`, `Trace Correlation`, and `DB Table Counts` come last, so read the tail or query `trace_events` directly for the failure window.
6. **Conclude from the strongest evidence.**

1. **Set the failure window.** Record the approximate local time, workspace, component, and any thread, Turn, request, process, or connection ID.
2. **Check operational logs.** Read the newest files around that window:

  --thread "D:\path\to\workspace\.craft\threads\active\thread_x.jsonl"

   - Apply `turn_state_replaced` by Turn ID and let it replace earlier incremental state for that Turn.
   - Apply `thread_rolled_back` before reporting Turns; ignore rolled-back tail Turns as current evidence.
   - Report model and provider history only as schema, boundary, count, source, reason, and validation metadata.
5. **Correlate state and traces.**
   - Read `trace_session_bindings` for `root_thread_id = thread_id`. The main session often has `binding_kind = threadMain`; subagents and maintenance forks may have different session keys.
   - Inspect `trace_sessions` counters, duration, finish reason, maintenance forks, and prompt drift.
   - Query `trace_events` by `session_key` and timestamp. Prioritize events with `type = 'Error'`, tool failures, unusual finish reasons, or a failed request immediately before the rollout `Error` item.
6. **Conclude from the strongest evidence.** Separate a confirmed root cause from an inference. Recommend the smallest durable fix and relevant regression test.

- **Finding**: root cause or most likely failure class.
- **Evidence**: 3-6 bullets with timestamps, rollout line/item IDs, trace event IDs, and table names.
- **Fix**: concrete remediation steps.
- **Residual risk**: what remains uncertain and what extra evidence would settle it.

+# Read-only, content-free inspection of one DotCraft thread's failure window.
+# Prints structure, enum-like metadata, numbers and string lengths only (no prompts/outputs/tool payloads).
+import json
+import pathlib
+import sqlite3
+import sys
+
+WS = pathlib.Path(r"F:\项目\nova-image-studio\.craft")
+THREAD = "thread_20260928_22oc7a"
+ROLLOUT = WS / "threads" / "active" / f"{THREAD}.jsonl"
+DB = WS / "state.db"
+LINE_LO, LINE_HI = 650, 676
+TS_LO, TS_HI = "2026-09-28T07:19:30", "2026-09-28T07:33:30Z"
+
+CONTENT_KEYS = {"text", "content", "arguments", "args", "result", "output", "reasoning", "summary", "message",
+                "prompt", "data", "image", "delta", "value", "input", "instructions", "preview", "body", "error",
+                "payload_text", "raw", "json"}
+META_HINTS = ("type", "kind", "status", "reason", "role", "_id", "id_", "turnid", "itemid", "time", "_at", "model",
+              "provider", "name", "source", "state", "phase", "boundary", "schema", "version", "mode", "code", "finish")
+
+
+def is_meta(key):
+    k = str(key or "").lower()
+    return k not in CONTENT_KEYS and (k == "id" or any(h in k for h in META_HINTS))
+
+
+def shape(v, key=None, depth=0):
+    if isinstance(v, dict):
+        return f"<dict {len(v)}>" if depth >= 6 else {k: shape(x, k, depth + 1) for k, x in v.items()}
+    if isinstance(v, list):
+        if depth >= 6:
+            return f"<list {len(v)}>"
+        out = [shape(x, key, depth + 1) for x in v[:6]]
+        return out + ([f"+{len(v) - 6} more"] if len(v) > 6 else [])
+    if isinstance(v, str):
+        s = v.strip()
+        if s[:1] in "{[" and len(s) > 1:
+            try:
+                return {"<json>": shape(json.loads(s), key, depth + 1)}
+            except ValueError:
+                pass
+        if is_meta(key) and len(v) <= 80 and "\n" not in v:
+            return v
+        return f"<str len={len(v)}>"
+    return v
+
+
+def dump(obj, limit=1400):
+    text = json.dumps(obj, ensure_ascii=False, default=str)
+    return text if len(text) <= limit else text[:limit] + f" …(+{len(text) - limit})"
+
+
+print(f"== rollout lines {LINE_LO}-{LINE_HI} (structure only) ==")
+with ROLLOUT.open("r", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
+    for n, line in enumerate(fh, start=1):
+        if n < LINE_LO:
+            continue
+        if n > LINE_HI:
+            break
+        try:
+            print(n, f"bytes={len(line.encode('utf-8'))}", dump(shape(json.loads(line))))
+        except ValueError as error:
+            print(n, "unparseable", error)
+
+con = sqlite3.connect(DB.resolve().as_uri() + "?mode=ro", uri=True)
+con.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
+
+
+def cols(table):
+    return [r[1] for r in con.execute(f"PRAGMA table_info({table})")]
+
+
+def row_view(row):
+    view = {}
+    for k in row.keys():
+        v = row[k]
+        view[k] = v if isinstance(v, (int, float)) or v is None else shape(v, k)
+    return view
+
+
+tcols = cols("trace_events")
+print("\n== trace_events columns ==", tcols)
+ts_col = next((c for c in tcols if c in ("timestamp", "created_at", "occurred_at", "ts", "time")),
+              next((c for c in tcols if "time" in c or c.endswith("_at")), None))
+where, params = [f"{ts_col} BETWEEN ? AND ?"], [TS_LO, TS_HI]
+if "session_key" in tcols:
+    where.insert(0, "session_key = ?")
+    params.insert(0, THREAD)
+rows = con.execute(f"SELECT * FROM trace_events WHERE {' AND '.join(where)} ORDER BY {ts_col}", params).fetchall()
+print(f"== trace_events {TS_LO}..{TS_HI}: {len(rows)} rows ==")
+for r in rows:
+    print(dump(row_view(r), 1800))
+
+for table, sql in (("thread_turns", "SELECT * FROM thread_turns WHERE thread_id = ?"),
+                   ("thread_items", "SELECT * FROM thread_items WHERE thread_id = ? ORDER BY rowid DESC LIMIT 8")):
+    print(f"\n== {table} columns ==", cols(table))
+    try:
+        for r in con.execute(sql, (THREAD,)).fetchall():
+            print(dump(row_view(r), 1200))
+    except sqlite3.Error as error:
+        print("query failed:", error)

Now I'm mapping out what's left across the remaining todo items: finishing the layout.tsx theme-color tweak to close out tokens-backdrop, then moving into primitives (utils, button, input, and the various Radix-based components), then the shell components like WorkspaceShell, mode tabs, dialogs, and gallery panels, and finally performance cleanup work.

I'm reminding myself to keep each response small and batch parallel edits rather than over-planning, since a prior attempt failed from too much upfront reasoning. Now I'm starting on the primitives, beginning with the utils.ts file where I'm extending tailwind-merge to account for custom shadow tokens defined in globals.css.

Writing button variant classes...

Defining button style variants...

In dark mode that's still a subtle brighten, which works fine. I'm also checking that consumer className overrides merge correctly with the extended twMerge config, and confirming the sidebar tool button override for box-shadow still applies cleanly. Now I'm defining the input field styles with border, background, padding, and file-input variants.

Actually, that risks showing a border on inputs meant to be borderless, so I'll skip the hover border effect. I'm also dropping the dark-mode background overrides since the base variant now handles them fine, favoring a consistent field background, and I'm dialing back the focus ring opacity from 50% to something more subtle like 25%.

For accessibility, the ring color border itself should serve as the primary focus indicator, with the glow as a supplementary cue — same treatment applies to the textarea. Now I'm styling the select trigger with a rounded field background, hover and focus-visible states, and a distinct border/background treatment when the popup is open.

I need to confirm that `data-[popup-open]` needs to become the `[data-popup-open]` attribute selector syntax in Tailwind v4, since Base UI sets that attribute directly on the trigger. Then for the select popup styling, I'm defining a floating panel with max-height, anchor-width sizing, and open/close animation states using the data-open and data-closed custom variants I confirmed are defined in the Tailwind config, checking whether Base UI's Select.Popup actually applies the data-open attribute needed for those animations to trigger.

Adjusting item padding and rounding for dropdown items...

Adjusting spacing on labels and separators...

I'm applying the nova-float class to the popover content and removing the redundant border utility, since the base border-color rule from the layer system gets overridden by nova-float's own border shorthand anyway.

Now I'm moving to the tooltip styling, swapping the medium rounding and plain background for a larger radius, tighter padding, medium font weight, and a drop shadow. Then updating the dialog overlay to use a semantic scrim color with a slightly longer duration, and starting to rework the dialog content's layout classes.

Also checking the DialogFooter styling - it's fine since backdrop-filter isn't an issue, and I don't need to worry about consumers passing custom background classes. Now looking at the footer's margin and border styling to see if it needs adjustment too.

For the tabs list, I'm keeping the layout classes but swapping the muted background variant for a track background token to match the new theme system.

For tab triggers, I'm adjusting transition properties to be more specific, updating text color states to use muted-foreground consistently, and switching the active shadow style to a lifted variant plus tweaking background states for active tabs...

Adjusting switch colors...

Simplest path: keep the thumb styling unchanged and just drop the dark-mode track override, since removing it preserves visible contrast against the faint unchecked state. I'll leave that alone and adjust the slider thumb's border and background opacity slightly instead.

For the toggle-group, I'm swapping the muted background for a track color and updating the pressed state to use a stronger surface color with a lifted shadow, plus broadening the transition to cover both color and background-color properties.

The badge stays unchanged, and I'm confirming the dropdown menu item's focus states work fine with the new accent tint. Now I'm getting ready to apply these edits carefully, making sure I match the exact original text from the files I read earlier before making changes.

Adjusting the base button classes...

I'm confirming the default variant now gets a proper hover state, and checking that primary buttons inside the params bar and theme toggle in the sidebar still behave consistently with existing overrides.

For select.tsx I need to edit three separate lines (trigger, popup, item) — since parallel edits on the same file could race, I'll do them sequentially or use larger multi-line matches. For the smaller primitive files like select, popover, tooltip, input, and textarea, it might be simpler to just rewrite them entirely rather than doing targeted edits.

But full rewrites risk introducing typos in unrelated code and cost more tokens than targeted edits, so I'm leaning toward keeping the approach surgical. For this pass I'll handle utils.ts with a quick write, then work through button.tsx's variant definitions using precise edits.

I want to avoid running parallel edits on the same file since concurrent read-modify-write could clobber changes, so I'll sequence multi-edit files carefully. Planning the batch: utils.ts, button.tsx's variant block, input.tsx, textarea.tsx, popover.tsx, tooltip.tsx, switch.tsx, and toggle-group.tsx's root and item styling, treating same-file edits as sequential rather than parallel to avoid lost updates.

Splitting the remaining primitives across four batches — button base styles, select/dropdown/dialog/tabs variants first, then their content sections, then item-level styling — keeping each batch quick and self-contained. Now writing the utils.ts import statement...

Still writing input styles...

Reconstructing the exact input styling string...

Comparing textarea styling changes...

Now checking popover.tsx, where I'm swapping the popover's border/shadow styling for a floating glass effect with rounded corners.

For tooltip.tsx, I'm adjusting the rounding, padding, and adding a medium font weight with a shadow to give it more depth.

For switch.tsx, I'm simplifying the unchecked background so it no longer needs a separate dark mode variant.

Now I'm moving to the toggle-group root styles...

Updating button variant styles...

I'll also update that small theme-color hex value tweak. Now marking tokens-backdrop as complete and moving primitives to in-progress, then sending the first batch with a brief note in Chinese.

The GifModeChoiceDialog overlay has the same structure, so the identical fix applies there too. Now I'm moving on to update the panel's className styling to match.

Locating that unique substring to swap in the updated class string, and double-checking that the transition and scale utilities behave correctly together in this Tailwind version.

Updating similar dialog panels...

Adding stop-propagation handlers and the panel container styling...

For ConfirmDialog I can apply a similar approach: the overlay and panel blocks are separated by a style section, so I'll edit them together as one contiguous block, relying on fuzzy matching to handle whitespace differences.

Still writing modal panel styles... I'm deciding to split this into separate edits — overlay first, then the panel — for safety, since the ConfirmDialog panel line is a unique substring I can target directly.

Still writing panel styles...

For ConfirmDialog I'll handle the overlay now and save the panel for the next batch. I'm also lining up the simpler single-edit perf cleanups: chip fixes in ImageHoverActions, AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, AttachmentChips, and GifFrameTuner, plus a careful find-replace in canvas-node-dialogs.tsx to drop the backdrop blur class.

I'm listing out the remaining files needing similar single-line edits — image-annotation-editor, WorkspaceHeader, fullscreen-image-viewer, canvas-toolbar, canvas-zoom-controls, canvas-context-menu, canvas-mention-editor, and AgentInputEditor. That's a large batch, but since each edit targets a different file, I can fire them in parallel without conflict, even though it adds up to a lot of tool calls in one go.

Now I'm working through the chip styling replacements across AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, PromptGallerySubcomponents, and ImageHoverActions — swapping the translucent white background and blur for a darker semi-transparent black with a subtle inset ring, while keeping hover and focus states intact. I need to double-check that combining the new ring styling with the existing focus-visible ring doesn't create a conflicting or overly busy visual effect.

For the remaining files, I'm mapping out separate edits: PromptGallerySubcomponents needs two distinct changes (chip in one spot, overlay background in another) so they'll go in different batches; AttachmentChips just needs its backdrop blur removed; and GifFrameTuner's fullscreen overlay should drop the blur and go with a solid background instead of the translucent one.

bumping to 18px blur with saturate should be similar cost given the small area, and the mini-map keeps its own treatment. This is a continuation of earlier work. So far I've reworked the global styles with tokens, glass components, and motion, updated the tailwind merge utility, and revised button, input, textarea, and popover components with consistent focus rings and field backgrounds. Now I need to keep going through the remaining components.

I'm continuing that same sweep across tooltip, switch, toggle-group, layout theme-color, and the workspace tabs and shell classes, then moving through dialogs (Gif choice, confirm, quick prompt), toast, select, tabs, dropdown-menu, and various editor and canvas components -- stripping unnecessary blur effects, standardizing floating-panel classes, and making several previously translucent surfaces opaque for the toolbar, zoom controls, message bubbles, and image galleries.

Now I'm dropping the blur on attachment chips and the prompt gallery scrim, and updating the hover overlay on the completed job card. For the second image-viewer overlay, I'm planning to wrap the Maximize icon in a glass-style circular chip with a translucent dark background and subtle ring, then update the overlay markup itself as a follow-up edit since both changes hit the same file sequentially.

Now moving to WorkspaceShell, I need two separate edits: adding a `nova-gallery-panel` class to the gallery wrapper div so the unlayered styles can override its border, background, and shadow at wider breakpoints, and updating the error toast portal to use `nova-float nova-toast` classes with adjusted border and radius so it inherits the popover foreground color properly.

I also still need to apply the chip edit in PromptGallerySubcomponents separately from the scrim change, and I'm deciding whether to refine the dropdown-menu item styling — bumping corner radius and padding across DropdownMenuItem, SubTrigger, CheckboxItem, and RadioItem for a slightly roomier, more modern look.

For consistency, I should also adjust the label padding so it aligns with the items' new spacing, and update the select item's radius and highlighted state to match the rest of the menu components.

Moving to tabs trigger styling: swapping `text-foreground/60` for `text-muted-foreground`, cleaning up the dark mode overrides that are now redundant, and replacing the shadow/border variant classes with a cleaner `shadow-lifted` approach for active states.

I could try one combined edit spanning that whole segment, but it's safer to do these as separate sequential replacements since the exact string is long and fuzzy matching may misfire.

Still writing tab styles...

I'm confirming this is one contiguous edit, and checking that the dark mode active-state styling for tabs doesn't conflict with my variant fix, since some of those border/background rules were already removed elsewhere. I also want to check the WorkspaceModeTabs component next.

I do want to double check that the unconditional gradient-over-popover background in `.nova-app-settings` still looks right on mobile where the sheet goes full-screen.

Same story for ImageGenerationWorkbench — the panel and prompt-surface classes get their border/background swapped via CSS variables, though I should check what background the inner Textarea ends up using since the consumer also passes its own bg utility.

Now I'm planning verification: run the full build with typecheck, run lint, then run the vitest suite covering WorkspaceHeader, TextToImageForm, S3AssetBrowser, and the CanvasEditor regression test to make sure nothing asserts on specific classes. After that, I'll copy the build output into the bench "after" folder, run the benchmark against both targets with three repeats, and compare the resulting screenshots before iterating on any remaining visual issues.

I'm also weighing whether to do a final rebuild without the desktop flag, since the normal dev build enables the PWA service worker while the desktop build disables it -- since `out/` is gitignored, leaving my last desktop-flavored build in place should be fine unless the user specifically deploys `out` for web use.

Actually, since the backend serves `out` directly, missing the PWA service worker would be a real functional difference for anyone running `npm start`. I should do one final normal build at the end without the flag so it regenerates the service worker and workbox files, restoring things to match the original state.

I should also clean up the temp bench directory in %TEMP% with all the baseline/after screenshots and profiles, but recursive forced deletes are blocked by policy. I'll try a non-forced removal and if that fails, just tell the user the path so they can clean it up themselves, while keeping the before/after screenshots accessible for their reference.

I'll settle on telling the user the folder holds before/after screenshots and can be deleted afterward, and I'll attempt removing the browser profile directories at the end without forcing it if blocked.

I confirm v4 handles bare-number opacity modifiers fine, and other utility classes like rounded corners and toast animations are properly defined. I'm also verifying that Tailwind's border utility correctly overrides the base glass border color for tone-specific elements, and that the hairline ring shadow gives enough definition against light backgrounds where the glass edge would otherwise be nearly invisible.

Checking further, dropdown SubContent, canvas toolbar, and mini-map components all correctly inherit the float/blur styling without conflicts, and I'm noting that removing text-popover-foreground from DialogContent needs a final pass to confirm nothing else depends on it.

I'm double-checking the dialog animation — the translate positioning for centering combined with the enter/exit transform animations shouldn't conflict since they're composed properly by the animation utility classes.

Now I'm checking the border radius: the app-settings class sets 20px at small breakpoint, unlayered so it overrides the responsive rounded utility, and this changes what the settings modal previously used at wider viewports.

I'm also tracing the shell's height and padding behavior across breakpoints—on mobile the padding utilities don't apply so full width works fine, and in agent-tab mode with dvh sizing the frame properly fills remaining space via flex-1, while other tabs use min-height screen so they're never smaller than the viewport.

Now I'm checking the frame's glass styling in both light and dark modes, confirming the rounded corners and translucent backdrop colors look right against the dark background. I'm also planning to review the disabled state of the image generation workbench when no API key is configured, which shows a subtle tinted icon chip.

I'm now considering whether the completed job card's icon edit can be merged into the same replaceAll pass as the overlay changes, checking whether the maximize icon markup that follows is unique enough to target directly.

I want the Maximize chip to have a subtle scale-in on hover, since it's cheap to add via a transform transition. I'm confirming the group-hover trigger is correctly tied to the parent media container so the effect activates properly.

Now I'll make this batch of edits and kick off the build afterward, then queue one more small batch before running the build again.
