payload.text:
This is just a tool continuation marker, not a new instruction, so I should keep going with the work already in progress. Recapping where things stand: globals.css is rewritten and compiling fine, and the first batch of primitives is done, including the popover, utils, toggle-group root, and layout theme-color update.

Now I'm working through the remaining primitives: button variants need `transition-all` swapped for an explicit transition list that includes translate so the active-press effect still animates properly, the toggle-group item's pressed state needs updated surface and shadow tokens, and the slider thumb styling needs a similar background and shadow adjustment.

I'm also mapping updates across select, dropdown-menu, dialog, and tabs: swapping muted/popover backgrounds for the new field/scrim/surface tokens, upgrading corner radii and ring styles to the nova-float treatments, and replacing implicit transition-all with explicit transitions where needed.

For tabs specifically, I need to strip out the dark: overrides on the active trigger since they'd now conflict with the new dark mode palette — dark:data-active:bg-input/30 would render nearly invisible against surface-strong, so those classes have to go, along with redundant dark:text-muted-foreground variants now that the base token handles it correctly in both modes.

Checking the other components — badge.tsx, button.tsx destructive variants, and dropdown-menu's destructive item styling all have dark: classes that remain reasonable and can stay untouched. Now I'm moving on to the shell components, tracing how WorkspaceShell.tsx applies wide-mode classes and bare workspace styling across the frame, workspace container, and gallery panel wrapper.

Continuing through more files: WorkspaceModeTabs.tsx needs updates to its wide and horizontal list classes, Toast.tsx needs a rewrite, and the dialog components (ConfirmDialog, QuickPromptDialog, GifModeChoiceDialog) need their overlay scrims and panels updated to use the new float-sheet styling. I'm also noting that PromptGallerySubcomponents.tsx and CompletedJobCard.tsx have overlay/hover styles that need the same scrim treatment, and several chip components (ImageHoverActions, AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, PromptGallerySubcomponents) share the same hover-chip pattern that should be swapped from a white/blur style to a darker ring-based background for better contrast and performance.

Removing more backdrop-blur instances...

Also reconsidering whether canvas-toolbar should keep real blur since it floats over the panning canvas where re-blurring on pan could matter more than in static popovers.

Now I'm moving to the remaining primitives batch — select, dropdown-menu, dialog, tabs, button base, toggle-group item — but since dropdown-menu and select have multiple edit spots per file, I need to be careful about doing parallel edits within the same file since ordering isn't guaranteed, so I'll edit one file at a time or combine edits per file into a single call.

I could use replaceAll for the shared item padding classes across dropdown items, bumping them from a tighter `rounded-md px-1.5 py-1` to a roomier `rounded-lg px-2 py-1.5`, which increases item height slightly for a more modern feel while keeping the inset padding untouched. That seems like a worthwhile but modest improvement, so I'll plan it into the batching.

For the button component, I want to swap `transition-all` for a more targeted transition list covering color, background, border, and translate properties, while keeping `focus-visible:ring-3 focus-visible:ring-ring/50` as-is since keyboard focus rings benefit from stronger visibility on buttons compared to inputs.

For the select trigger, I'm updating the background to use `bg-field`, switching hover and open states to `bg-surface-hover`, adjusting the focus ring opacity to `/25` for consistency with inputs, and narrowing the transition properties similarly. I'm checking that the hover brightening effect works correctly in both dark and light modes given the new surface tokens.

Then I'm moving through several more component tweaks: adding a `nova-float` class and rounding to the dropdown menu content while dropping the old ring/shadow styling, switching the dialog overlay to `bg-scrim` with a slightly longer duration, renaming the tabs list background to `bg-track`, and starting on similar token updates for the toggle group item styles.

Beyond the CSS token pass, I'm also planning the next batch of file edits — a full rewrite of Toast.tsx, and for ConfirmDialog.tsx I'm weighing whether to do separate edits for the overlay and panel classNames or one larger edit spanning both sections since they're separated by other style lines; a single combined edit is riskier since the old text has to match exactly, but I already have the file contents from an earlier read to work from.

I'm reworking the overlay's fade to use a background-color transition (transparent to scrim) instead of opacity, so it doesn't become a backdrop-filter root and block the panel's blur from seeing the page behind it, while the panel keeps its own opacity/scale fade unaffected.

The GifModeChoiceDialog overlay has the same structure, so the identical fix applies there too. Now I'm moving on to update the panel's className styling to match.

Locating that unique substring to swap in the updated class string, and double-checking that the transition and scale utilities behave correctly together in this Tailwind version.

Updating similar dialog panels...

Adding stop-propagation handlers and the panel container styling...

For ConfirmDialog I can apply a similar approach: the overlay and panel blocks are separated by a style section, so I'll edit them together as one contiguous block, relying on fuzzy matching to handle whitespace differences.

Still writing modal panel styles... I'm deciding to split this into separate edits — overlay first, then the panel — for safety, since the ConfirmDialog panel line is a unique substring I can target directly.

Still writing panel styles...

For ConfirmDialog I'll handle the overlay now and save the panel for the next batch. I'm also lining up the simpler single-edit perf cleanups: chip fixes in ImageHoverActions, AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, AttachmentChips, and GifFrameTuner, plus a careful find-replace in canvas-node-dialogs.tsx to drop the backdrop blur class.

I'm listing out the remaining files needing similar single-line edits — image-annotation-editor, WorkspaceHeader, fullscreen-image-viewer, canvas-toolbar, canvas-zoom-controls, canvas-context-menu, canvas-mention-editor, and AgentInputEditor. That's a large batch, but since each edit targets a different file, I can fire them in parallel without conflict, even though it adds up to a lot of tool calls in one go.

Now I'm working through the chip styling replacements across AgentImageGallery, AgentMessageBubble, PromptGallerySubcomponents, and ImageHoverActions — swapping the translucent white background and blur for a darker semi-transparent black with a subtle inset ring, while keeping hover and focus states intact. I need to double-check that combining the new ring styling with the existing focus-visible ring doesn't create a conflicting or overly busy visual effect.

For the remaining files, I'm mapping out separate edits: PromptGallerySubcomponents needs two distinct changes (chip in one spot, overlay background in another) so they'll go in different batches; AttachmentChips just needs its backdrop blur removed; and GifFrameTuner's fullscreen overlay should drop the blur and go with a solid background instead of the translucent one.

I'm also spotting the same pattern in image-annotation-editor's fullscreen container, and noticing that WorkspaceHeader and fullscreen-image-viewer both have a header bar with the semi-transparent background plus blur that needs the blur stripped, though I want to double check how that header nests inside its own blurred parent overlay since stacking backdrop-filters could behave differently than a single flat one.

Given that nesting, when the header sits inside the blurred fullscreen overlay, its own blur is really re-blurring whatever image content pans underneath it rather than the page behind everything — so removing that inner blur just stops the panned image from getting a second blur pass under the bar, which is fine to cut.

Continuing to swap out the border/shadow/blur combos across the canvas toolbar, zoom controls, context menu, and mention editor for the simpler nova-float style...

I'm also checking the CompletedJobCard hover overlays — the two duplicate absolute-positioned dark overlays with a centered Maximize icon that fade in on hover — to see if they need the same treatment.

Since these are near-duplicate blocks in the same file, I'll edit them one at a time to avoid conflicting matches. Redesigning the overlay with a gradient backdrop and a circular badge holding the Maximize icon for better contrast...

Now shifting to WorkspaceShell, which needs five separate edits across the shell classes, frame, workspace, gallery wrapper, and error portal sections — I'm planning the sequence for those.

I'm weighing whether parallel edits to the same file are actually safe, given uncertainty about tool execution order, and deciding to stick with the cautious sequential approach from before.

For WorkspaceModeTabs, I'm merging the adjacent wide-list and trigger edits into one batch, while keeping the horizontal list edit separate since it's further down.

I'm swapping out the active-state utility classes for the new data-active styling, replacing the old bg-card/shadow treatment with the surface-strong variant and group-data selector pattern.

So the TSX change is technically optional but I'll keep it for consistency and to avoid fighting with the CSS. Now I'm looking at the horizontal tab list styling with scrollbar hiding and overflow handling...

Base components batch one is done (buttons, inputs, Popover, Tooltip, switch). Next are the remaining component base styles and the shell. Different files go out in parallel; any file that needs several edits gets one edit per round to avoid overwriting.

payload.text:
This is a continuation of earlier work. So far I've reworked the global styles with tokens, glass components, and motion, updated the tailwind merge utility, and revised button, input, textarea, and popover components with consistent focus rings and field backgrounds. Now I need to keep going through the remaining components.

I'm continuing that same sweep across tooltip, switch, toggle-group, layout theme-color, and the workspace tabs and shell classes, then moving through dialogs (Gif choice, confirm, quick prompt), toast, select, tabs, dropdown-menu, and various editor and canvas components -- stripping unnecessary blur effects, standardizing floating-panel classes, and making several previously translucent surfaces opaque for the toolbar, zoom controls, message bubbles, and image galleries.

Now I'm dropping the blur on attachment chips and the prompt gallery scrim, and updating the hover overlay on the completed job card. For the second image-viewer overlay, I'm planning to wrap the Maximize icon in a glass-style circular chip with a translucent dark background and subtle ring, then update the overlay markup itself as a follow-up edit since both changes hit the same file sequentially.

Now moving to WorkspaceShell, I need two separate edits: adding a `nova-gallery-panel` class to the gallery wrapper div so the unlayered styles can override its border, background, and shadow at wider breakpoints, and updating the error toast portal to use `nova-float nova-toast` classes with adjusted border and radius so it inherits the popover foreground color properly.

I also still need to apply the chip edit in PromptGallerySubcomponents separately from the scrim change, and I'm deciding whether to refine the dropdown-menu item styling — bumping corner radius and padding across DropdownMenuItem, SubTrigger, CheckboxItem, and RadioItem for a slightly roomier, more modern look.

For consistency, I should also adjust the label padding so it aligns with the items' new spacing, and update the select item's radius and highlighted state to match the rest of the menu components.

Moving to tabs trigger styling: swapping `text-foreground/60` for `text-muted-foreground`, cleaning up the dark mode overrides that are now redundant, and replacing the shadow/border variant classes with a cleaner `shadow-lifted` approach for active states.

I could try one combined edit spanning that whole segment, but it's safer to do these as separate sequential replacements since the exact string is long and fuzzy matching may misfire.

Still writing tab styles...

I'm confirming this is one contiguous edit, and checking that the dark mode active-state styling for tabs doesn't conflict with my variant fix, since some of those border/background rules were already removed elsewhere. I also want to check the WorkspaceModeTabs component next.

Checking the dialog footer too — `bg-muted/50` on the glass sheet gives a subtle mint band in light mode, which is fine to leave. I'm considering whether the `-mx-4` without `-mb-4` causes spacing issues since the footer sits below content padded with p-4.

SettingsModal itself needs no TSX changes — the `nova-float-sheet` class flows through DialogContent, and `.nova-app-settings` already overrides the background and disables backdrop-filter, so the existing prop combination (`p-0 pt-0 gap-0 sm:max-w-5xl` plus rounding) merges fine. I do want to double check that the unconditional gradient-over-popover background in `.nova-app-settings` still looks right on mobile where the sheet goes full-screen.

Moving on, HistoryJobList needs nothing, and AgentChatWorkspace's classes are already fully covered by the unlayered CSS overriding border, background, shadow, and radius. Same story for ImageGenerationWorkbench — the panel and prompt-surface classes get their border/background swapped via CSS variables, though I should check what background the inner Textarea ends up using since the consumer also passes its own bg utility.

Now I'm planning verification: run the full build with typecheck, run lint, then run the vitest suite covering WorkspaceHeader, TextToImageForm, S3AssetBrowser, and the CanvasEditor regression test to make sure nothing asserts on specific classes. After that, I'll copy the build output into the bench "after" folder, run the benchmark against both targets with three repeats, and compare the resulting screenshots before iterating on any remaining visual issues.

I'm also weighing whether to do a final rebuild without the desktop flag, since the normal dev build enables the PWA service worker while the desktop build disables it -- since `out/` is gitignored, leaving my last desktop-flavored build in place should be fine unless the user specifically deploys `out` for web use.

Actually, since the backend serves `out` directly, missing the PWA service worker would be a real functional difference for anyone running `npm start`. I should do one final normal build at the end without the flag so it regenerates the service worker and workbox files, restoring things to match the original state.

I should also clean up the temp bench directory in %TEMP% with all the baseline/after screenshots and profiles, but recursive forced deletes are blocked by policy. I'll try a non-forced removal and if that fails, just tell the user the path so they can clean it up themselves, while keeping the before/after screenshots accessible for their reference.

I'll settle on telling the user the folder holds before/after screenshots and can be deleted afterward, and I'll attempt removing the browser profile directories at the end without forcing it if blocked.

Now I'm double-checking visual details post-build: the dark-mode active tab pill styling looks visible and correct, the tooltip's light-background/dark-text treatment matches the previous behavior, and I'm verifying whether Tailwind v4's opacity modifier syntax properly supports the toast's success-color transparency value.

I confirm v4 handles bare-number opacity modifiers fine, and other utility classes like rounded corners and toast animations are properly defined. I'm also verifying that Tailwind's border utility correctly overrides the base glass border color for tone-specific elements, and that the hairline ring shadow gives enough definition against light backgrounds where the glass edge would otherwise be nearly invisible.

Checking further, dropdown SubContent, canvas toolbar, and mini-map components all correctly inherit the float/blur styling without conflicts, and I'm noting that removing text-popover-foreground from DialogContent needs a final pass to confirm nothing else depends on it.

I'm double-checking the dialog animation — the translate positioning for centering combined with the enter/exit transform animations shouldn't conflict since they're composed properly by the animation utility classes.

Now I'm checking the border radius: the app-settings class sets 20px at small breakpoint, unlayered so it overrides the responsive rounded utility, and this changes what the settings modal previously used at wider viewports.

I'm also tracing the shell's height and padding behavior across breakpoints—on mobile the padding utilities don't apply so full width works fine, and in agent-tab mode with dvh sizing the frame properly fills remaining space via flex-1, while other tabs use min-height screen so they're never smaller than the viewport.

Now I'm checking the frame's glass styling in both light and dark modes, confirming the rounded corners and translucent backdrop colors look right against the dark background. I'm also planning to review the disabled state of the image generation workbench when no API key is configured, which shows a subtle tinted icon chip.

Let me line up the remaining batch of edits: updating the completed job card's overlay gradient and chip, adjusting the workspace shell gallery wrapper, tweaking the prompt gallery chip styling, fixing a tabs trigger class, standardizing dropdown menu item padding and rounding, and updating select item spacing and disabled states.

I'm now considering whether the completed job card's icon edit can be merged into the same replaceAll pass as the overlay changes, checking whether the maximize icon markup that follows is unique enough to target directly.

I want the Maximize chip to have a subtle scale-in on hover, since it's cheap to add via a transform transition. I'm confirming the group-hover trigger is correctly tied to the parent media container so the effect activates properly.

Now I'll make this batch of edits and kick off the build afterward, then queue one more small batch before running the build again.
Two small batches of edits remain. This one finishes the result card hover chip, the prompt gallery panel, the tab text colors, and the spacing on menu and dropdown items.

I still need to fix the checkbox/radio item padding for consistency, then move on to popover, tooltip, dialog, tabs, switch, slider, and toggle-group components. I'm also making the checkbox/radio dropdown items rounded and adjusting their padding, replacing both occurrences at once with consistent spacing.

Since sequential edits within the same file might race, I'll prioritize the checkbox/radio fix now and hold off on the label edit for a separate pass.

I'll sequence this into batches since the build needs to run after everything else: first batch handles the three main edits, then the dropdown label edit, then finally the build itself, since running them all in parallel risks race conditions.

payload.text:
Recapping the state: tests are passing (78 across 16 files, with some pre-existing act() warnings), but lint is failing with 17 problems—8 errors and 9 warnings, including a "cannot update ref during render" issue in the image annotation editor file.

Also PromptGalleryAccess and reverse-prompt-config errors, plus useAgentChat—none of these are in lines I actually edited (I only touched a className on line 630 of the editor). I want to confirm these are pre-existing issues rather than something I introduced, so I'm thinking through how to safely verify this without risky operations like git stash, maybe by just checking whether the flagged line numbers overlap with my actual changes.

Next I need to run the full benchmark across both targets with three repetitions, which will take roughly eight minutes given the number of scenarios and perf measurements per key. I'm weighing whether the exec tool has a timeout that could interrupt this, since the earlier no-perf baseline run did complete successfully.

Since foreground execution risks hitting a timeout, I'll run this in the background with output piped to a log file and poll it periodically. I'm also considering adding settings and dropdown captures to the dark wide scenario for better screenshot coverage, accepting the extra ~36 seconds this adds since both targets will run identical scenarios.

I'll skip trying to capture toast or confirm-dialog states since they're hard to trigger reliably. Once the benchmark finishes, I want to review a handful of key before/after screenshots across the light and dark wide/agent scenarios to spot-check the changes.

Then, after iterating on any visual issues, I need to figure out whether a normal rebuild is required at the end to restore the PWA service worker in the `out` directory, since my desktop build likely didn't include it — I'm trying to recall whether the existing `out` folder from before I started was itself a desktop build or a standard one.

Both the original `out/` and my desktop build produced 54 files, so file count alone doesn't tell me if sw.js was present either way. Since `sw.js` and `workbox-*.js` live in `public/` and are gitignored but currently present, Next.js copies them into `out/` regardless of whether the PWA flag was set — meaning `out/` gets the service worker file either way, and the real difference must lie in whether the service worker is actually registered/active rather than whether the file exists.

With PWA disabled, the client bundle wouldn't include the SW registration script, so a desktop build served by the backend would lack offline/PWA registration even though sw.js exists on disk. To be safe, I'll run a final normal `npm run build` with PWA enabled to regenerate `public/sw.js`/workbox files and produce an `out/` that matches what a standard build would look like, in case the app is later run via `npm start` serving `out/` directly.

I should double-check that these gitignored artifacts (sw.js, workbox files, next-env.d.ts) aren't inadvertently modifying tracked files like tsconfig.tsbuildinfo — I'll run `git status --short` after all builds to confirm nothing tracked changed. I also want to understand how the Electron desktop app actually consumes the frontend build.

Actually, this probably isn't necessary — the build artifacts (sw.js, workbox files) regenerate automatically on every normal build, and the user will rebuild anyway when they run the app since dev scripts trigger a fresh build first.

Now I'm thinking about cleanup: the temp benchmark directory has baseline/after copies, profile dirs, screenshots, and reports. I need to check whether deleting these counts as a "forced delete" requiring approval, since I recall being told forced deletes aren't permitted without interactive confirmation.

My plan is to try a plain recursive removal (no -Force flag) on the specific temp subpaths I created, since it's my own scoped directory and low-risk, and just report the path to the user if it gets blocked. I'm also reconsidering whether to preserve the before/after screenshots so the user can review them.

I'm weighing whether an inline visualization comparing before/after screenshots is feasible—embedding them as base64 thumbnails could work, but the raw PNGs are too large to embed directly without downscaling first.

I could add a "thumbs" capture mode using JPEG compression at reduced scale to shrink each screenshot to ~70-100KB, keeping the total HTML manageable at a few hundred KB. That extra effort seems worthwhile since showing a visual before/after comparison is a much stronger way to demonstrate the UI improvements than describing them in text.

Actually, embedding base64 images would mean pasting hundreds of KB directly into my output through WriteFile, which is impractical, and reading that file back would flood context too — so I need another approach, maybe referencing images by relative path instead of embedding them.

I'll skip the inline visualization idea since it's too risky, and instead just point the user to the screenshot folder for before/after comparison. I'll save screenshots to a TEMP folder rather than the repo's gitignored output directory, and let the user know they can delete it once they're done reviewing.

For the lint check, I'm running eslint with JSON output piped through a small Node script that parses the results and prints each error/warning with its file, line, and rule ID.

I'm second-guessing the piping behavior in PowerShell though—since file paths contain Chinese characters, I need to think about whether native-to-native pipes in PowerShell 7.4+ preserve raw bytes correctly or if encoding issues could corrupt the JSON before it reaches the parser.

Actually the worktree approach is too fiddly since ESLint's config resolution and node_modules wouldn't work properly outside the base path. Cross-referencing changed lines against flagged lines is sufficient: if flagged lines weren't touched by my diff, those errors pre-date my change. I should also check git status to confirm builds didn't dirty tracked files, then move on to updating the bench scenario for dark settings/dropdown screenshots before launching the benchmark in the background.

I'm adjusting the `web-wide-gen-dark` scenario config to add dropdown and settings flags, confirming the settings button text is still findable in web mode, and checking that the shorter viewport height doesn't cause issues with compact media rules. I'm also considering whether to add a toast screenshot by triggering a prompt copy action.

For a delete confirmation dialog screenshot, I'm thinking of clicking a card's delete button to trigger a glass ConfirmDialog, then adding a step to locate it via a title attribute containing '删除', wait briefly, capture the screenshot, and dismiss it with Escape or a cancel click.

I could check the lint cross-reference in parallel while the bench runs. For the bench edits, I'll add a confirm flag to the light scenario and add a confirm step after the dropdown step that finds the delete button by title or aria-label containing '删除', clicks it, waits, then takes a screenshot.

Then I click the '取消' button to cancel the dialog and wait briefly, catching any errors into a confirmError field. But I'm worried that if clicking cancel fails, the dialog stays open with body position fixed, which could distort perf measurements at rep 0 since the history scroller element would still be scrollable underneath — I may need to reload the page after the confirm step to avoid contaminating those results.

Right, shots only fire at rep 0, so reps 1-2 just load and count without issue. I could also fold the dark settings screenshot into the dark scenario by adding settings and dropdown flags, closing the dialog with Escape which base-ui handles reliably, and then define a separate light-confirm scenario for the confirm dialog case.

For the delete confirm dialog test, I'm clicking cancel rather than confirm, so nothing actually gets deleted, and the seeded data lives in a disposable profile anyway. For running the benchmark, I'll launch it in the background with repeat=3, redirecting output to a log file I can poll and read back later rather than blocking on it directly.

I also want to run a lint check alongside checking git diff and status to see what's changed. Then I need to edit bench.mjs to add the new scenario entries, likely as a couple of sequential edits to the same file since I'm adding both the scenario table and the corresponding test cases.

I'll plan three quick rounds: first lint/git plus the scenario edit, then the runScenario edit, then launching the bench, since the two edits are far apart in the file and can't be merged easily.

Actually, keeping the confirm dialog demo is worth it — it's a real test of the frosted glass and scrim transition, so I'll implement it rather than skip it.

Now I'm writing the lint command that runs eslint with JSON output to a temp file, then parses it with a small node script.

I'm confirming argv[1] behaves as expected with node -e, and checking that the temp path is ASCII-safe. Now I'm editing the SCENARIOS entry for the wide dark web generation scenario in bench.mjs.

Adding a new light-theme confirm scenario...

I'll send this first batch now, noting that tests pass (78/78) and lint shows 8 errors that I need to confirm are pre-existing rather than newly introduced.

Looking at the attached images now, the light-mode dropdown looks good with its frosted glass pill trigger and translucent menu panel showing the two options clearly. Now I'm checking the hover card's gradient overlay treatment in light mode.

For the dark settings dialog, the sheet with rounded corners and gradient sheen on the header looks solid, but I'm noticing the active "模型配置" tab has a bright mint-green border box around it that looks like a focus ring rather than intentional active-state styling — likely because the dialog auto-focuses the first tab on open, triggering focus-visible styles unintentionally.

The rectangular outline is likely the TabsTrigger's focus-visible styling, which I didn't modify, so it's probably pre-existing behavior triggered by the dialog's auto-focus rather than something introduced by my changes. I could verify against the baseline dark settings screenshot if it's cheap enough to check.

Looking at the rest of the settings modal: the model catalog panel has a clean bordered box, the mint "保存设置" primary button glows nicely in dark mode, the "检查模型" outline button reads as a glass pill, and the select triggers show dark field boxes with chevrons — all looking solid. The dialog itself sits dark and near-opaque against the dimmed page scrim.

But I notice the confirm screenshot is missing — `web-wide-gen-light-confirm--confirm.png` isn't in the listing, only the non-confirm shot, suggesting the confirm step failed. I suspect the delete button isn't matching my filter for '删除' in the title/aria-label/text, since the CompletedJobCard toolbar might use different labeling.

From the hover screenshot, the toolbar icons look like import-to-canvas, image, download, copy, retry, and the X delete button — likely titled "清除记录" or "删除记录". I'll grep to confirm.

Checking rep 1 perf numbers: web-gen-light history looks roughly equal between after and baseline, but web-wide-gen-light shows after slower than baseline in both reps so far, which is a bit concerning and worth digging into further.

Consistently the wide-mode history scroll runs 15-40% slower per frame in uncapped mode, and dark wide shows a similar slowdown. I'm considering possible causes — maybe the result cards now use a gradient background via a CSS variable instead of a solid color, which could add slight raster cost per new tile, or the box-shadow inset on the result card class might be contributing too.

At DPR 1.5 all scrollers get composited, so the panel background doesn't repaint during scroll — but the scroller's contents still get rasterized into tiles as they scroll, and since the history list itself has no opaque background, its translucent gradient cards get rasterized onto transparent tiles composited over the panel below.

The fixed `body::before` layer with `will-change: transform` adds a full-viewport composited layer drawn every frame, similar in cost to when that background was part of the root layer. The wide image-gen workspace being transparent makes no real difference either. I'm also considering the removal of the wide-mode opaque card background override that had blended the card color with the background color.

For the cards now using translucent gradients, the opaque-vs-transparent distinction doesn't affect compositing cost, only raster cost, and since GPU rasterization is enabled, gradient fills are cheap despite being shader-based rather than solid fills. Transform transitions on result cards are irrelevant at rest. Now I'm thinking through the history panel's new rounded corners and overflow-hidden with a box-shadow ring, since a rounded-corner clip on an ancestor of a composited scroller typically requires a mask layer.

Actually the baseline already had the same overflow/border-radius structure just at 16px instead of 20px, so there's no meaningful change there. I'm confirming this was already inside the wide-mode media query in the baseline too, so nothing new happens at 1440px width. Other elements like the active job list panel's gradient background and the toolbar's color-mix background remain static and unaffected.

Now I'm looking at scrollbar styling — the thin custom scrollbar previously had an invalid `scrollbar-color` value that got dropped, falling back to default colors, but now with valid custom colors set, Chrome switches from native theme painting to Blink-painted scrollbar layers for composited scrollers.

Custom scrollbars styled via ::-webkit-scrollbar might disable composited thumb animation, forcing main-thread repaint each scroll frame, though I'm unsure if Blink still composites these via PaintedScrollbarLayer. I'm also noting that since baseline's scrollbar-color declaration was invalid and dropped, Chrome 121+ would fall back to the ::-webkit-scrollbar rules already defined on the container.

Actually, since scrollbar-width was set to "thin" in baseline, Chrome ignores the custom ::-webkit-scrollbar styling and just renders a native thin scrollbar with default colors, while the updated version adds a custom scrollbar-color on top of "thin" — both are standard, composited scrollbars, so the cost should be comparable. Now I'm turning to a font change, since font-mono now maps to Cascadia Code or Consolas.

The card meta row text likely isn't monospace, so that impact is minor. I'm also considering the fixed grain backdrop tiled across the viewport — since it's a static composited layer with will-change, it only rasterizes once, and at higher DPR the texture size grows to roughly 12MB but is still just drawn as a single textured quad per frame.

Beyond that, adding this backdrop layer means the root layer becomes transparent and now needs blending against it, so instead of one opaque full-screen quad, the frame now composites two full-screen quads with blending. On an iGPU that's roughly 0.1-0.3ms extra per frame — noticeable if running uncapped where frame budgets are tight, but insignificant under normal 60Hz vsync.

Since viz has occlusion culling enabled for opaque quads, and the backdrop layer is marked contents-opaque because its background color fully covers the layer bounds, the occluded canvas background quad below gets culled entirely — confirming that path works out fine.

Splitting the layers this way now separates the root background into layer A, the opaque backdrop into layer B, and the app contents (including all the non-opaque panel glass backgrounds) into layer C, which spans the full screen and requires blending each frame since it's transparent where no panel exists. Previously these were combined into a single opaque root layer, so this split introduces one extra full-screen blended quad per frame — roughly +0.2ms on an iGPU at this resolution.

Comparing against the baseline dark settings screenshot, that mint outline on the first tab is pre-existing, not a regression I introduced. I also notice the baseline uses a native light scrollbar while mine has a themed thin scrollbar, which is an improvement. The delete button's title text is "移除."

I need to fix my confirm filter to catch "移除" instead of "删除." Looking at the perf numbers across repetitions, wide-mode light and dark scenarios show consistent regressions of roughly 0.4-0.6ms average frame cost, and the long-frame percentages are also higher after the change, though the absolute counts of janky frames are close enough that this might just be virtualization mount overhead rather than a real regression. I'm now checking the normal web-mode timings too, where light history after-values look slightly worse than baseline in one rep but comparable in another.

Given the user's constraint that overall performance can't be affected, I'm considering whether the fixed backdrop layer with `will-change: transform` in wide mode is adding an unnecessary composited layer plus forcing content transparency/blending — since in wide mode the document itself doesn't scroll, the baseline could paint the shell background straight into the root layer as a single opaque layer. Removing `will-change: transform` might let that pseudo-element paint into the root layer when there's no scrolling, but I need to think through how Chrome's compositing behaves differently for fixed-position elements when the viewport actually is scrollable versus not, since that determines whether this fix would help or hurt in normal mode.

Removing `will-change: transform` seems like the right call since fixed elements still get composited automatically when the root scrolls, avoiding repaint costs in normal mode, while in wide mode (non-scrollable root) it stays uncomposited like the baseline. I'm now checking whether other changes — the new box-shadow with an added hairline ring, and the gradient background on result cards versus the baseline's solid fill — might also affect rasterization cost in the wide history panel scroller.

The measured 0.5ms difference could just come from the extra composited layer during scroll, so the empirical test is to strip out `will-change` and re-measure. I also want to look at the `body::before` composited layer behavior at higher device pixel ratios.

Since the root layer now has transparent regions, it's no longer opaque and needs blending against the backdrop layer beneath it — removing `will-change` would make it opaque again, saving a full-screen composite pass. I'm also questioning whether Chrome actually composites fixed elements the way I remember in scrollable documents, since normal mode's scroll numbers don't clearly confirm that.

So Chrome likely composites position:fixed elements automatically when the document is scrollable, to avoid repaint on scroll, regardless of will-change. I could verify this empirically by testing normal window scroll behavior with and without will-change and comparing.

Actually, a cleaner solution is to only apply will-change conditionally: keep it active when the document itself scrolls (non-wide mode), since in wide mode the document has overflow hidden and doesn't scroll, so no separate layer is needed there.

On the other measurements, I'm noting the settings dialog scroll numbers vary a bit between runs, but since that dialog doesn't use the live blur effect in my version, the difference is likely unrelated noise rather than something caused by my change.

My plan: fix the CSS so will-change only applies during scroll, fix the sidebar padding, fix the bench confirm filter, then rebuild and run a targeted bench across the key wide-mode scenarios against baseline with a few repeats, keeping the earlier full run for the summary. I need to wait for the current bench run to finish first since it's using the same Chrome ports and a second concurrent run would conflict.

While that finishes on its remaining scenarios, I can safely edit CSS and rebuild since the build output goes to frontend/out while the running bench serves from temp copies. I'm scoping the will-change promotion to only apply in normal (non-wide) mode so wide mode doesn't pay for an extra composited layer it doesn't need.

I'm also reasoning through the sidebar status element's padding to align the queue summary text with the button icons above it — adding padding-inline of 12px so the 8px sidebar padding plus that inset lines up with the button's own 12px padding, matching visual alignment at 20px.

Now I'm updating the bench script's confirm filter to match delete/remove buttons by title, aria-label, or text content, checking for either "删除" or "移除", and starting to check for an open dialog by querying for fixed inset overlay elements.

Since the two CSS edits (will-change and status padding) are far apart in globals.css, I'm deciding to space them across turns rather than combine, running the will-change edit alongside the bench edit now and saving the status padding edit plus build for the next step.

It's worth just testing the will-change theory directly rather than reasoning about it further, since it's cheap to verify. My changes also add no live backdrop-filter blur at rest in either version, only when floating layers are open, which is worth noting in the report.

The baseline screenshot has the same mint rectangle on the first settings tab, so that was already there and my changes didn't cause it. The history cards' delete button is titled "移除", not "删除", which is why the confirm-dialog step never triggered.

On performance, all three rounds show wide-mode history scrolling a bit slower than baseline (about +0.3–0.6ms per frame with the frame rate uncapped). My read on the cause: the new fixed backdrop always carries `will-change: transform`. In wide mode the page itself never scrolls, so this only adds one more full-screen compositing layer per frame. Baseline painted that background straight into the root layer. The fix is to promote the layer only when the page scrolls, and I'll measure again afterwards to confirm.

payload.text:
Looking at the full run medians, web-gen-light history looks equal or slightly better after the change, but web-wide-gen-light history seems to regress somewhat, with p95 rising from 5.7 to 7.1.

I'm also seeing style recalc time consistently rise across scenarios, roughly 25% during scroll—likely because virtualization mounts/unmounts day groups, triggering more style recalcs. I'm trying to figure out which selectors could be responsible; the universal scrollbar selector should be cheap since it's a single rule, and the dark-mode `:where()` variant selectors should also be bucketed efficiently by class, so they shouldn't be the bottleneck either.

Each result card's gradient background needs var() resolution at style time, and both baseline and new code use color-mix, so that's more per-element computation. I'm also wondering whether the ~80 additional root custom properties matter, but since they're inherited via a shared pointer structure, they likely don't add per-element cost unless individual elements set their own variables.

Since Tailwind's shadow utilities set non-inherited `--tw-*` variables per element with copy-on-write semantics, the cost of my new shadow utilities on buttons should stay modest rather than compounding.

I'm ruling out font-family inheritance and dark-variant utility overhead as cheap, and starting to suspect the recalc cost sits somewhere in the style measurement itself rather than the CSS rules.

Checking whether animations tied to history-list-wide, waiting/failed cards, or the sidebar's rise effect could be contributing—but these seem unchanged from baseline since they've already completed by measurement time with backwards fill applied.

A finished animation on an ancestor shouldn't force descendant style recalcs, so that's probably not it. The transition utilities resolve similar var()-based timing and duration values either way, so they should be roughly equal too — the ~150ms difference across thousands of scroll frames works out to a tiny per-frame style cost that doesn't feel like the main contributor.

The frame-time increase looks more compositor/GPU-driven since it's uncapped, so I should stop chasing style recalc. The p99 gap in dark mode (33.2 vs 17.2ms) is more telling — with uncapped frames, long frames mostly come from virtualization mounting new day groups, and with translucent gradient cards plus a composited backdrop layer, the new tiles being rasterized are no longer simple solid colors, which could explain the heavier tail.

For the wide-mode scroll path specifically, I'm now thinking through two structural changes: the body::before layer promotion (via will-change) creates a full-screen extra translucent layer, making the root layer non-opaque and forcing full-screen blending — this is fixed in after2 by removing will-change in wide mode, which should restore the root layer to opaque and match baseline structure. I also want to check the history panel's glass effect as a second contributor.

I'm now verifying that the card gradient backgrounds are similarly translucent to the baseline's color-mix cards, and that alpha values roughly match so this isn't the source of the discrepancy — that checks out fine. I'm also noting the scrollbar-color fix on the virtual scroll container now paints correctly.

The result card now has two shadows at rest versus none in the baseline, adding a small raster cost when tiles render, plus the history panel's rounded clip. I'm also comparing toolbar backgrounds and card glass effects between baseline and new versions, which look roughly equivalent, then checking the grain tile setup.

I'm now tracing whether the root layer repaints during scrolling in wide mode — since the history list scrolls as a composited layer, scrolling itself shouldn't invalidate the root. But the virtualizer's visible-day tracking updates a header chip, which does trigger a small repaint region in the root layer, meaning the backdrop behind it re-rasters too. The SVG grain is a cached image so redrawing it is cheap, but I'm still weighing the cost of the radial gradient underneath.

I'm confirming normal mode looks fine too — the scroll timings there stay near or below baseline, and at rest neither mode has live backdrop-filter elements since menus and dialogs are closed. Now I'm noticing that `nova-float` is applied to canvas toolbar controls that stay mounted even when the tab is hidden, so I want to check whether the hidden tab panel actually gets `display: none` from the underlying Tabs implementation.

I'm reasoning through why the backdrop count stays at 0/0 even for the canvas toolbar — computed style should still resolve for display:none subtrees, but since baseline also shows 0 for the canvas toolbar, it's likely the canvas editor itself isn't mounted until its tab becomes active, so this is consistent behavior rather than a regression.

Fonts show the expected fix: baseline resolves to a fallback sans stack (confirming the bug), while after correctly resolves to a proper monospace stack. React error #418 appears equally in both versions, confirming it's pre-existing and unrelated to my change, and CSS size grew by about 7% which seems acceptable.

Now I'm planning the next comparison run — baseline vs after2 across several wide viewport scenarios with multiple repetitions, and considering whether to also include the original "after" build as a third target to isolate the effect of the will-change property.

Estimating timing per scenario given navigation, tab switches, and settings interactions, I'm calculating that two targets at three reps each would take roughly 7-8 minutes, versus over 11 minutes with three targets, so I'll start with just baseline vs after2 at repeat=3.

I'll keep the interleaving order simple and check that the target ports and output filenames are named correctly. I still need to review several screenshots from after2, including the confirm dialog and sidebar alignment, plus several remaining desktop and agent variant shots I haven't looked at yet.

While the targeted bench runs, I'll view those pending screenshots to check for visual issues, keeping in mind the prior "after" screenshots are still mostly valid since the CSS tweaks (will-change, status padding) don't meaningfully change visuals — so I want to confirm wide mode looks identical without will-change applied.

Also, toggling wide mode causes just a one-time repaint from the layer change, which is fine, and normal mode's blending cost from the translucent frame was already fine in the benchmark numbers. I'm now launching the targeted benchmark in the background across the remaining scenarios to confirm these conclusions hold.

While that runs, I'll check the after screenshots — they're reasonably sized PNGs so image token cost stays low. I'm also thinking ahead to the cleanup plan: after the final benchmark, I need to decide whether a normal build without the desktop flag is necessary to restore standard PWA registration in the output directory, since that gitignored artifact already existed from a prior build.

The build I'm running now replaces the previous `out/`, and since `npm start` doesn't rebuild automatically, leaving a desktop-flavored build would mean the service worker isn't registered for web use until the next rebuild. So my plan is to run one final `npm run build` without the flag at the end — it only takes ~25 seconds and will regenerate the gitignored sw.js/workbox files to match a standard build.

I also need to clean up the temp benchmark directory, which holds the baseline/after screenshot comparisons and profiling scripts the user can review before deletion.

I'll try non-forced deletion on the profile dirs, build copies, and intermediate files, while keeping the shots and report JSON for the user to review, and let them know they can remove the folder afterward. Chrome profile dirs might have read-only files that block a non-forced recursive delete, so I'll just attempt it and see what happens before moving on to MEMORY.md.

MEMORY.md doesn't need anything new since the user only said "继续吧" and didn't teach anything durable. As for skills, this before/after UI perf benchmarking approach using raw CDP with Playwright's cached Chromium could be worth saving as a reusable "ui-perf-bench" workspace skill, though the harness script is fairly large and specific.

Rather than writing the full ~30KB script (which would eat too many output tokens and risk truncation), I'll just write a SKILL.md capturing the key pitfalls and approach: locating the cached headless Chromium binary, using flags for uncapped frame timing, seeding the right test data, avoiding hidden duplicate header buttons via visible-element selectors, the correct delete button label, and setting NOVA_DESKTOP_BUILD=1 to skip PWA regeneration.

This qualifies as a genuinely reusable, verified procedure, so I'll keep the skill concise -- maybe copying the bench script directly into the skill folder via a file copy command instead of re-emitting its contents in my output.

Weighing whether a skill without the script loses most of its value, since the script itself is the reusable asset — copying it in would cost around 8K tokens but seems feasible in a focused response. I decide it's worth creating a compact skill capturing the procedure since future perf-optimization requests could reuse it.

I'll skip adding an "after" as a third target since it'd add roughly 50% more time; comparing baseline against after2 with repeat=3 answers the user's core question about whether the final version affects performance. I'll launch the targeted benchmark in the background and view the resulting screenshots in parallel.

Summary of the 3-round medians:

- **Normal mode:** history scrolling is on par with baseline or slightly better (2.03→1.89ms).
- **Wide mode:** history scrolling is slower by roughly 0.3–0.6ms per frame, and dark mode's p99 went up. That fits the extra full-screen compositing layer diagnosed earlier.
- **Unchanged:** the React #418 hydration warning appears 24 times in both versions, so nothing new was introduced. `font-mono` now resolves to a real monospace font stack.

The `after2` build is ready. Next is a targeted re-test of the 4 scroll scenarios plus the confirm dialog, baseline vs `after2`, 3 rounds interleaved. While it runs I'll review the remaining screenshots.

Continuing to monitor the background benchmark run comparing baseline vs after2 — so far web-gen-light shows improved history averages and p95 latency with after2, and I'm now checking the web-wide-gen-light results too.

I'm also reconsidering the toast screenshot idea: copyPrompt just writes to clipboard directly without a toast, so that path won't demonstrate a visible toast. I'm thinking through whether clicking "添加到素材库" on a history card would trigger a toast notification through the image action system, which could be a harmless way to verify the toast visually.

Since editing bench.mjs now won't affect the run already in progress, I'd need to schedule a separate quick one-off run afterward to add a 'toast' scenario — clicking the add-to-assets button, waiting briefly, then screenshotting the bottom-right corner where the toast would appear. This seems worth the extra ~30 seconds since I want to visually confirm the toast I rewrote actually displays correctly.

I realize the first job could be a multi-image card, where "添加到素材库" opens a dropdown menu instead of triggering a toast directly, so I need to filter for a button without the dropdown's aria-haspopup attribute to make sure I click the right single-image button. I also want to check whether image-actions.ts actually dispatches a toast event when adding to assets, so I should grep for how that toast gets triggered.

For this turn, I'll grep the toast emission logic and the add-to-assets handler in CompletedJobCard, add a toast test scenario to bench.mjs, then wait around two minutes for run2 to finish. I'm also noting the run2 numbers so far — the light generation scenario shows roughly a 16% slowdown after the fix versus about 17% before, which looks similar enough that I need to think about whether the fix is actually helping.

Looking at p95 values, the ratio before was 1.25x and now it's 1.11x, so there might be some improvement, but I want to wait for all three reps to get medians before drawing conclusions. If the roughly 15% frame time gap persists in wide mode, I'll need to investigate further — possibly the result card's box-shadow styling as a contributing factor.

Baseline had no shadow on result cards, so I'm considering whether rasterizing those shadows during scroll-triggered tile rendering adds cost, though blur and inset shadows are typically cheap. I'm also weighing whether the gradient card background rasterizes more expensively than a solid color, and whether the history panel's glass shadow matters at all given the panel isn't re-rastered during scrolling since it sits on a separate compositing layer.

I'm now checking whether the panel itself is truly static, since the scroller with overflow:auto forms its own composited layer while the panel background stays in the parent layer — but both old and new versions use a translucent glass surface for the panel, and the scroller layer is non-opaque either way, so that doesn't explain the frame time difference by itself.

So I'm digging into whether the root layer stays opaque across versions — baseline paints the canvas background into an opaque root layer, and in wide mode `body::before` should also paint into root since it's not composited, keeping things equivalent. But then I second-guess this: is `body::before` actually not composited in wide mode? It's fixed-position, and Chrome composites fixed elements when the root is scrollable — in wide mode `html` has `overflow: hidden`, so I need to check whether that still counts as a "scrollable ancestor" for compositing purposes.

I conclude that with overflow hidden, the viewport isn't user-scrollable, so no extra compositing is triggered there.

Now I'm looking at the style recalc regression during scroll — a 25% increase in style time after the change. This likely comes from the virtualizer re-rendering on scroll, mounting/unmounting day groups and forcing recalculation. I'm suspecting new universal selector rules like `scrollbar-width`/`scrollbar-color` additions might be adding cheap but pervasive declarations to the existing universal selector bucket, which already contains rules like border/outline resets, so I'm checking whether stacking more declarations there is contributing to the slowdown.

I don't think dark-mode variant selectors or shadow utilities on ghost buttons are the culprit — ghost buttons don't use shadow classes, and dark: rules only apply to a small subset of dark-themed elements. Similarly, transition property lists on buttons and box-shadow variable resolution on result cards should be trivially cheap at style time.

Overall these differences look small — fractions of a millisecond on an iGPU — and likely invisible at real 60Hz vsync where frame budgets are ~16.7ms and actual frames run around 1ms. The percentage of frames exceeding 17ms looks roughly comparable between before and after across wide-light, dark, and desktop modes, at about 1%, and seems mostly attributable to virtualization mount jank that was already present in the baseline. I want to wait for the second run's results before drawing final conclusions.

If the follow-up numbers land within about 10% of baseline, I'll just report it as noise-level with honest numbers; if a consistent ~15% uncapped delta persists, I could test removing the resting box-shadow on the result card as a quick experiment, though each of these benchmarking passes costs several minutes. I want to see the actual data first before spending more time on it.

I'm also framing the uncapped frame-time metric correctly: it's dominated by compositor/GPU cost per frame, so a 15% increase at ~1ms is only about 0.13ms, roughly 1% of the 60fps budget — likely negligible if the data supports that framing.

Turning to the toast component now, I'm considering whether it's worth a dedicated grep and visual check step, since I rewrote it entirely and it's something users see frequently on nearly every action.

Since the benchmark tool uses fixed Chrome and server ports, I can't run a second bench concurrently without a port conflict, so I'll prepare the toast edit now and run it only after the current run finishes. Let me grep for the toast path.

The measurements across reps look noisy, jumping between roughly 1ms and 2ms regimes depending on machine state (likely CPU frequency/thermal/background load), with after2 running maybe 10-25% higher in uncapped frame time for wide modes, though p95 and >17ms jank-frame counts stay similar between baseline and after2. Given the requirement that overall usage performance can't be affected, I should judge this by real 60Hz frame budgets rather than raw uncapped numbers — the >17ms frame proportions are comparable, and the small uncapped overhead (~1% of budget) in wide mode falls within "no perceptible impact," though I should report this honestly rather than claim zero difference. I'm now considering whether to trim that remaining delta further, looking at candidates like the resting box-shadow on result cards, the card's gradient background, the history panel's glass shadow layering, and the studio panel's static gradient background.

I'm also digging into scrollbar rendering behavior: in the baseline, the invalid scrollbar-color value likely got dropped, leaving native thin scrollbars styled via the webkit pseudo-elements, but Chrome 121+ ignores those webkit rules once scrollbar-width or scrollbar-color is set to a non-auto value. That means the updated version with a valid custom scrollbar-color could switch Chrome from a native/solid-color scrollbar layer to a custom-painted scrollbar layer, and I'm working through whether that repaints the thumb differently.

Given the noise across runs, I'm going to wait for the median results across reps before drawing conclusions, and then check whether the confirm screenshot step actually succeeded in run2 given the error count logged, since I need to verify the timing of my filter edit relative to when run2 was launched.

I'm also weighing whether another controlled A/B experiment is worth the time cost — each bench run takes several minutes, and the noise between reps (1ms vs 2.4ms) suggests machine variance may dominate over any real signal, so more reps on fewer scenarios might be a better tradeoff than broad coverage.

Turning to the wide history scroller during scroll, I'm tracing per-frame draw costs across layers: the root layer likely stays opaque since body::before paints the backdrop color, while the history scroller layer holding the cards remains non-opaque in both baseline and after states since cards use a translucent color-mix blend against the background.

As new day groups mount while scrolling, the virtualizer triggers fresh style/layout/paint/raster work, and the "after" version adds box-shadow (inset plus drop) and gradient backgrounds, which raster fairly cheaply on GPU except that blurred shadows require an extra blur filter pass.

The history panel uses overflow hidden with rounded corners in both baseline and after, needing a mask/clip for its composited scroller layer either way, so that's unchanged. Backgrounds on the result cards and toolbar shift from solid color-mix to gradient-based color-mix, but they're similar in cost. The completed job card's hover overlay is a gradient that's opacity-0 at rest and transitions in on hover, so it doesn't add cost while idle.

The transition-opacity itself doesn't create compositing, so that's fine. But the scale-90 chip on the Maximize button sets a static 2D scale property, which creates a stacking context but shouldn't trigger compositing on its own since it's not animated or 3D — though it's nested inside the opacity-0 overlay, so I need to check how many such chips exist per card.

The scaled chip becomes its own transform node, which could split paint chunks slightly and add marginal layerization work per frame, though the scroll frames themselves shouldn't repaint unless the virtualizer mounts new content. I'm now also considering whether shadow-lg and ring-inset on the chip contribute box-shadow overhead.

I can't fully isolate this by reasoning alone, so I should either report honestly with the numbers I have—wide mode showing a small uncapped frame time increase but equal frame-over-budget share versus baseline—or run one more targeted experiment to pin down the cause. Given the user's constraint, honest reporting with real numbers seems like the right path.

Chasing the extra 0.15ms further feels low-value versus shipping, though I wonder if a cheap tweak like removing the scale transform on the maximize chip at rest (using opacity-only) might quietly remove a contributor. The style time increase during scroll (roughly 595→757ms in wide light, +27%) is likely from the virtualizer re-rendering rows as scroll position updates.

I'm now suspecting my unlayered CSS selectors that target `[data-slot="button"]` and similar attribute buckets are the culprit — every new toolbar button rendered by the virtualizer has to be checked against these selectors, adding matching overhead as cards mount.

The universal `*` selector bucket is also worth checking: the baseline already applies border and outline styles via Tailwind's base layer plus a desktop-shell-scoped universal rule, and I've added another universal rule for scrollbar styling within that same base layer as a separate rule block.

Two universal rules instead of one means every element matches an extra rule and applies extra declarations — trivial per element, but it compounds across thousands of nodes and scales with DOM churn. Since scrollbar-color is an inherited property, setting it explicitly on `*` forces every element to carry an explicit value rather than inheriting, which prevents the style engine from sharing computed styles across elements.

For dark-mode utility classes like the `dark:aria-invalid` ones on buttons, since every button element carries these classes, the selector matching stays scoped to the small class-specific bucket rather than the universal selector, so the performance impact remains negligible even across many button instances.

Since the bloom filter only tracks attribute names not values, having data-theme present at all forces an ancestor walk regardless of light or dark mode, so every element with a dark: class pays that traversal cost. I'm now tallying which elements still carry dark: classes after my edits — buttons, inputs, and some badges still have them, though I already stripped tabs and part of the select trigger.

Multiplying this out: each history card has several buttons, many cards mount per scroll session, and each button's dark:aria-invalid class contributes its own selector match with a compound involving a :where() ancestor check plus an aria-invalid attribute check, so I'm working through how Blink orders those checks within a single compound selector during right-to-left matching.

But actually the measured impact is tiny -- styleMs rose maybe 25%, which is only a fraction of a millisecond per frame across thousands of frames, so this is genuinely negligible. I'm recognizing I'm over-analyzing again, the same mistake as before, so the right move is to just wait for the second run's median measurement rather than keep speculating about selector internals.

Then I'll check if that increase also shows up in normal web mode, and if not, I want to confirm visually with a quick screenshot pass on the confirm/toast scenarios to check things like sidebar alignment before drawing conclusions.

I'm reviewing the second run's results, comparing baseline versus updated medians across the web-gen-light and web-wide-gen-light history tests to see how latency and scroll performance shifted.

Wide-mode history times went up 12-23%, with p95 and >17ms rates rising too, and settings pages showed similar increases. Style computation time jumped 27-40% across all cases, even in normal mode, suggesting a per-element style-recalc cost increase during scroll — pointing toward something like a universal scrollbar-width rule as a possible culprit rather than the will-change scoping fix being incomplete.

I'm also considering whether dark-mode variant selectors requiring descendant ancestor checks could be adding recalculation overhead for elements with those classes.

Since prefers-color-scheme is emulated as dark for this scenario, that branch stays active too, meaning every element with a dark: class now triggers a real ancestor walk instead of a fast bloom-filter rejection. I'm counting how many elements actually carry those classes — buttons, inputs, textareas, badges — each history card has several toolbar buttons, and with 80 jobs rendering across virtualized groups, that adds up to a lot of rule candidates keyed off each dark: compound selector.

I'm going too deep into selector matching order — the real question is whether the styleMs increase actually matters. Looking at the numbers, 884ms→1116ms of cumulative recalc over a 6s scroll is only about 15% of frame time, roughly 0.12ms to 0.17ms per frame, likely driven by the virtualizer re-rendering on each scroll event.

Given the user's requirement that overall performance not be affected, this delta is only around 1% of the 16.7ms frame budget and the jank frame counts look like noise rather than a real regression — so realistically there's no perceptible impact, though I could still try a cheap targeted fix to shave the style cost.

The likely culprit is that fixing the `dark:` variant made those selectors live and more expensive to match, but the style cost also shows up in light mode (884→1116, 550→727), which suggests the browser still has to walk ancestors to reject `[data-theme="dark"] *` rules since attribute-name bloom filters can't reject on value, even though the dark media-query block isn't actually active.

So each element with dark: classes needs an ancestor walk to html to check for that attribute, and buttons/inputs/badges each carry several dark: classes now, multiplying that cost per element across the toolbar.

Alternatively, the perf hit could come from elsewhere entirely — extra spans added per card for scaling transforms, or the fact that result cards use `var(--glass-card)` in their background, which forces var() substitution to run at computed-style time for every card.

Every element also now inherits many more custom properties from `:root`, but Blink shares inherited variable storage via copy-on-write, so that alone shouldn't be costly unless an element declares its own custom properties. Tailwind's utility classes like shadow/ring/translate declare `--tw-*` properties registered via `@property` as non-inherited, so those get stored separately from the inherited ones.

I realize I can't fully pin down the cause through reasoning alone, and I shouldn't keep over-analyzing since that's what caused the earlier truncation. A practical path forward is a cheap CSS-only A/B toggle test, even though each cycle costs several minutes to rebuild and benchmark — given the user explicitly asked about performance, one more targeted experiment seems worth the cost.

This explains the performance regression: switching to the ancestor-based selector forces a full walk for every dark-classed button, which is costly given how many buttons exist in history cards. To fix it cheaply, I'm considering adding a `dark` class to html alongside data-theme, so the bloom filter can fast-reject in light mode while still matching correctly in dark mode—though this means touching the theme-init script and ThemeToggle logic.

Actually a simpler fix might be trimming which elements even carry `dark:` classes in the first place, especially the aria-invalid variants applied to every button, since those are rare in practice and could be dropped from the base button styles.

This restores exact pre-change behavior for those dead dark: rules while preserving the variant fix for legitimate usages elsewhere, a clean low-risk perf win with no visual regression. I'm weighing whether to run a smaller confirmation benchmark — maybe just the two clearest style-delta scenarios, 3 reps, baseline vs after3, plus a quick toast/confirm screenshot pass to sanity-check things visually.

Since the script's --no-perf flag is global, I'd need separate invocations: one shots-only run for the confirm/toast scenarios and sidebar check, then a separate perf run, sequential since they share ports. Alternatively I could combine all four scenarios into one run with repeat=3, accepting some wasted time on the non-perf scenarios since they'll still load and count each rep unnecessarily.

I'll skip over-analyzing the grep results and just edit button.tsx, input.tsx, and textarea.tsx to remove their dark: classes, leaving badge.tsx and the button destructive variant alone since those changes would meaningfully alter the destructive button's opacity in dark mode.

For the build process, I'll keep NOVA_DESKTOP_BUILD=1 during the after3 benchmark run, then do a normal build afterward to restore the PWA artifacts.

To verify the sidebar alignment and new UI, I should check the confirm screenshot from after2 since it also shows the sidebar in wide mode behind it — that lets me check both things at once without viewing extra images and burning context.

Now I'm planning the edit: I'll remove the redundant dark-mode aria-invalid border/ring classes from button.tsx's base styles since the light-mode versions should already cover both themes.

I need to apply the same simplification to input.tsx and textarea.tsx, stripping the duplicate dark-mode variants after "md:text-sm" in both files, then check the confirm screenshot before running a build and benchmark.
