I'm defining a helper function that checks the error type and message content to decide whether a non-streaming retry should be attempted.

I'm weighing whether to retry broadly on any 400/404/405/415/422/501 status regardless of the message content — reasoning that a 400 usually means the request was rejected without billing, so a cheap retry without streaming is safe even for things like moderation blocks or unrecognized models, since worst case it just wastes an extra request.

I should also track stream support per base URL in memory so future calls skip streaming for endpoints known to fail with it, though concurrent requests won't benefit from this immediately. I'm also considering that a stream failure could stem from an error embedded in the SSE payload itself, like a moderation rejection surfaced during event parsing.

For 5xx errors or mid-stream network drops, I shouldn't auto-retry non-stream since the image may have already been generated and billed upstream — retrying risks double-charging. I'll limit automatic retries to clear 4xx unsupported-type responses and parse failures, not transient server or connection errors.

I'm weighing options for making the timeout cover the full response body read, not just headers: proxy/model calls need a shorter timeout while image downloads need a much longer one, and text proxy currently just uses the default. Since the body is read immediately by response.text() in the image parsing paths, the simplest fix seems to be adding a mode to fetchWithTimeout that keeps the timer alive until the body is consumed, rather than restructuring every call site.

That approach feels hacky, so let me reconsider the auditor's finding about timeouts not limiting total request time — once headers arrive, only undici's 30-minute idle timer between chunks applies, and for image generation that's a reasonable enough ceiling since indefinite body trickling is mostly a theoretical edge case rather than the real problem.

The more concrete issue is that model listing and download routes wait the full 30 minutes when they shouldn't, so per-route timeouts would fix that. I'm weighing whether to build a fetchWithTimeout wrapper that also handles body completion, versus just passing AbortSignal.timeout directly into fetch to keep things simple.

Passing AbortSignal.timeout directly seems cleanest since it stays active through both headers and body reads and cleans itself up when fired, with no meaningful leak risk. I'm defining a wrapper that combines a timeout-based abort signal with any caller-provided signal, ensuring the deadline spans the whole request including body streaming, not just until headers arrive.

For 5xx errors or mid-stream network drops, I shouldn't auto-retry non-stream since the image may have already been generated and billed upstream — retrying risks double-charging. payload.text:
Build passes with 80 tests passing, but lint shows 11 errors versus a baseline of 8 -- the 3 new ones all trace back to my changes in useAgentChat.ts and useWorkspaceJobs.ts, where state updates inside layout effects are triggering the set-state-in-effect rule.

I'm weighing whether to suppress these with justified eslint-disable comments, or follow the project's existing pattern of wrapping the setState in queueMicrotask like usePersistedSettings and useWideMode do. I'm reasoning through the timing: a microtask queued from a layout effect would still flush before the browser paints, since layout effects run synchronously within the commit and microtasks drain before the next paint opportunity -- so this should be safe, though I need to check which update lane React would assign to it.

Given the complexity of tracing update priorities through microtasks, I think the cleaner path is to keep the synchronous setState directly in the layout effects, since that's the pattern React's own docs recommend for reading/measuring before paint, and just add targeted eslint-disable comments explaining why.

I'm also weighing switching the model-availability check to useSyncExternalStore instead, since that's the idiomatic way to read an external store with a server snapshot and avoids tripping the lint rule altogether — subscribing to the registry-updated event, using the cached availability check as the snapshot, and falling back to false on the server.

This is getting too tangled to verify without testing, so the pragmatic path is to keep the sync setState inside useLayoutEffect since that's guaranteed to run before paint per React's docs, and just add eslint-disable comments with clear justification rather than restructuring further. That keeps the lint count at the baseline of 8. I'm locating the three call sites needing disable comments, starting with the refreshModelAvailability call inside the layout effect in useWorkspaceJobs.ts around line 50.

Recounting line numbers, I trace the effect block through the earlier edits to figure out that line 219 corresponds to `setWebSearchEnabled(...)`, the first synchronous setState call flagged inside that effect.

Since I'm unsure if the rule flags only the first setState per effect or all of them, the safer approach is to wrap the entire effect body with a block-level eslint-disable/enable pair for the set-state-in-effect rule, so every setState call inside is covered regardless.

Adding disable/enable comments...

Since only setJobs there is synchronous and flagged, a single next-line disable before line 58 covers it, and I can bundle both edits in one contiguous range. For useAgentChat, I'm checking which calls in that effect actually get flagged — setWebSearchEnabled at line 219 needs a disable, while refreshApiKeyState apparently doesn't.

I'll wrap the whole effect block with a disable/enable pair since I already know its exact text, then re-run lint to confirm we're back down to 8 errors. After that I want to move to backend work in parallel: adding per-route timeouts via AbortSignal.timeout to fetchWithTimeout and its callers, handling upstream cancellation on client disconnect for the text proxy, broadening stream fallback with per-baseUrl memory, and updating normalizeError to preserve status/upstream text while classifying timeouts.

I'm confirming line offsets shifted by prior edits so my next fetchWithTimeout edit targets the correct location, then rewriting that function to use AbortSignal.timeout.

AbortSignal.any needs Node 20.3+, which both dev and packaged Electron satisfy since the backend runs via utilityProcess or a node child process. I also need to check that the error handling still works correctly, since timeouts now produce a DOMException named 'TimeoutError' instead of the old 'AbortError', so I should verify normalizeError's regex catches both.

I'm also checking that a mid-body timeout still propagates correctly to callers as a timeout error, and that the image generation timeout now spans the entire request including body reading, which should be fine since image generation realistically finishes well under 30 minutes. Server tests using mock upstreams should be unaffected by this change.

Now I need to add specific timeout values to the remaining per-route fetch calls — the models endpoint fetch should get a 20-second timeout, and the image download fetch should get a 120-second timeout, editing those specific lines in the code.

Since edit tool matches by unique text rather than line numbers, I don't need to worry about line shifts from prior edits, just confirm each snippet is unique in the file.

Next I need to look at the text proxy cancellation loop around the relevant section, and then broaden the stream-fallback retry logic in generateNovaImage to check for unsupported streaming errors more generally.

I'm reasoning through when a stream fails after the upstream already generated an image—things like a missing image in the response, invalid JSON, or specific 4xx codes that aren't auth/quota/rate-limit related—since those cases shouldn't be retried the same way as network or server errors where billing might duplicate.

For genuine 400 content-policy rejections or 404 unsupported-model errors, retrying via the non-stream path just repeats the same failure harmlessly, costing one extra round trip but no double billing. That seems like an acceptable tradeoff given the per-baseUrl memory prevents this from happening repeatedly.

I'm setting up a set to track base URLs where streaming isn't supported, and in the image generation function I only fall back to the non-stream request and record the base URL as unsupported once that fallback actually succeeds -- avoiding mistaking a bad key or moderation failure for a streaming incompatibility.

I'm reconsidering the memory key though: instead of just baseUrl, keying by baseUrl plus model might be more accurate since some relays route different models to different upstream channels. I also want to check how this interacts with existing tests, like the one checking a response_format error for b64_json and the partial_images streaming test.

Since each test likely spawns its own server process with a separate temp DB, memory shouldn't leak across tests, so my change should be safe — I'll just run the backend test suite to confirm. Then I need to check where normalizeError is used, probably in the task processing error handler.

I'm defining normalizeError to keep upstream HTTP error text intact (truncated if too long), and to detect timeout-related errors by checking error name, cause code, or message patterns, returning a Chinese "请求超时" style message for those cases.

For network-level failures I'm matching common fetch/connection error codes and messages to return a friendly "网络连接失败" message including the code if available, otherwise falling back to truncating the raw error message if it's too long.

I should double-check whether the frontend's failure classification logic depends on matching these exact Chinese error message strings, since changing wording could break existing tests that check for '网络连接失败' or '请求超时' patterns—so I need to keep those prefixes consistent.

I also realize there's a subtler bug: an upstream HTTP error like "504 Gateway Timeout" would previously get matched by the timeout regex and misleadingly reported as a request timeout, so I should fix the classification order to check status codes before falling back to message pattern matching.

I still need to check whether normalizeError's messages align with existing backend tests, and to add a timeout to the queue-status fetch in backend-process.js which currently has none. For graceful shutdown, I'm considering wiring a shared abort signal into all upstream fetch calls so in-flight requests can be cancelled when the server stops, rather than just waiting or force-killing after 8 seconds.

Adding a global shutdown AbortController would make in-flight tasks reject quickly on abort, so the "wait for running tasks" step during shutdown finishes fast before closing the database. I need normalizeError to detect shutdown-triggered aborts specifically and return a distinct message like "服务正在退出，任务已中断，请重新生成" instead of the misleading timeout message, and then confirm that on next startup, initDatabase properly cleans up any queued/processing entries left behind.

Now I want to actually check the relevant code sections: server.js's proxy handler and shutdown routine, backend-process.js's stop logic, and the task handling itself to verify these assumptions before proposing a fix.

I'm planning to add a shutdown-aware AbortController for upstream fetches, wiring it into fetchWithTimeout so requests get cancelled cleanly during shutdown, reusing the existing isShuttingDown flag. I'll make the fetchWithTimeout edit first since the other changes touch the same file in multiple places and need to be sequenced separately.

I'm combining all the abort signals so the fetch cancels on timeout, shutdown, or an external signal. Though now I'm second-guessing whether AbortSignal.any could cause a memory leak, since the shutdown signal lives forever and older Node versions had issues retaining dependent signals from long-lived sources.

That leak was actually a known Node issue that got fixed in later versions, and since this is running on Node 22/24 via current Electron, it shouldn't be a problem. I'm now checking that other fetchWithTimeout call sites pass proper init objects, defaulting to an empty object when none is given, and tracing where it's used for the streaming text proxy endpoint.

For that streaming case, the timeout deadline should cover the entire stream duration since a chat stream running over 30 minutes would be unusual, and I want to make sure a client-close event properly triggers an AbortController to cancel the upstream fetch. I also want to double check the frontend hydration story — the AssetsWorkspace component being dynamically imported with ssr:false means it never risks a hydration mismatch, but I should check whether GIF/ReversePrompt components, which are still server-rendered, have any storage-reading initializers that could cause the same issue.

My grep pattern for state initializers reading from storage might have missed variants like conditional window checks, so I should verify using the bench harness that counts React error #418 occurrences after a fresh build, running it against the current desktop build output on a couple of scenarios. Then I'll move through: fixing the lint issues in useWorkspaceJobs and useAgentChat, editing the fetchWithTimeout logic in server.js, and reading through the text proxy, shutdown, and backend-process stop regions along with the task-failure message handling.

For the useWorkspaceJobs fix, I'm adding an eslint-disable comment above the state-restoring calls in the layout effects, explaining that they intentionally restore stored state before first paint. For useAgentChat, I'm still working through the effect that checks for a text model since the image step reports missing models separately.

Wrapping up parsing stored preferences into state, catching storage errors gracefully, and setting up a listener to refresh the API key state when the model registry updates, with cleanup on unmount.

I'm double-checking that useEffect is still used elsewhere in useAgentChat after this refactor—confirming other effects like syncing imageModelRef still exist, so no unused import issues after the build passes.

Now I want to search task-failure.ts for network/timeout-related patterns, and check server.js for error normalization usage, shutdown flags, and graceful shutdown handlers like SIGTERM.

Both the build and the 80 unit tests pass. Lint shows 11 errors against 8 at baseline, and the 3 extra ones are mine. They're all the `set-state-in-effect` rule, triggered by restoring stored state inside `useLayoutEffect`.

That's deliberate: setting state in a layout effect is the approach React documents for "read before the first paint", and it's what makes the restored screen appear without a flash. So I'm keeping it and adding a scoped exception with the reason to the rule instead of changing the implementation.

I'm also starting on the backend. `fetchWithTimeout` now uses `AbortSignal.timeout`, so the deadline covers the whole request including the response body, and all in-flight upstream requests are cancelled together when the app exits. Meanwhile I'm reading the text proxy, the exit flow, and the frontend's failure-classification rules, so that changing error messages doesn't break its checks.

payload.text:
Lint is back to baseline levels. Now I'm adding client-close cancellation to the text proxy by wiring an AbortController to the response's close event so I can cancel the underlying fetch when the client disconnects early.

I need to make sure the error handling accounts for this abort case specifically — checking if the abort came from the client rather than a timeout, so I don't try writing a response to an already-closed connection.

Then for the models proxy endpoint, I want to guard against `sendJson` outputting "null" when the upstream response body is empty, falling back to a small error object instead.

Also checking the image download call to confirm its timeout is properly set to 120 seconds and that I'm targeting the right line since there's a similar fetch call for Bing images nearby.

Good, confirmed that snippet is unique enough for the edit tool to match safely. Now for the stream fallback logic in generateNovaImage, I want to track which base URL and model combinations don't support streaming so I can skip retrying them, falling back to the non-streaming request when a target is known to be unsupported.

I'm extending the retry logic to also catch cases where the stream returned but had no usable image data or invalid JSON, treating those as retryable. But I realize there's a subtlety—if the upstream actually generated the image but returned it in an unrecognized format, retrying non-stream risks double-billing, so I need to think through that edge case carefully.

Given the tradeoff, I'll accept the small risk of double billing since it only happens once per target per session with the per-target memory approach, and it's better UX than making the user retry manually. I also need to check the existing backend test for stream fallback behavior around the partial images environment variable.

Now I'm turning to rewriting the error normalization function to preserve upstream HTTP status codes and text instead of letting keyword matching rewrite them into misleading timeout or network messages.

Adding network error handling...

I want the timeout message to be generic rather than tied to a specific number, since different routes have different limits — something like "请求超时，请稍后重试" so it stays accurate across models and image generation paths.

Now I'm checking abort handling: previously any 'abort' matched the timeout branch, but AbortError itself doesn't include 'timeout' in its message, so I need to trace when it actually fires — it happens when the combined AbortSignal's timeout signal triggers, causing fetch to reject with that TimeoutError DOMException as the reason.

For safety, I'll also map name === 'AbortError' into the timeout branch as a conservative fallback, matching the old behavior, since shutdown aborts get caught earlier by their own branch anyway. I'll keep the 'terminated' mapping for dropped connections, and confirm the frontend classifier correctly treats timeout as non-terminal while server restart is terminal.

Now I want to check whether error messages get wrapped elsewhere — things like "API 请求失败:" prefixes from parseGptImageResponse should pass through normalizeError unchanged, and similar provider-specific messages should fall through fine too. I should grep the existing server tests to see if they assert on specific normalizeError output strings so I don't break them.

I'm reasoning through the shutdown sequence: aborting the upstream controller right after setting the shutdown flag should make running tasks reject quickly, their handlers mark items failed with the shutdown message via normalizeError, the DB gets updated, and then the pending promises settle fast so checkpoint and close can proceed.

I'm also considering edge cases — tasks that partially completed before abort might end up marked 'completed' with a warning rather than 'failed', meaning initDatabase won't touch their images on restart. But tasks still sitting in QUEUED state at shutdown time never got aborted, so they'll remain queued and need to be marked failed on the next startup.

For confirming this is intended behavior, aborting only happens when stopServer runs on app quit, and the desktop app should already prompt the user before quitting if tasks are pending, so this aligns with expectations. I also want to add a timeout signal to the getQueueStatus fetch call in backend-process.js, and make sure the 8-second kill timeout still comfortably covers the faster abort-based shutdown. Since I'm making several edits to server.js, I should apply them one at a time rather than in parallel to avoid conflicts.

Editing the same file in parallel risks conflicts, so I'll stick with sequential EditFile calls rather than shell scripting workarounds. This turn I'll tackle the text proxy and models proxy edits together since they're adjacent.

Planning the order: after this combined edit and the backend-process getQueueStatus edit, I need to grep server.test.js for error assertions, then handle normalizeError, generateNovaImage, stopServer, and download in later turns, followed by running backend/desktop tests and checking frontend build and bench hydration.

Writing the combined proxy replacement...

Setting up abort handling and streaming response piping...

I'm reasoning through edge cases: whether 'close' fires correctly on normal completion versus disconnection, and confirming that ending an already-destroyed response is safely guarded by checking writableEnded first.

I'm writing the catch block to check if the response is already destroyed or ended before sending an error, distinguishing timeout errors (504) from other proxy failures (502). I'm double-checking that both `res.destroyed` and `writableEnded` are covered so a client abort doesn't trigger a write-after-end crash.

For the models proxy endpoint, I'm setting up a fetch with a 20-second timeout, safely parsing the JSON response, and falling back to an error object if parsing fails or the request times out. I'm deciding to inline the timeout constants as literals rather than defining named constants, to avoid extra edits.

I'm now checking that when upstream returns 200 with non-JSON content, the fallback error still results in a reasonable frontend message about not finding models in the list. I want to verify the test file's expected error strings for network failures and timeouts, then move to updating the queue-status fetch in backend-process.js to ensure it never blocks tray quit operations.

Now I'm updating the todo list: marking lazy-loading work complete since canvas, assets, gallery, and settings modules use dynamic imports, and jszip is loaded dynamically in AgentImageGallery, while gifenc stays static since it's small. Virtualization is pending final verification, and I'm moving on to the backend queue-status task.

I'm weighing whether to make the abort controller resettable for in-process restarts, but since main.js's restart logic actually stops the child process and forks a new one rather than reusing the module in-process, that extra edit likely isn't necessary — the module simply isn't designed for repeated start/stop cycles within the same process.

Editing seed template...

Now I'm looking at generateNovaImage, which routes requests to the appropriate API protocol based on the frontend's protocol field, resolving the base URL and handling the OpenAI-style path with size resolution and streaming logic.

Then it catches errors from unsupported streaming and falls back to a non-streaming request, logging a warning when that happens. I'm adding a set to track base URL + model combinations whose streaming failed previously, so future requests to those targets skip streaming entirely...

Writing retry logic...

On success I mark that target as stream-unsupported going forward. I'm weighing whether an HTML response (likely from a misconfigured endpoint) should also trigger the fallback, but since a wrong URL would fail non-stream too, I decide to exclude HTML detection and instead keep the retry condition focused on missing image data in the response.

I also want to catch invalid JSON responses and certain 4xx codes (400, 404, 405, 415, 422, 501) as retry triggers, since these often indicate transient issues like moderation blocks or unsupported models where retrying without streaming might still succeed. If the fallback attempt also fails, I'll surface that non-stream error since it tends to be more informative anyway. I need to place the module-level tracking set and helper function before the generateNovaImage definition, and note where the existing upstreamShutdownController is declared for reference.

Now I'm checking whether existing tests still pass with this change — tracing through the stream-then-fallback scenario confirms the same request count and behavior as before, so the retry logic shouldn't break that test case.

Looking at the shutdown handler edit, I'm reordering it to abort in-flight upstream requests immediately rather than waiting, since the desktop shell kills the process after 8 seconds — I need to verify this abort happens before the HTTP server close and doesn't disrupt existing shutdown tests.

I'm also checking that failed tasks from the abort still write to the DB safely (before it closes) and that WebSocket broadcasts to closing sockets are already guarded elsewhere in the code, which they appear to be. This turn covers the generateNovaImage and bench.mjs edits; the stopServer change will follow next.

That message is just a harness artifact, so I'll continue. The build passes and startup JS dropped noticeably, from 1787 KB down to 1317 KB, about a 26% reduction, with the page chunk shrinking from 721 to 453 KB and the large 902 chunk no longer showing up in the top list, replaced by a smaller 984 chunk around 197 KB. I'll stop the server now.

Next I need to run backend and desktop tests via the root test:desktop script, which covers server, storage, backup-service, s3-service, updater, and main tests. I also want to rerun the frontend vitest suite and confirm lint stays clean, since my last lint pass covered all the frontend edits including the AgentImageGallery and HistoryJobList changes, and the disable comments added afterward shouldn't affect test results—though it's cheap enough to rerun anyway. I'm also noting that one frontend test actually reads server.js source text directly to check for specific strings, so I need to keep that in mind when verifying.

I'll target the desktop build path, confirming the fs handling works fine with Unicode directory names and that the desktop-flag build skips PWA service worker registration for the bench. For scenarios, I'm covering web-wide-gen-light, web-agent-light, and desktop-wide-gen-light, noting the fake bridge routes config.get through localStorage so I need to check how the registry caching path behaves for desktop.

I'll skip a comparative perf run since there's no baseline build to measure against, and instead focus on hydration checks and mounted card counts at perDay=80. I also want to verify the web-gen-light scenario since it exercises history and hydration behavior, and I'm working out expected mounted card counts under the wide three-column layout.

Rather than measuring a "before" state, I can reason from the old code directly: since overscan covered whole day groups, all 80 cards in a single-day group would have mounted, versus the new virtualized approach which mounts only visible plus overscan rows. I'll note this as a code-derived comparison rather than an empirical one, then do a final PWA build to restore the output directory before checking git status and diffs.

Now I want to update the todo list and prepare the final report, but first I should verify desktop tests pass, check that server tests still work with the normalizeError changes, and run the desktop test suite, frontend tests, and the hydration benchmark in parallel since they use separate ports and shouldn't conflict.

I'm running the bench with the four light scenarios in the foreground since prior shots-only runs completed quickly enough to stay within timeout limits.

I'm double-checking that the `--targets=final@...` argument parses correctly since the target path itself has no '@' character, and confirming perDay=80 just puts all jobs on day zero which is fine since the new frontend reads seeded jobs from localStorage/IDB on each scenario's page reload. I'm also writing a small script to print per-run results from the report — scenario name, errors, mounted cards, DOM node counts, and any settings or dropdown errors.

The desktop scenario uses a fake config bridge backed by localStorage with an empty model registry, so it should still show the "API key not configured" card same as before — this bench doesn't really exercise the model-configured hydration path since no models are set up, but that's fine since the original issue was about jobs text. I'm also planning to run the desktop test suite from root and filter the output for summary lines since it could be long.

Build passed, and the lazy loading measurably shrank the startup bundle: the first page load now fetches 1317KB of JS instead of 1787KB, a 26% cut. The page bundle alone went from 721KB to 453KB. Every backend change is in.

Final verification now, three things in parallel:

- **Backend + desktop tests:** `test:desktop`, which includes the backend task and stream-fallback tests.
- **Frontend unit tests:** one of them checks the `server.js` source code, which has changed, so it needs a rerun.
- **Browser run:** load the new build to confirm the React #418 hydration error is gone. I put all 80 history jobs on the same day to count how many cards the row-level virtualization actually mounts.

payload.text:
That backend lint error is pre-existing and unrelated to my changes, just shifted line numbers from my edits. Frontend now passes all 80 tests and the build succeeds with PWA support restored to normal.

Now let me pull a final git diff stat to summarize which files changed, and re-run the test suite once more to get accurate pass/fail counts for the report. I'll wrap this up with the final Chinese summary covering both batches of fixes, confirming the build and tests are green.

I'm also noting the caveats worth flagging: the real Electron IPC sync gains weren't measured against the fake bridge used in benchmarking, the streaming fallback path was only covered by existing backend tests, and the abort/exit path wasn't manually exercised. The desktop app still needs a rebuild via `npm run desktop:dev`, and I should mention that concurrency defaults to 8 with tasks beyond that queuing, configurable through the NOVA_TASK_CONCURRENCY env variable.

Other user-facing behavior changes worth calling out: configuring only an image model still allows saving, while Agent/reverse-inference checks depend on whether a text model is available; switching templates now preserves custom Base URL and name, but saving fails if Base URL is empty; the model test checks whatever is currently being edited with a 20s timeout; canvas, materials, and prompt plaza now lazy-load on first open causing a brief delay; desktop backend concurrency is now 8; in-progress tasks get marked as interrupted on shutdown with a "server restarted" message; and upstream HTTP errors now surface both status code and upstream text. None of this has been committed yet, and the temp bench directory still has leftover files from earlier runs.

I've already saved the two key facts to memory. Now I'm considering whether to patch the nova-ui-perf-check skill with newly discovered pitfalls — like using --perDay=80 to force jobs onto a single day for testing row virtualization, noting that structure.mountedCards tracks mounted history cards, and that web-* scenarios should show zero hydration errors after the fix. This seems like a cheap, worthwhile addition alongside the git/test call.

Also I realize the existing pitfall about the React #418 hydration warning being expected on every load is now stale since the fix resolved it — I need to correct that entry to say #418 was fixed and any recurrence would indicate a regression. So my plan is: patch the skill to replace the stale #418 line and add the new harness options, then run git diff --stat plus the desktop test counts, and mark the todo complete.

The desktop app still needs a rebuild via `npm run desktop:dev`, and I should mention that concurrency defaults to 8 with tasks beyond that queuing, configurable through the NOVA_TASK_CONCURRENCY env variable.

Other user-facing behavior changes worth calling out: configuring only an image model still allows saving, while Agent/reverse-inference checks depend on whether a text model is available; switching templates now preserves custom Base URL and name, but saving fails if Base URL is empty; the model test checks whatever is currently being edited with a 20s timeout; canvas, materials, and prompt plaza now lazy-load on first open causing a brief delay; desktop backend concurrency is now 8; in-progress tasks get marked as interrupted on shutdown with a "server restarted" message; and upstream HTTP errors now surface both status code and upstream text. None of this has been committed yet, and the temp bench directory still has leftover files from earlier runs.

I've already saved the two key facts to memory. All the work across both batches is done, so now I need to write the final summary for the user in Chinese, organized by what changed, how it was verified, noticeable behavior differences, and any remaining risks, with file references included.

I'm noting the two changes that were dropped per the user's earlier instruction, item #12 and the web deployment security items, now recorded in MEMORY.md as out of scope.

I'm going through the performance fixes: caching the model registry so desktop no longer does synchronous IPC and key decryption on every call, debouncing job list saves with a flush on page hide, fixing the hydration mismatch by restoring state in layout effects instead, and adjusting desktop concurrency along with disabling preview frames by default.

Now I'm reviewing the settings changes: template switching preserves the customized Base URL and name while letting model ID follow the template, blocking saves on empty Base URL, and separating validation so image-only setups check the image model while Agent features check the text model, plus giving the model check a clearer timeout and error message.

For batch 2, I'm confirming the lazy-loading work cut startup JS from 1787 KB to 1317 KB and the page chunk from 721 to 453 KB, and the row-level virtualization in the history job list now mounts only a handful of cards instead of all eighty. I'm also looking at the backend fetch timeout deadline logic that was added.

Now I'm covering the remaining backend hardening: the proxy cancels upstream requests on client disconnect, stream fallback logic is broadened and remembered per base URL/model while avoiding retries on auth or rate-limit errors, error normalization preserves upstream status codes, and shutdown now aborts in-flight requests and marks interrupted tasks before the DB closes.

Finally I'm checking the verification results — builds pass, TypeScript is clean, and I'm noting the frontend test suite (80 passing) and desktop/backend tests (29/29) before looking into the lint warnings.

I'm noting the remaining lint issues (scoped disables for layout-effect state changes, one pre-existing backend error) and browser sanity checks with zero hydration errors.

I'm listing user-visible behavior changes: gallery load delays, image task concurrency limits with an override env var, immediate task interruption on quit, upstream error details surfacing, and settings validation tweaks.

I'm flagging what's unverified, especially that registry cache gains haven't been measured on real Electron since the benchmark uses a fake bridge without IPC or decryption.

I'm also noting the retry/error classification paths for stream fallback and shutdown weren't tested against a real upstream or real quit, that virtualization row counts were only estimated from code, and gifenc remains in the startup bundle. I'm cross-checking which items from the original batch list are actually done versus still pending.

For batch 15, the model check with draft/timeout/message works but the "试生成" button I suggested wasn't added, and the API key in query string remains unchanged since it's local-only. For batch 2, lazy loading is done except gifenc is still eager, row virtualization and timeouts are done, text proxy cancel works, fallback/error classification is done, and exit uses abort—but I need to check whether interrupted task images actually get deleted on next start given the abort behavior.

I should note I didn't verify whether finished items in multi-image tasks are preserved when abort happens partway through, and item 6 (desktop ref images to data URL at startup) wasn't part of my batch plan so I shouldn't mention it as complete.

I could add a brief "not done yet" note covering 6, 16 (unsaved-changes prompts, delete confirmation, corrupted registry handling), and 17 (per-model stream/headers/timeout), kept as one concise line. I also need to mention changes aren't committed yet, and that the temp folder still has leftover benchmark scripts and screenshots that could be cleaned up.

I'll also briefly note that I recorded two lessons in MEMORY.md, and that the nova-ui-perf-check skill got patched — both worth a passing mention but not the focus of the final answer.

Now I'm drafting the actual response in Chinese: an opening line on the outcome, then sections grouping changes by 性能/设置/后端 with bullet links, a 验证 section, a 使用上会注意到的变化 section, and finally what's unverified or remaining — aiming for moderate length overall.

I've confirmed all tests pass but nothing's committed yet, and per the instructions I only recorded in project memory that the text model fills only the key and uses local client mode, leaving the address and web deployment security items untouched this time. For performance, I added an in-memory cache to model config reads so the desktop app only does synchronous IPC and key decryption on first load and save, refreshing on settings changes or registry updates, always returning copies so callers can't mutate the cache; the task list also now batches writes every 400ms, flushing immediately on page hide or close.

I also fixed a recurring React #418 hydration error on every launch by restoring the task list, model availability state, and the two agent toggles after the first frame but before paint, avoiding a flash of empty state. The infinite canvas, my assets, and prompt plaza now only load and mount on first open, staying mounted afterward.

Settings modal now loads after the page is ready, and jszip in the agent gallery only loads when "package download" is clicked, cutting startup JS from 1787KB to 1317KB (26% less). I also virtualized the history list by row so that with 80 tasks in a day, only 14 cards mount in wide mode and 5 in regular mode.

For settings, switching built-in templates now preserves any custom Base URL and display name edits, while model ID still follows the template.

I'm making sure image models can't save with an empty Base URL (it errors instead of silently defaulting to aioss.cc), and that configuring only an image model is enough to save — image/animation generation checks for an image model while agent and caption-reversal check for a text model. The "check model" function validates whatever's currently being edited with a 20-second timeout, and warns that some relay sites don't list all their models when one isn't found in the list.

On the backend and desktop side, I'm reducing desktop concurrency from 50 to 8 with the queue status reflecting the real cap, no longer requesting unused preview frames by default, and making the timeout cover the entire request including the read phase.

Response body timeouts differ by type: 20 seconds for model lists, 5 minutes for result image downloads, and still 30 minutes for image generation. Closing a conversation now cancels the upstream request for text agents. I'm loosening streaming fallback logic — when image data can't be read, or the upstream returns 400/404/405/415/422/501 due to request format issues, it retries once non-streaming, then remembers that combination of address and model to skip streaming for the rest of the run; but auth, quota, rate-limit, and 5xx errors don't get retried, to avoid duplicate charges. Errors now keep the original upstream status code and message instead of being rewritten to "request timeout" based on keyword matching. On exit, in-flight upstream requests are aborted first, and tasks get marked "server restarted, task interrupted" in the database before it closes, with a 2-second timeout added to reading queue status during tray exit. Then I'm verifying that both builds — desktop and the production build with PWA — pass along with the TypeScript check.

Frontend unit tests (80) and desktop/backend tests (29) all pass; one test that checked the old fallback statement directly against server.js source code needed its assertion updated to match the new logic. payload.text:
Item #12 isn't actually a bug since only the key is meant to be fillable for text models by design, so I'll leave that as is. Items #18/#19 about security are out of scope too since deployment is desktop-only with server and client on the same local machine, bound to 127.0.0.1 with a token. Now I'm moving on to start making the actual batch of fixes.

I'll split the work into two batches to keep responses manageable given output limits: batch 1 covers items 1, 2, 3, 7, 13, 14, 15, and batch 2 covers items 4, 5, 8, 9, 10, 11. Before continuing, I should record these two standing facts the user just taught me -- that text model config intentionally only exposes the key field, and that deployment is desktop-client-only with both server and client running locally -- into MEMORY.md so future sessions don't misflag these as issues. Let me check the current memory file contents first.

For the actual implementation, I'm working through item 1: adding a registry cache in the renderer's `loadRegistry()`, invalidated on save and on the registry-updated/storage events. I need to be careful about whether callers mutate the returned registry object directly, since a shared cached reference could get corrupted -- I'm weighing returning a structured clone versus freezing the object, and checking how something like SettingsModal actually consumes the loaded registry before deciding.

I also need to make sure the cache gets invalidated when other paths write the registry key directly (like backup restore flows), and think about whether returning a cheap structured clone of a small registry object is the safest way to avoid mutation bugs entirely.

I'm keeping scope tight to just the caching change rather than adding a JSON.parse try/catch guard, since that's an unrelated correctness improvement the user didn't ask for. On the desktop side, the cache should also cut down repeated decryption calls in the sync IPC path since loadRegistry gets reused across hasAnyApiKey and getStoredApiKey.

For job persistence, I'm planning to debounce saveJobs writes with a trailing delay and flush them on pagehide/visibility-hidden events, moving the logic into job-store.ts with a module-level timer rather than doing the save as a side effect inside the setJobs updater. The main risk is losing very recent updates if the app crashes within the debounce window, but since the desktop app hides to tray instead of truly closing, the renderer stays alive long enough for the timer to fire.

I also want to check usePersistedSettings.ts:67, which seems to persist on every keystroke — I'll debounce that too once I look at it more closely.

For the hydration mismatch, I'll fix useWorkspaceJobs by initializing state with empty defaults (empty array, false) instead of reading storage synchronously during render, then loading the actual stored jobs and API key status inside the mount effect to avoid mismatching the static HTML.

I'm now tracing the timing between the boot loader removal and the jobs effect's setJobs call, since both fire around mount — worried about a possible flash of empty state if the loader is removed before the jobs re-render commits. Need to think through how React 18 batches passive effect updates to confirm the ordering is safe.

Beyond that, I'm considering whether other hydration mismatches exist, particularly around the image-generation panel's server-rendered "0 items / no dates" placeholder versus client-loaded job data.

Similarly, the API key check via `hasAnyApiKey()` in a `useState` initializer would return false on the server but true on the client if keys exist, flipping the workbench between the "not configured" card and the actual form—another mismatch source worth fixing the same way. I should grep for other components using `useState(() => ...)` with storage reads, then verify the fix by rerunning my bench harness and confirming the React #418 error count drops to zero.

For concurrency, I'm considering setting `NOVA_TASK_CONCURRENCY` in the backend process env to something like 6, but noticing the queue status display currently reports the global limit rather than the effective configured concurrency, which could confuse users into thinking more capacity is available than actually is.

On streaming, the default enables it, but I'm questioning that given the relay behavior — with aioss.cc, the sunburst request took 145s just to get headers back in stream mode, which suggests the relay wasn't forwarding headers early anyway, so streaming wasn't providing the keepalive benefit it's supposed to.

For non-streaming, flare took 27s vs 20s streaming, likely just noise. Non-streaming avoids SSE parsing edge cases, but there's a risk with Cloudflare-fronted relays that timeout long non-streamed requests around 100s — and since sunburst took 146s, that could trigger a 524 error. However, aioss.cc's server header shows openresty rather than Cloudflare, so that particular risk may not apply here.

Given the uncertainty, I think the better move for item 7 is to keep streaming on by default since it was a deliberate choice and some relays benefit from early keepalive headers, rather than trying to parse SSE incrementally which adds complexity. But I'm also worried about memory — buffering the full stream when partial_images=1 means an extra ~1MB+ partial image on top of the final one, and since the UI doesn't actually render those partial frames, requesting them just wastes bandwidth and memory. Setting partial_images to 0 by default would preserve the streaming keepalive benefit while dropping the wasted partial frame data.

I confirm partial_images 0-3 is valid, and if we omit the param when it's 0, OpenAI defaults to only sending the completed event — this halves stream payload in cases where relays honor it. This matches what I told the user in the report: turn off streaming preview frames by default since they're not shown anyway, and also lower concurrency on desktop to help with memory. For batch 2's fallback logic, I should broaden it to cover any stream failure that isn't just a client abort.

I'm reconsidering whether incremental SSE parsing is even needed — if concurrency drops to around 6 and partial frames aren't requested, peak memory stays manageable at roughly 6 times twice the image size, which seems fine. Now I need to settle on the actual concurrency number: the auditor suggested somewhere between 4 and 8, but I also have to weigh upstream relay rate limits against local desktop usage patterns with multiple queued tasks.

With images running 10-20MB base64 each and 8 in flight, peak memory hits around 160-320MB, which is acceptable. I'm leaning toward 8 rather than 6 so typical parallel submissions don't get queued unnecessarily, especially since relay rate limits often cap concurrency anyway — I'll make it configurable via an environment variable. This should be set in backend-process.js since the user is only using client mode, not by changing the server default.

Now I need to fix the queue status display to reflect this effective limit.

For the preset switching issue, I want handleUpdateImageModel to fill in protocol, modelId, limits, and advanced settings from the template since those are model-specific, but for name and baseUrl I should only overwrite them if they're empty or still match the previous preset's default — preserving anything the user has customized, like a personalized baseUrl or name.

So the untouched-field rule keeps template filling working while preserving user edits, but this gets trickier for modelId—if someone customizes it and then switches templates, they may actually want the new template's model id applied rather than kept.

Actually, the real bug was that switching templates could leak the relay key to aioss.cc because baseUrl got reset. The minimal fix is to avoid overwriting baseUrl when the user has set a custom, non-default value, and I should apply similar logic to name and modelId.

I'm also checking how empty baseUrl gets handled downstream — normalization falls back to preset or fixed defaults, and incomplete models with empty baseUrl are flagged and excluded during save validation, so I need to make sure at least one complete model remains before persisting.

So the fix should preserve undefined vs empty-string distinction when falling back — undefined means use preset default, empty string means user intentionally cleared it and it should stay incomplete, correctly marked as needing completion.

For persistRegistry, I'll add a validation check: if a model has an API key but no baseUrl, flag it with an error like "图片模型「X」缺少 Base URL" so the user gets clear feedback before saving.

Now I'm looking at whether saving should still be allowed with only image models configured and text models left empty — checking where hasAnyApiKey requires both image and text keys, since that gates the workbench UI's disabled state, and I want to relax the requirement so image-only setups work.

I realize text-dependent features already gate themselves separately via `requireDefaultConfiguredTextModel`, which throws a specific error when text models aren't configured. So changing `hasAnyApiKey` to use `||` instead of `&&` would let image-only workspaces unlock the image workbench without breaking text feature gating, but I need to check all the consumers—AgentChatWorkspace, ReversePromptForm, GifGenerationWorkspace—to see if loosening this flag has unintended side effects on them too.

I'll add hasCompleteImageModel() and hasCompleteTextModel() helpers alongside hasAnyApiKey, then expose hasImageModel/hasTextModel from useWorkspaceJobs so WorkspaceShell can disable the image workbench and agent/reverse-prompt panels based on the right model type, keeping GIF generation tied to the image model. I also need to double check that handleSubmitError still correctly triggers the MissingApiKeyDialog for the '请先配置 API 密钥' message.

For the SettingsModal's onApiKeyChange flow, I'm thinking the cleanest fix is to expose a refreshModelAvailability() function from useWorkspaceJobs and have WorkspaceShell pass that as the callback, so saving settings refreshes both model flags instead of just the old single boolean.

For the model checking issue, I want checkModelsAvailability to accept an optional draft config so it validates the unsaved form state, not just saved config, plus add a 20-second timeout to the fetch and apply the same timeout on the backend proxy models call.

For unlisted models, rather than adding a "try generate" test button which costs quota and adds UI complexity, I'll just improve the error message to explain that some proxy sites don't list all available models — simpler and sufficient given what was accepted for this batch.

Moving to batch 2: implementing lazy loading with next/dynamic for the Canvas, GIF, Assets, ReversePrompt, and PromptGallery workspace components.

I realize keepMounted tabs would still load these dynamic chunks immediately after hydration, defeating the purpose. To truly defer them, I need to change the mounting strategy so a workspace only mounts on its first activation, then stays mounted afterward — though this affects cross-tab interactions like importing tasks into Canvas from another tab.

I'm checking whether components like AssetsWorkspace and GifGenerationWorkspace depend on background events or props before they're actually visited, since lazy mounting only works cleanly if they properly initialize their state on mount rather than needing to be active earlier.

The riskiest issue is deferred mounting delaying resumption of in-progress GIF jobs at startup — I need to verify whether useGifWorkflow resumes pending jobs on mount, and whether ReversePromptForm has similar resume logic, before deciding to track visited tabs with a lazily-populated set.

For implementation, I'm planning to track visited tabs in state, defaulting to the active tab, and add new tabs as they're visited. Heavy tab content would use dynamic imports for code-splitting, loaded only on first visit — with the default Agent tab and core image-generation/history components staying statically mounted, while Canvas, Assets, ReversePrompt, GIF, and PromptGallery become dynamic and mount-on-visit, unless I find they have background startup responsibilities I need to check for via grep.

I'm also considering how heavy libraries like jszip, gifenc, fflate, and localforage get pulled in — if they're only imported by the lazily-loaded workspace modules, they'll naturally fall out of the initial bundle, but I need to verify none of the shared startup code (like download utilities) pulls them in directly, and convert those to dynamic imports if so.

For row-level virtualization in HistoryJobList, I'm planning to flatten the current day-group structure into individual rows — a header row per group plus chunked rows of jobs — and virtualize at that granularity with per-row-type size estimation and dynamic height measurement, while preserving the existing scroll-to-day and visible-day-key behavior. I want to check the existing test file to see what it currently covers before making this change.

Then for timeouts, I'm thinking about setting per-route limits alongside an overall deadline for upstream requests.

Now I'm digging into fetchWithTimeout's cleanup timing: since it clears the abort timer once headers arrive but the caller reads the body afterward, the timeout doesn't actually protect body reads. I'm weighing whether to keep the timer alive until body consumption finishes, but since the body is a stream read by the caller rather than internally, hooking into its completion isn't straightforward without wrapping the response stream itself.

Before redesigning, I want to check the actual call sites and their timeout needs — the models proxy uses a 20s timeout, image downloads use 2 minutes, the prompt gallery has its own dedicated timeout constant, and the streaming text proxy should keep its long 30-minute window since it's not a simple request/response.

For item 9, I'm planning to add an AbortController tied to the client's connection close event around the text proxy code, so the upstream request gets cancelled if the client disconnects.

Now I need to merge that controller's signal with any signal fetchWithTimeout already accepts, likely using AbortSignal.any support in newer Node versions, and I should look at how the current read/write loop works before deciding whether to keep it or replace it with a pipeline.

For item 10, I'm thinking about broadening the stream fallback logic beyond just regex matches — considering which error types (parse failures, missing image data in the response) should also trigger falling back to a non-streaming retry.

I also need to weigh the tradeoffs carefully: retrying could double the cost if the image was already generated but the SSE just failed to parse, but leaving it failed forces the user to manually retry anyway at the same cost, so a safe rule might combine the existing regex match with parse-failure and certain HTTP status conditions like 400/404/405/415, while excluding auth, quota, and moderation-related failures where retrying wastes resources.

I'm also considering caching per-baseUrl stream support status in memory so future requests skip straight to non-stream mode once a failure pattern is detected, and improving error normalization to retain the original message alongside the HTTP status rather than collapsing everything into a generic timeout message.

I want to distinguish real timeout errors (AbortError, network cause codes like ECONNRESET or connection timeout errors) from upstream errors that merely mention "timeout" in text but are really HTTP failures with a status code that should be preserved.

Then I'm turning to exit handling: an 8-second kill window on shutdown and cleanup logic that deletes incomplete images from interrupted tasks when the process restarts.

On shutdown I need to abort in-flight requests via a shared AbortController, mark running tasks failed within a single transaction, close the db, and exit quickly, while preserving images for tasks that already completed. I also need to check server.js's shutdown logic, the database's interrupted-task handling on init, and the backend-process stop routine, then plan to run the desktop test suite after making these backend changes since this is a lot of work to pace across turns.

Now I want to set up a fresh todo list before diving in, saving memory notes first. I'm sketching a batch of initial tasks around caching the model registry in the renderer, debouncing job-list persistence with a flush on pagehide, and starting on hydration-related work.

For batch one, I'm planning fixes for the hydration mismatch by deferring job/model-availability loading until after mount, handling desktop backend concurrency limits with partial images and effective queue limits, and settings behavior around preset switching, base URL validation, and separate image/text availability checks. For batch two, I'm outlining lazy-loading heavy workspaces and libraries, adding row-level virtualization to the history list, backend improvements like per-route timeouts and stream fallback with error classification, and finishing with a verification step covering build and tests.

Before touching code, I need to update MEMORY.md with two durable notes: the text model intentionally only requires an API key with a fixed endpoint at aioss.cc (not a bug), and the deployment is desktop-client-only, so web/Docker security concerns are out of scope. Since memory updates need to happen before continuing the task, I'll read MEMORY.md, set up TodoWrite, and kick off the parallel reads for batch one now.

I still need to check several files: the model registry load/save functions, settings persistence and hasAnyApiKey logic, the SettingsModal's registry persistence and check-models handler, the task client's model availability check, server queue status, and backend process environment handling. I should also grep for raw usages of the model registry key and related useState initializers.

Given the context budget, I'll keep reads targeted and start writing the first batch of edits now, keeping my reasoning brief going forward.

Got it. The fixed address for text models is intentional, so I'll leave it as is. Since you only use the client (desktop) mode, where the backend listens only on the local machine and requires a token, the two web-deployment security items are out of scope too. I'll record both points in the project memory so they don't come up as issues in future reviews.

Then I'll start on batch one and work in small steps: read the relevant code, change one area, verify it, and move on to the next area.

I'm weighing options for making the timeout cover the full response body read, not just headers: proxy/model calls need a shorter timeout while image downloads need a much longer one, and text proxy currently just uses the default. Since the body is read immediately by response.text() in the image parsing paths, the simplest fix seems to be adding a mode to fetchWithTimeout that keeps the timer alive until the body is consumed, rather than restructuring every call site.

That approach feels hacky, so let me reconsider the auditor's finding about timeouts not limiting total request time — once headers arrive, only undici's 30-minute idle timer between chunks applies, and for image generation that's a reasonable enough ceiling since indefinite body trickling is mostly a theoretical edge case rather than the real problem.

The more concrete issue is that model listing and download routes wait the full 30 minutes when they shouldn't, so per-route timeouts would fix that. I'm weighing whether to build a fetchWithTimeout wrapper that also handles body completion, versus just passing AbortSignal.timeout directly into fetch to keep things simple.

Passing AbortSignal.timeout directly seems cleanest since it stays active through both headers and body reads and cleans itself up when fired, with no meaningful leak risk. But I need to handle the case where the caller also supplies its own signal (like a client-close abort), which means combining signals with AbortSignal.any.

I should confirm error naming: AbortSignal.timeout produces a TimeoutError DOMException rather than AbortError, but the existing normalizeError regex for abort/timeout messages should still catch it fine.

Now I'm working out per-endpoint timeout values: 30 minutes for the overall request deadline, which suits both the text proxy streaming chat and prompt gallery sources; 2 minutes for image downloads; 20 seconds for the models proxy endpoint. I'll leave the Bing/picsum fetches alone since they likely already pass their own timeouts.

I'm defining a wrapper that combines a timeout-based abort signal with any caller-provided signal, ensuring the deadline spans the whole request including body streaming, not just until headers arrive.

Checking whether image generation, chat streaming, or file downloads could legitimately exceed the timeout after headers — all seem fine within the 30-minute bound, and the unref'd timer behavior in Node is also fine. Now I need to look at the text proxy's client-close cancellation logic around lines 2127-2160, and then move on to broadening stream fallback and error classification.

I want to widen the fallback condition beyond just the regex match for unsupported streaming errors, so it also triggers when the stream response can't be parsed (missing image data or invalid SSE) or when upstream returns specific error codes with stream-related messages. I'm defining a helper function that checks the error type and message content to decide whether a non-streaming retry should be attempted.

I'm weighing whether to retry broadly on any 400/404/405/415/422/501 status regardless of the message content — reasoning that a 400 usually means the request was rejected without billing, so a cheap retry without streaming is safe even for things like moderation blocks or unrecognized models, since worst case it just wastes an extra request.

I should also track stream support per base URL in memory so future calls skip streaming for endpoints known to fail with it, though concurrent requests won't benefit from this immediately. I'm also considering that a stream failure could stem from an error embedded in the SSE payload itself, like a moderation rejection surfaced during event parsing.

For 5xx errors or mid-stream network drops, I shouldn't auto-retry non-stream since the image may have already been generated and billed upstream — retrying risks double-charging. I'll limit automatic retries to clear 4xx unsupported-type responses and parse failures, not transient server or connection errors.

For error normalization, I need to preserve upstream HTTP status codes instead of guessing from keyword matches, since messages like "504 upstream timeout" were being mangled into generic timeout text. I'm rewriting normalizeError to check for the API failure pattern first and truncate long messages, then fall back to checking error name and cause code for timeout/network classification.

I should check whether normalizeError applies to model-list timeouts too, or just image generation errors, since the 1800-second message is specific to that context. I also need to look at the shutdown handling flow: server.js waits for running tasks before closing the db, backend-process.js force-kills after 8 seconds, and initDatabase deletes files for interrupted tasks, which might wrongly delete completed item images too. The fix should preserve completed items and only clean up files for items that weren't finished.

I'm weighing whether to change task-completion behavior so partially-finished tasks report 'completed' with a warning instead of 'failed', preserving completed images rather than deleting them, but that's a bigger change than I have budget for. Given the constraints, I'll scope the shutdown fix down to something simpler, like adding a timeout to the backend status fetch.

I'm weighing whether to suppress these with justified eslint-disable comments, or follow the project's existing pattern of wrapping the setState in queueMicrotask like usePersistedSettings and useWideMode do. I'm reasoning through the timing: a microtask queued from a layout effect would still flush before the browser paints, since layout effects run synchronously within the commit and microtasks drain before the next paint opportunity -- so this should be safe, though I need to check which update lane React would assign to it.

Given the complexity of tracing update priorities through microtasks, I think the cleaner path is to keep the synchronous setState directly in the layout effects, since that's the pattern React's own docs recommend for reading/measuring before paint, and just add targeted eslint-disable comments explaining why.

I'm also weighing switching the model-availability check to useSyncExternalStore instead, since that's the idiomatic way to read an external store with a server snapshot and avoids tripping the lint rule altogether — subscribing to the registry-updated event, using the cached availability check as the snapshot, and falling back to false on the server.

This is getting too tangled to verify without testing, so the pragmatic path is to keep the sync setState inside useLayoutEffect since that's guaranteed to run before paint per React's docs, and just add eslint-disable comments with clear justification rather than restructuring further. That keeps the lint count at the baseline of 8. I'm locating the three call sites needing disable comments, starting with the refreshModelAvailability call inside the layout effect in useWorkspaceJobs.ts around line 50.

Recounting line numbers, I trace the effect block through the earlier edits to figure out that line 219 corresponds to `setWebSearchEnabled(...)`, the first synchronous setState call flagged inside that effect.

Since I'm unsure if the rule flags only the first setState per effect or all of them, the safer approach is to wrap the entire effect body with a block-level eslint-disable/enable pair for the set-state-in-effect rule, so every setState call inside is covered regardless.

Adding disable/enable comments...

Since only setJobs there is synchronous and flagged, a single next-line disable before line 58 covers it, and I can bundle both edits in one contiguous range. For useAgentChat, I'm checking which calls in that effect actually get flagged — setWebSearchEnabled at line 219 needs a disable, while refreshApiKeyState apparently doesn't.

I'll wrap the whole effect block with a disable/enable pair since I already know its exact text, then re-run lint to confirm we're back down to 8 errors. After that I want to move to backend work in parallel: adding per-route timeouts via AbortSignal.timeout to fetchWithTimeout and its callers, handling upstream cancellation on client disconnect for the text proxy, broadening stream fallback with per-baseUrl memory, and updating normalizeError to preserve status/upstream text while classifying timeouts.

I'm confirming line offsets shifted by prior edits so my next fetchWithTimeout edit targets the correct location, then rewriting that function to use AbortSignal.timeout.

AbortSignal.any needs Node 20.3+, which both dev and packaged Electron satisfy since the backend runs via utilityProcess or a node child process. I also need to check that the error handling still works correctly, since timeouts now produce a DOMException named 'TimeoutError' instead of the old 'AbortError', so I should verify normalizeError's regex catches both.

I'm also checking that a mid-body timeout still propagates correctly to callers as a timeout error, and that the image generation timeout now spans the entire request including body reading, which should be fine since image generation realistically finishes well under 30 minutes. Server tests using mock upstreams should be unaffected by this change.

Now I need to add specific timeout values to the remaining per-route fetch calls — the models endpoint fetch should get a 20-second timeout, and the image download fetch should get a 120-second timeout, editing those specific lines in the code.

Since edit tool matches by unique text rather than line numbers, I don't need to worry about line shifts from prior edits, just confirm each snippet is unique in the file.

Next I need to look at the text proxy cancellation loop around the relevant section, and then broaden the stream-fallback retry logic in generateNovaImage to check for unsupported streaming errors more generally.

I'm reasoning through when a stream fails after the upstream already generated an image—things like a missing image in the response, invalid JSON, or specific 4xx codes that aren't auth/quota/rate-limit related—since those cases shouldn't be retried the same way as network or server errors where billing might duplicate.

For genuine 400 content-policy rejections or 404 unsupported-model errors, retrying via the non-stream path just repeats the same failure harmlessly, costing one extra round trip but no double billing. That seems like an acceptable tradeoff given the per-baseUrl memory prevents this from happening repeatedly.

I'm setting up a set to track base URLs where streaming isn't supported, and in the image generation function I only fall back to the non-stream request and record the base URL as unsupported once that fallback actually succeeds -- avoiding mistaking a bad key or moderation failure for a streaming incompatibility.

I'm reconsidering the memory key though: instead of just baseUrl, keying by baseUrl plus model might be more accurate since some relays route different models to different upstream channels. I also want to check how this interacts with existing tests, like the one checking a response_format error for b64_json and the partial_images streaming test.

Since each test likely spawns its own server process with a separate temp DB, memory shouldn't leak across tests, so my change should be safe — I'll just run the backend test suite to confirm. Then I need to check where normalizeError is used, probably in the task processing error handler.

I'm defining normalizeError to keep upstream HTTP error text intact (truncated if too long), and to detect timeout-related errors by checking error name, cause code, or message patterns, returning a Chinese "请求超时" style message for those cases.

For network-level failures I'm matching common fetch/connection error codes and messages to return a friendly "网络连接失败" message including the code if available, otherwise falling back to truncating the raw error message if it's too long.

I should double-check whether the frontend's failure classification logic depends on matching these exact Chinese error message strings, since changing wording could break existing tests that check for '网络连接失败' or '请求超时' patterns—so I need to keep those prefixes consistent.

I also realize there's a subtler bug: an upstream HTTP error like "504 Gateway Timeout" would previously get matched by the timeout regex and misleadingly reported as a request timeout, so I should fix the classification order to check status codes before falling back to message pattern matching.

I still need to check whether normalizeError's messages align with existing backend tests, and to add a timeout to the queue-status fetch in backend-process.js which currently has none. For graceful shutdown, I'm considering wiring a shared abort signal into all upstream fetch calls so in-flight requests can be cancelled when the server stops, rather than just waiting or force-killing after 8 seconds.

Adding a global shutdown AbortController would make in-flight tasks reject quickly on abort, so the "wait for running tasks" step during shutdown finishes fast before closing the database. I need normalizeError to detect shutdown-triggered aborts specifically and return a distinct message like "服务正在退出，任务已中断，请重新生成" instead of the misleading timeout message, and then confirm that on next startup, initDatabase properly cleans up any queued/processing entries left behind.

Now I want to actually check the relevant code sections: server.js's proxy handler and shutdown routine, backend-process.js's stop logic, and the task handling itself to verify these assumptions before proposing a fix.

I'm planning to add a shutdown-aware AbortController for upstream fetches, wiring it into fetchWithTimeout so requests get cancelled cleanly during shutdown, reusing the existing isShuttingDown flag. I'll make the fetchWithTimeout edit first since the other changes touch the same file in multiple places and need to be sequenced separately.

I'm combining all the abort signals so the fetch cancels on timeout, shutdown, or an external signal. Though now I'm second-guessing whether AbortSignal.any could cause a memory leak, since the shutdown signal lives forever and older Node versions had issues retaining dependent signals from long-lived sources.

That leak was actually a known Node issue that got fixed in later versions, and since this is running on Node 22/24 via current Electron, it shouldn't be a problem. I'm now checking that other fetchWithTimeout call sites pass proper init objects, defaulting to an empty object when none is given, and tracing where it's used for the streaming text proxy endpoint.

For that streaming case, the timeout deadline should cover the entire stream duration since a chat stream running over 30 minutes would be unusual, and I want to make sure a client-close event properly triggers an AbortController to cancel the upstream fetch. I also want to double check the frontend hydration story — the AssetsWorkspace component being dynamically imported with ssr:false means it never risks a hydration mismatch, but I should check whether GIF/ReversePrompt components, which are still server-rendered, have any storage-reading initializers that could cause the same issue.

My grep pattern for state initializers reading from storage might have missed variants like conditional window checks, so I should verify using the bench harness that counts React error #418 occurrences after a fresh build, running it against the current desktop build output on a couple of scenarios. Then I'll move through: fixing the lint issues in useWorkspaceJobs and useAgentChat, editing the fetchWithTimeout logic in server.js, and reading through the text proxy, shutdown, and backend-process stop regions along with the task-failure message handling.

For the useWorkspaceJobs fix, I'm adding an eslint-disable comment above the state-restoring calls in the layout effects, explaining that they intentionally restore stored state before first paint. For useAgentChat, I'm still working through the effect that checks for a text model since the image step reports missing models separately.

Wrapping up parsing stored preferences into state, catching storage errors gracefully, and setting up a listener to refresh the API key state when the model registry updates, with cleanup on unmount.

I'm double-checking that useEffect is still used elsewhere in useAgentChat after this refactor—confirming other effects like syncing imageModelRef still exist, so no unused import issues after the build passes.

Now I want to search task-failure.ts for network/timeout-related patterns, and check server.js for error normalization usage, shutdown flags, and graceful shutdown handlers like SIGTERM.

Both the build and the 80 unit tests pass. Lint shows 11 errors against 8 at baseline, and the 3 extra ones are mine. They're all the `set-state-in-effect` rule, triggered by restoring stored state inside `useLayoutEffect`.

That's deliberate: setting state in a layout effect is the approach React documents for "read before the first paint", and it's what makes the restored screen appear without a flash. So I'm keeping it and adding a scoped exception with the reason to the rule instead of changing the implementation.

I'm also starting on the backend. `fetchWithTimeout` now uses `AbortSignal.timeout`, so the deadline covers the whole request including the response body, and all in-flight upstream requests are cancelled together when the app exits. Meanwhile I'm reading the text proxy, the exit flow, and the frontend's failure-classification rules, so that changing error messages doesn't break its checks.

I'm also noting the caveats worth flagging: the real Electron IPC sync gains weren't measured against the fake bridge used in benchmarking, the streaming fallback path was only covered by existing backend tests, and the abort/exit path wasn't manually exercised. The desktop app still needs a rebuild via `npm run desktop:dev`, and I should mention that concurrency defaults to 8 with tasks beyond that queuing, configurable through the NOVA_TASK_CONCURRENCY env variable.

Other user-facing behavior changes worth calling out: configuring only an image model still allows saving, while Agent/reverse-inference checks depend on whether a text model is available; switching templates now preserves custom Base URL and name, but saving fails if Base URL is empty; the model test checks whatever is currently being edited with a 20s timeout; canvas, materials, and prompt plaza now lazy-load on first open causing a brief delay; desktop backend concurrency is now 8; in-progress tasks get marked as interrupted on shutdown with a "server restarted" message; and upstream HTTP errors now surface both status code and upstream text. None of this has been committed yet, and the temp bench directory still has leftover files from earlier runs.

I've already saved the two key facts to memory. Now I'm considering whether to patch the nova-ui-perf-check skill with newly discovered pitfalls — like using --perDay=80 to force jobs onto a single day for testing row virtualization, noting that structure.mountedCards tracks mounted history cards, and that web-* scenarios should show zero hydration errors after the fix.
